**The 18-19 gap now has a year with no furlough in it.** That gap outranking
every statutory gap had been seen only in 2021-22, a year carrying a named
contaminant, and this station declined to explain anything with that
contaminant. 2018-19 runs from April 2018 to March 2019, entirely before the
pandemic, and it shows the same thing. The contaminant does not account for

**The 19 to 20 flat spot does not repeat in the added year.** Read on the
three-year average the fall from 19 to 20 was 3.6 pp, the smallest step
between 16 and 22. Per rate year that step reads 10.2, 4.9, 1.7 and 6.1 pp,
and it is the smallest step in its year only in 2021-22. In 2018-19 it is
10.2 pp, the same size as the steps on either side of it. The three-year
average is arithmetically right and it carries less than it appeared to: the
shape is in three of four rate years and it is deepest in the year with the
contaminant. It is not withdrawn, its scope is narrower. An average that
pools rate years hides the spread between them, which is what printing the
object rather than the summary is for.

| B35-2 origin-side arm, bovine carrier | **superseded** | superseded by B35-6 |

**Two things stay open at closing and belong to no verdict above.** Swine tongues
are a candidate the same pull dropped out: China 37.19 / Japan 31.37 / Mexico
26.48 per cent, all twelve months, unit values 1.87 / 3.23 / 2.33 dollars per kg,
with no low-cost swap between the three because access for frozen offal is
granted plant by plant. It carries a September 2022 break on the China leg that
prices cannot resolve and rule text can. B35-4 was registered and never run.

**The independent count came out the other way round.** The gate arithmetic
divides by the square root of the step count, and monthly series are serially
correlated, so the count was measured rather than assumed. The residual
difference series has negative low-order autocorrelation and a long-run variance
ratio of 0.7417, so the effective count is larger than the nominal one. Dividing
by the square root of the raw month count is conservative on differenced monthly
data, not optimistic. It is worth one pass over residuals already on disk
wherever an arm books a month count.

### B35 — the D23 gate on the swine-tongue candidate, answered by arithmetic

`nothing fetched` `read from this station's own record` `a pre-opening gate, not a station reading`

**B35 closed with one candidate open and one precondition: read the rule text for the
September 2022 break on the China leg and decide between "access opened" and "two
goods under one code".** The rule text was chased through five source classes and not
reached. **The one dated document covering the period, USMEF's foreign-trade-barriers
filing to USTR of 28 October 2022 — six weeks after the break, from the body whose job
is tracking exactly this — names no 2022 access event for pork offal.** The
Chinese-language customs announcement class is robots-blocked from here.

**The gate did not need it.** The question is whether the three anchors price one
physical thing across the break, and the test is whether the break is tongue-specific.

**It is not.** On the China leg, in the same months: tongues x9.69 in monthly volume
with unit value 3.384 -> 1.552; **skins cold-start, zero for eight months then 1,447
tonnes a month; head meat dies, 2,890 tonnes a month down to 726.** Feet (x0.92) and
offal-nesoi (x0.85) do not move.

**The other two anchors, same code, same split, do not move**: Japan 3.179 -> 3.387
(x1.065), Mexico 2.368 -> 2.260 (x0.954). A US-side code revision would hit every leg
at once, so this is a China-leg event rather than a reclassification.

**The mixture decomposition names the new flow and finds where it came from.** If the
old flow continued at its own pre-break rate, the implied new flow is 10,741,500 kg at
**$1.341/kg**; head meat on the same leg priced **$1.219/kg** before the break, ten per
cent away, and lost 8,656,944 kg over the same four months. **Price and quantity both
line up.**

**Verdict: two goods under one code, in its sharpest form — not a code that always held
two goods, but goods moving between codes on this leg from September.** No claim is
made about the mechanism; the gate only asked whether the anchors price one thing, and
they do not.

**The candidate arm is not closed, it is narrowed to January through August.** The
registered caveat on it tightens with that: the D22 independent count over an
autocorrelated monthly series was already flagged as not twelve, and it is now not
eight either. That count and the resolution floor come before the arm opens.

### B35 — what the September break is: contents moving between two codes, on a leg that has no break of its own

`nothing fetched` `same cached pull as the gate above` `ten criteria, all pass`

**The gate above settled that the anchors do not price one thing across the break. This
asks the next question: which part of the tongue line is tongue, and what exactly broke.**

**First the scope, because the file this reads is one where getting it wrong changes the
answer.** The destination wildcard returns the dimension's index table, and that table
carries continents, trade blocs and one world total alongside the countries: **1,153 of
2,296 rows are aggregates.** Summing every returned row inflates the tongue tonnage by
**6.058x**, because Asia, Pacific Rim, APEC, OECD and the world total each count China's
share again. **The atom rule is four digits, all numeric, not starting 00**, and the
check the pitfall ledger asks for is now a criterion rather than a comment: the atoms sum
to the world-total row on **all 84 commodity-months, worst relative difference 0.000e+00**.
The gate above is unaffected: it reads three named countries, and all three are atoms.

**Where the rise is.** Tongues across all countries go 1,743.9 to 4,322.6 tonnes a month
(x2.48) while the non-China leg goes 1,434.8 to 1,328.1 (x0.93). **The China leg carries
1.041 of the increment — more than all of it, because the rest of the world fell.** A
US-side revision hits every leg; the other legs' tongue unit value sits between $2.42 and
$2.93 all year and never moves.

**The anatomical control, which needs no yield assumption.** One tongue, one heart and
four feet come off every hog, so those three quantities are locked at the animal and any
movement in a ratio between them is a statement about the export mix or the code
boundary. Hearts and feet are both inside 0206.49 and neither is alleged to have moved.
**Tongue over foot moves x1.75 (log 0.560) while the heart-over-foot control moves x0.90
(log 0.103)**; on the China leg tongue over heart goes 2.18 to 36.63. The reading is the
ordering of the two log sizes, not a line drawn on either.

**The sharpest object here needs neither anatomy nor outside data: the union of the two
codes is continuous where each member is not.** If a boundary moved between exactly two
codes and nothing else happened, the pair is invariant. On the China leg the tongue unit
value ranges **do not overlap** (3.212-3.764 against 1.419-1.950); head meat's own price
ranges **do** overlap; and the ranges of the two codes **taken together** overlap
(1.211-1.627 against 1.418-1.802). **A demand episode inside one good cannot produce that
shape**: it does not leave the pair invariant while breaking one member. Head meat's price
never moves at all, only its volume, so the product that moved was priced as head meat
throughout.

**How much of the post-break tongue line is not tongue.** Both endpoints are measured on
this leg before the break: old tongue $3.3838/kg, head meat $1.2189/kg. Writing each
post-break month as a mixture of the two, **and running the eight pre-break months
through the same arithmetic as a control**:

```
share of the tongue line pricing like head meat
  pre-break control    -0.176 to +0.079      scattered about zero
  post-break            0.662 to  0.907

implied real tongue flow, post-break   386 - 609 t/mo
observed tongue flow,     pre-break     79 - 699 t/mo
implied mixed-in                     2,533.7 t/mo
head meat's own loss                 2,164.2 t/mo      ratio 1.171
```

**The tongue flow itself never moved.** The residual is printed rather than smoothed: the
mixed-in tonnage exceeds head meat's loss by 17 per cent, so either a third source exists
or the moved product priced slightly off the head-meat line. **Neither changes the
reading, and the sweep says so rather than an argument**: moving the second endpoint
across $0.90 to $1.60/kg leaves the mean not-tongue share between **0.705 and 0.982**.

**What broke, stated as a rank inside each series rather than a line across both.** A
pre/post mean cannot separate "the leg stepped up in September" from "the leg climbed all
year and only the mix broke". Among the eleven month-on-month steps of 2022, **August to
September is rank 1 of 11 in the China-leg tongue unit value** (log step -0.655, next
largest 0.318) **and rank 9 of 11 in the whole leg's tonnage** (log step -0.080, the leg's
largest step being +0.206). The leg's monthly total climbs from 18,295 to 32,788 tonnes
between January and August and then runs flat, with no step at the break.

**One thing happens the same month that a boundary move cannot produce**: skins to China
are exactly zero for eight months and then 86.7, 1,283.1, 1,936.1, 2,481.9 tonnes. **A
line cannot cold-start from an exact zero because a code boundary moved.** More than one
thing happened on that leg in September, and no claim about mechanism is made here.

**Step or spike is registered and not run, with both outcomes given readings before the
test.** One year cannot separate a code or registration change from a demand episode;
2021 and 2023 can. `api.census.gov` is outside the egress allowlist of both shells
available to the session that wrote this, and the 2022 cache was fetched on the machine
that owns the data directory, where the same fetcher resumes.

### B35 — step or spike, run on three years: it is a step, and the move is larger than one year showed

`36 months, 2021 to 2023, fetched on the machine that owns the cache` `six criteria, all pass`

**The test above registered this one and wrote readings for all three of its outcomes
before the pull.** One year cannot separate a code or registration change from a demand
episode. Three can.

**"Looks like" is made operational by interval overlap on the China-leg tongue unit
value**, the same instrument the continuity criterion used, and an overlap test has no
threshold to choose.

```
2021          2.305 - 3.617     overlaps the pre-break window
2022 Jan-Aug  3.212 - 3.764
2022 Sep-Dec  1.419 - 1.950
2023          1.066 - 1.582     overlaps the post-break window
2021 against 2023               no overlap
```

**The branch that fires is STEP**, and no second branch is readable.

**Head meat to China does not shrink, it ends.** 81,424 to 26,023 to 713 tonnes a year,
monotone, **four months of 2023 at exactly zero**, and **2021's thinnest month is 8.7
times 2023's thickest.** Recorded but not adjudicated: head meat was already falling
inside 2021, from 10,868 tonnes in July to 1,839 in December, then held near that level
through the first half of 2022 before ending. The September 2022 step is the last step
of a longer process, and one year of seasonality cannot carry a verdict on the rest.

**Slaughter is excluded with no weight assumption at all.** One tongue and four feet come
off every hog, so the tongue line and the foot line are two meters reading the same
animal count, and the reading is each line against itself across years rather than
against the other.

```
China leg, 2021 -> 2023
feet         161,704 -> 171,058 t   x1.058    the slaughter meter, unmoved
tongues        4,940 ->  63,057 t   x12.765
skins          1,261 ->  19,263 t   x15.277
offal nesoi   34,968 ->  46,447 t   x1.328
hearts         3,987 ->   1,780 t   x0.447    the other direction
```

**Log sizes 2.547 against 0.056.** A change in slaughter cannot produce that.

**Three years correct one word in the reading above.** The one-year view read this as head
meat moving into tongues. On this horizon head meat empties into more than one place:
skins move x15.277 over the same span and hearts move the other way. **It is a wider
re-coding rather than a two-code swap**, and the continuity criterion still holds because
tongues' main source on this leg is still head meat: over all 36 months the tongue unit
value spans 3.53x while the two codes together span 1.75x, with the 2021 and 2023 tongue
ranges disjoint and the union's overlapping. **1.75 is not 1.00, and that is why the word
changes**: the pair is far tighter than either member, not conserved.

**The anatomical ceiling, with its limitation stated because it is real.** One tongue to
four feet bounds tongue tonnage over foot tonnage at w_tongue / (4 w_foot), which runs
0.114 to 0.321 across the 25 weight pairs swept. **The China leg reads 0.0305 in 2021,
below the ceiling on all 25, and 0.3686 in 2023, above it on all 25.** Exports are not
production, so a part exported at a higher fraction than another can lift this ratio
without any re-coding; **the reading that carries weight is the two meters above, which
does not take that limitation.**

**What the tongue line requires in head, printed and not compared here.** This record
neither fetches nor asserts a US slaughter figure. At 0.25 to 0.45 kg a tongue the 2023
world tongue line requires **326.2 down to 181.2 million head, with no domestic
consumption at all**, against 85.1 down to 47.3 million for the same line in 2021. Written
as a threshold rather than a point estimate so a reader can complete it with the slaughter
figure they trust; **none of the six verdicts rests on it.**

**The arm's disposition.** Not closed. 2022 is confined to January through August as
registered; 2021 and 2023 may be used whole; **and 2023 must pass the gate again on its
own, because on that leg this code is no longer carrying the same good.** The independent
count and the resolution floor still come first.

### B35 — the demand side, which is right about hearts and wrong about tongues

`same panel, nothing fetched` `two external inputs, both sourced` `eight criteria, all pass`

**The reading above excluded slaughter by comparing two meters of one animal. That is a
statement about supply and it leaves demand untouched.** Tongue and heart are not the
same product to a buyer, they sit in different kitchens at different price points, and a
demand divergence between them is ordinary rather than anomalous. This section measures
that alternative instead of arguing with it.

**On hearts the demand account is what the data shows.** World exports rise x1.174 while
China's fall x0.447 and every other destination rises x6.196, China's share going 0.873 to
0.332, with the line sitting at 0.084 to 0.100 of US production in every year and no
physical anomaly anywhere. **That is a destination and demand shift, and this is what one
looks like on this instrument.**

**On tongues the demand account makes a prediction and the data refuses it.** A demand
shift against a supply position fixed by slaughter moves quantity and price the same way.
On the China leg the tongue line's quantity moves **x12.765 while its unit value moves
x0.451**, $2.864 to $1.292 a kg.

**One code, one origin, two prices, and this reading needs no weight, yield or slaughter
figure at all.**

```
2021   China leg $2.30-3.62 /kg      everywhere else $1.92-2.56     overlap: yes
2023   China leg $1.07-1.58 /kg      everywhere else $2.07-2.41     overlap: no
```

**In 2021 China paid a premium for this code. In 2023 it pays 0.574 of what everyone else
pays, and the rest of the world goes on paying a tongue price.**

**The physical ceiling, and a criterion-shape error the control caught.** One tongue comes
off one hog, so production is slaughter times a tongue's weight and exports cannot exceed
it. Slaughter is USDA NASS commercial head, 128,985,900 / 125,321,700 / 127,971,000;
yields are from a 196-hog by-product study, tongue 0.25 +/- 0.04 kg, heart 0.42 +/- 0.05,
fore feet 0.85 and hind feet 1.01.

```
exports over production   tongues  0.660   0.997   2.549
                          feet     0.728   1.013   0.766
                          hearts   0.084   0.047   0.100
```

**The first version of the control asserted that feet and hearts sit at or below one, and
feet came back at 1.013 in 2022.** The numbers did not change when that was fixed; the
verdict shape did. **A trade cut is not an anatomical cut** — a traded trotter carries part
of the shank, a traded tongue may or may not carry the root and throat trim — so a
dissected yield does not bound a traded tonnage exactly, and a line drawn at exactly 1.0
is the zero-width threshold that criterion-shape discipline forbids. **The reading is now
the ordering of the multiple**: the trade cut costs the controls at most 1.013 times the
anatomy while the tongue line asks for 2.549 times, **2.52 times more allowance than any
control needs.**

**And the weight cancels out of the ratio between years, which is where the reading
actually rests.** A traded tongue weighs the same in 2021 and 2023, so:

```
tonnage x3.833   slaughter x0.992   ->   export rate x3.864, whatever a tongue weighs
```

**For 2023 to sit at or below every tongue in the country, 2021 must have been at or below
0.259 of them** — three quarters of US pork tongue left unexported in a year when the line
was already shipping at $2.40 a kg. This does not declare an impossibility; it writes down
the two things that must hold together: a traded tongue of at least 0.6372 kg **and** a
2023 export rate of 100 per cent of national production.

**Monthly, against slaughter by month, 2022 only, because that is the year with a measured
monthly figure.** The world tongue line runs 0.544 to 0.795 of the country's tongue
production from January to August, **1.055 in September**, and 1.093 to 2.255 after. **It
crosses its own physical ceiling in the break month the gate named, and does not come back
under it.**

**One route stays open and is registered rather than closed by argument**: exports exceed
domestic production only if nothing was imported and re-exported. The imports side of the
same feed decides it, and all three outcomes carry readings written first, **one of which
voids this whole section.** An argument exists and is deliberately not used as one:
imported tongue must be bought at a tongue price and this line's unit value fell to head
meat's, so re-export would have to be loss-making. That is reasoning; the pull is a
measurement. **The pull ran on 2026-09-13 and the voiding branch is excluded by arithmetic.**
`b35_reexport_pull.py`, selftest 15 of 15, three years of the imports side of the same feed.
**The tongue line does not exist on that side**: the import schedule carries one basket,
`0206490000` offal of swine edible frozen nesoi, where the export schedule splits the heading
into tongues, hearts and skins. Two schedules do not register the same classes, so the quantity
the pull named cannot be read there at any price, and its absence is recorded as not readable
rather than as zero. **A bound needs no such split.** Every kilogram of frozen swine offal the
country imported is an upper bound on the part of it that was tongue, and nothing can be
re-exported that did not come in, so the whole basket enters at its ceiling. The 2023 gap is
49,545 t and the whole basket is 18,534 t, **0.374 of it**: even if all of it were tongue and
all of it left again, the ratio only falls from 2.5486 to 1.6138 and stays above one. No share
is borrowed from anywhere. The origins are Canada, Mexico, Denmark, Spain and Chile, with no
China leg. **The argument that was registered and deliberately not used is now a number**: the
basket landed at $2.34 a kg while the China leg of the tongue line shipped at $1.29, so
re-export would run at a loss of that order; it is reported and not leaned on, because a basket
average is not a tongue price. **What the bound does not cover** is tongue entering under
another heading, above all 0206.30 fresh or chilled, and leaving frozen; that basket has not
been pulled, so the bound covers the frozen route only.

**Checked in passing**: China's Decree 248, the overseas-establishment registration regime
often reached for here, took effect 1 January 2022 and covers meat in its recommendation
pathway. **It does not line up with a September break.**

### B35 — the gates before the tongue arm opens, and the one that shuts it costs nothing

`nothing fetched` `six criteria, all pass` `the arm closes on a count, not on a number`

**Two gates were owed before this arm opened. Running them first meant running the two
counting gates that come before both, and those are what settled it.**

**The window is better than the record expected.** Confined to 2022 the arm had eight
months. On the three-year panel the span where this code carries one good on every leg is
**2021-01 through 2022-08, twenty consecutive months**, with Mexico at 42.4 per cent,
Japan 28.3 and China 21.0, **each present in all twenty**, and the next destination at
2.5. The read-out's opening cell asked for twelve months and two anchors.

**And the arm closes anyway, on four vertices and three edges.**

```
one origin, three destinations, one edge per leg
V = 4    E = 3    b1 = E - V + 1 = 0
```

**A star has no independent loop, and an obstruction of the H1 kind lives on a loop.** No
amount of price dispersion on this carrier can form one, whatever the prices do and
however clean the data is. **This costs nothing, needs no data, and is decisive, which is
why it runs before the floor and the count rather than after them.**

**The class count says the same thing from the other side.** A square needs two classes at
each of two positions; this feed gives one buyer class per destination, so the square sum
has no second term to difference against. **What the carrier supports is reachability and
dispersion.**

**The object, printed rather than judged.** One code, one origin, three destinations,
twenty months: the dearest anchor runs **1.247 to 1.610 times the cheapest, mean 1.450,
and the gap never closes**. The ordering is stable — China dearest in 16 of 20, Japan in
4, **Mexico cheapest in 18 of 20 and dearest in none.**

**The floor is measured, not asserted.** 18 of 116 destination-months land within 1e-4 of
a whole cent per pound against a uniform expectation of 0.02 per cent, so the grid is one
cent a pound, **$0.0220 a kg**. The thinnest monthly gap between dearest and cheapest is
$0.537 a kg, **24.3 times that floor**, and the mean gap is 45.6 times it. **Gate six
passes wide.**

**Where this reading sits.** A scalar field with one potential per position writes any set
of star prices as `price(j) = potential(j) - potential(origin) + freight`. **Both accounts
give the same answer here, which is the common-answer cell**, recorded as ours and not as
a debt; the ordering principle says it is the last place to spend next, which is a
statement about what to do and not about what this is worth.

**Two reshapes are named and neither is fetched.** A **second origin** shipping the same
good to the same three destinations gives V=5, E=6, **b1=2**, two independent loops, and a
loop sum makes the scalar field's prediction of exactly zero readable on this carrier;
EU, Brazilian and Canadian export-by-partner series are where that would come from. A
**second class inside one destination** would give a genuine square, and that needs the
importing side's own reporting, a different channel from this one.

### B35 — the reshape closes too, on one line in three tariff schedules

`nothing fetched` `four criteria, all pass` `the gate is a reading, not a measurement`

**The gate record closed the arm on a count and registered the reshape that would fix it:
a second origin shipping the same good to the same three destinations gives b1 = 2.** This
runs that reshape's own gate before anyone fetches, and the gate is the question of
whether a document exists in which a second origin names the same good.

**It does not. The split lives only in the US ten-digit national extension.**

```
United States    HS10 national statistical extension   6 lines under 0206.49   splits it
European Union   CN8                                   1   "0206 49 00 Other"
Brazil           NCM8                                  1   "0206.49.00 Outras"
Canada           Canadian Export Classification, 8dg   1   "0206.49 00 --Other KGM"
```

Three origins checked, three single lines. **A second origin can ship the same good and
cannot name it, so a cross-origin loop can only be built on 0206.49 whole.**

**And 0206.49 whole is a mixed basket, which is a number here rather than a principle.**
The six US ten-digit lines inside it span **$0.794 to $3.593 a kg on the China leg over
the window, a factor of 4.52.**

**Splitting the cross-destination unit value gap at that shared level, month by month.**
China minus Mexico, only lines present on both sides, coverage 0.928 and 0.895 of each
side's tonnage across four to six common lines:

```
composition share of the total magnitude   min 0.188   mean 0.374   max 0.513
months in which composition opposes price  20 of 20
```

**The sharpest month is 2022-08: the observed gap is $0.221 a kg while the price part is
$1.235 and the composition part is -$1.302.** The visible gap is 18 per cent of the price
signal, and how much the basket cancels moves from month to month. **At the shared level a
unit value comparison reads the mix.**

**The B35 design excluded the NESOI line from a cross-destination comparison for exactly
this reason, in one sentence and with no number. This supplies the number and extends the
same reason to the whole of 0206.49.**

**Three routes could reopen it and none is taken here**: a commodity whose six-digit line
is effectively one good, which is a search over the nomenclature rather than over this
carrier; an origin publishing a comparable statistical subdivision, which none of the
three largest pork exporters outside the US does and which this file does not claim to
have exhausted; or the destination's own customs detail, a different channel and the same
one a second class inside a position would need. **Building the loop on 0206.49 whole is
not a route, and criteria 2 and 3 price it rather than waving it off.**

| | criterion | kind | detail |
|---|---|---|---|
| PASS | B35-SO-1 the granularity, read off three schedules | instrument | US 6 lines, EU / Brazil / Canada 1 line each |
| PASS | B35-SO-2 how mixed the shared level is | own_reading | six lines spanning $0.794 to $3.593, a factor of 4.52 |
| PASS | B35-SO-3 what the basket contributes on its own | own_reading | composition 0.188 to 0.513 of the magnitude, opposing price in 20 of 20 months |
| PASS | B35-SO-4 the routes that would reopen it | bookkeeping | three named, and the one that looks open is priced |

`experiments/b35_second_origin.py --selftest`, `results/b35_second_origin.json`


## B62 — an information edge that stays up while the number it carries goes away

A Zimbabwean rate publisher posted every trading day from July 2019 to July 2021. Each
post prints several quoted rates for that day, one of them computed from a single share's
price in Harare against its price in London and Johannesburg. **Three dated things
happened to that number and none of them happened to the publisher**: the transfer link
between the two listings was suspended, then the Harare price stopped being produced when
the exchange suspended the share, then the share was left out when trading resumed.

**So this carrier separates two things a single "was the information available" index
cannot separate: the state of the edge that carries a number, and the state of the number
it carries.** Nothing was fetched for this station; the data was closed in an earlier
round.

### B62: three states of a carried object, all under an intact channel

`nothing fetched` `six criteria, all pass` `states found without using any of the dates`

**Four posts are filed under a date at which their own page layout did not exist yet.**
One rail appears on 167 posts running from January 2020 to July 2021, and the only four of
those before June 2020 are 4, 5, 11 and 12 January; after them the rail's next appearance
is 144 days later. **A rail that only starts at some date is a stamp on the page, and a
post carrying that stamp while dated before it is filed under the wrong day.** The
judgement uses which fields are present and no value at all, so it cannot be talked into
agreeing with a story about the values; the values agree independently, since those four
posts print a parallel rate of 108 to 111 where the genuine January post prints 23.7.
**Dropping them takes the zero state from three separate runs to one** — left in, the
series appears to lose the number twice in January and get it back.

**The three states fall out of the series' own signatures, with no date supplied**: a
value that changes, a value that repeats to the cent, a value printed as zero.

```
live    x19    2019-07-22 .. 2019-08-23
stale   x 1    2019-08-26
live    x101   2019-08-27 .. 2020-07-10
stale   x16    2020-07-13 .. 2020-08-04
absent  x146   2020-08-05 .. 2021-07-23
```

**What separates the long repeat from the short one is not a length, it is whether it
comes back.** The 2019 repeat is one post and returns to live; the 2020 repeat is sixteen
and is followed by the zero state, which runs to the end of the archive.

**The reading that makes any of it mean something is free and has no assumptions in it:
on those very posts, the same publisher prints other rates that move.**

```
over the 16 frozen posts    zimrates 7 distinct values,  90.00 -> 98.00
                            interbank 4 distinct,        65.87 -> 76.76
over the 146 zero posts     zimrates 25 distinct,        95.00 -> 135.00
                            interbank 25 distinct,       80.46 -> 86.79
```

**One number is reprinted to the cent sixteen times while two others on the same page keep
moving.** The channel is demonstrably up, so what changed is the thing it carries. The
selftest seeds a world where the co-rails are frozen too, and the criterion fails there; a
criterion that passes either way reads nothing.

**The boundaries the series found on its own land one post after the dated events**: the
freeze starts 13 July against a trading suspension on 29 June, the zero starts 5 August
against a resumption on 3 August that left the share out, and the last live post is 10
July. **Neither date defined either state.**

**What this carrier cannot show, named rather than glossed**: the archive has one 63-day
hole, 27 February to 30 April 2020, and it covers the first of the three events. The other
two fall on days the publisher posted. **This station reads the second and third levels
and does not claim the first.** The first version of that criterion said the hole sat at
none of the events; the count was right and the sentence was wrong, and it was fixed
before the record was written.

**What the carrier gives the framework.**

| | the edge carrying it | the number carried |
|---|---|---|
| before 29 June 2020 | up | live |
| 29 June to 3 August | **up, posting daily** | **a stale copy reprinted verbatim sixteen times** |
| after 3 August | **up, and other numbers on the same page update** | **printed as zero, 146 times** |

**The third level is not silence.** Silence is no message; this is a message whose content
is that the number does not exist. An object with one index for whether information is
available has nowhere to put these three states: it records "available" in all three.
**That is the cell where the rival has no object rather than the wrong answer**, so it
banks a new fact and scores no contest.

| | criterion | kind | detail |
|---|---|---|---|
| PASS | B62-1 posts filed under the wrong date | instrument | four caught on fields not values; zero state goes from three runs to one |
| PASS | B62-2 three states from the series' own signatures | known_answer | live 120, stale 17, absent 146; the terminal run never returns to live |
| PASS | B62-3 the channel across all three states | own_reading | one 63-day hole, covering one of the three events and neither of the other two |
| PASS | B62-4 the same post carries numbers that move | known_answer | 7 and 4 distinct co-rail values over the freeze, 25 and 25 over the zeros |
| PASS | B62-5 the found boundaries against the dated events | own_reading | freeze from 13 July, zero from 5 August, each the first post after its event |
| PASS | B62-6 what this carrier cannot show | bookkeeping | the transfer-link suspension falls inside the hole and is not claimed |

`experiments/b62_carried_vs_carrier.py --selftest`, `results/b62_carried_vs_carrier.json`


## B45 — two pools for one plate, same city, same period

Guangzhou allocates ordinary-car plates through two legs running in the same month: a free
lottery and a paid auction. The published rules make the split a third party's doing
rather than the applicant's (one application code, one method per period), forbid lending,
leasing, transferring or inheriting an indicator, and fix each pool's size by notice. Two
prices for the same object with no low-cost swap between them, which is what the carrier
needed and what its rule text already established.

### B45: the registered comparison is not identified, and the split says so in numbers

`nothing fetched` `160 periods, 2013-05 to 2026-08` `four pass, one premise fails`

**The registered comparison.** The standard account is an indifference condition: the
marginal applicant is indifferent between paying P now and waiting T periods for a free
plate, so P = T x (the price of time). Its comparative static needs no value for the price
of time — the win rate rises, the wait shortens, P should fall. The framework says the two
legs are two edges with no loop, so no such constraint exists.

**The floor, measured, and the two series do not share one.** All 160 minimum prices are
exact multiples of 100 yuan, so the bid grid is 100; only 2 of 160 average prices are,
which is what a computed mean looks like. The average runs 10,338 to 57,283 yuan, three
orders above the grid. **Resolution is not the constraint here.**

**A quarter of the panel is pinned to the floor, and the biggest lever sits inside it.**
The auction has a published reserve of 10,000 yuan and the minimum price sits exactly on
it in **40 of 160 periods**. A price pinned at its floor cannot fall, so those periods
cannot refute a prediction that it should. **The largest policy move in the whole panel is
July 2025, indicators 3,000 to 12,000, a fourfold rise that takes the win rate from 0.2028
to 0.8300 per cent — and the price is at the reserve on both sides of it.** The
second-largest, the July 2024 cut from 4,500 to 3,000, is censored on one side too.
**Both genuine regime changes are unreadable.**

**And the registered regressor splits into a half that is exogenous and a half that is the
outcome's own driver.** The win rate is indicators over applicants, and applicants respond
to the same demand that sets the price.

```
                          slope       se        t
win rate (as registered)  -0.4888   0.1763   -2.77
  indicators, exogenous   -0.3829   0.2282   -1.68
  applicants, endogenous  +0.5924   0.2750   +2.15
```

**The half that is not exogenous is the one carrying the significant coefficient**, and it
is 42.2 per cent of the regressor's variance against the exogenous half's 62.3 (they do
not sum to one because the halves covary, the cross term being -4.5 per cent). **More
applicants and a higher price are the same demand seen twice, and that alone produces the
standard account's sign.** This is the shared-driver category error, and it is recorded as
a premise that fails: per the criterion-kind discipline, that means the criteria resting on
it have no object to judge, not that either account was refuted.

**It is not scored against the framework and it must not be.** An earlier station in this
repository manufactured a loss cell by mistaking an identification failure for a rival's
win; the discriminant that catches it is asking whether the thing being scored is a rival's
point prediction at all, and here nothing was scored.

**What is left of the exogenous variation, printed rather than assumed.** Only three policy
moves exceed 0.2 log points and escape the censoring, and **all three fall in July** — the
indicator count was cut to a floor every July in the early years, so that is one annual
pattern seen three times, and anything else moving with the calendar rides along.
**Exogenous variation on this leg is one seasonal cut plus two censored regime changes.**

**The arm is not closed, and it is at its ceiling on this leg.** More periods buy nothing:
the panel is already the entire carrier, and the limit is that within one leg the win
rate's denominator is the demand that sets the price. **Two routes out are named**: the
same city's organisation lottery and organisation auction; and the three other cities
running the same two-pool structure, whose sources are not yet reached.

**Two limits added after the first pass, both of which sharpen what this carrier can and
cannot be asked.**

**The indifference condition presumes a marginal person who is trading off, and this
carrier's population is not that.** Purchase timing here is set by when a car is actually
wanted, not by the cost of waiting, and both of these cities have strong enough public
transport that a private car is genuinely deferrable; the same person is a waiter in one
period and a buyer in the next. **Entering a free lottery costs almost nothing, so the
applicant pool contains a great many people with no near-term intention to buy at all.** So
the denominator of the win rate is not "how many people want a plate this period", it is
"how many people took a free option". That is a deeper objection than the endogeneity
measured above: an exogenous denominator would still not be the T that the indifference
condition needs. It also means periods are not independent draws, because people move
between the two roles across them, which is a count this station has not done.

**And the organisation leg is linked to the individual leg by a substitution the data
cannot see.** A company car and a personally bought plate are substitutes: if the employer
pays, the employee takes it, and that is firm demand rather than consumer demand. The
numbers separate who bid in which pool; **they do not separate why someone was absent from
the other one.** The cross-leg comparison is still cleaner than two halves of one ratio,
but it is not clean, and the direction of what remains is unknown. **The cross-city route
does not carry this problem.**

| | criterion | kind | detail |
|---|---|---|---|
| PASS | B45-1 the two tables join | instrument | 160 periods; Feb 2020 carries two rows in both tables and Jan none, so the early row is January postponed |
| PASS | B45-2 the floor, measured | instrument | bid grid 100 yuan on the minimum, 1 on the computed average; range three orders above it |
| PASS | B45-3 censoring, and where the lever falls | known_answer | 40 of 160 at the reserve; the 4x policy move sits inside the censored region |
| **FAIL** | B45-4 is the comparison identified | **premise** | **Void.** the endogenous half carries the significant coefficient; the registered reading has no object |
| PASS | B45-5 what exogenous variation remains | bookkeeping | three large uncensored moves, all in July, so one annual pattern rather than three shocks |

`experiments/b45_two_pools.py --selftest`, `results/b45_two_pools.json`


## B36 — a quota that does not bind, an expiry date that does, and the same switch thrown twice

A trade quota was written for 2026 on a coordinate the exporting country cannot
change: the average market share over July 2021 to June 2024. The station opened
on the United States because that leg was cheap to pull, and it closed on that
leg at once for a reason the design had not anticipated. Everything after that
came from following the reason rather than the quota.

### B36: the quota does not bind on this leg, and what killed the flow is a registration date

US beef to China ran at quota scale for four years (176.1, 208.3, 166.1 and
157.3 million kg for 2021 to 2024, against a 2026 quota of 164,000 tonnes) and
then collapsed in 2025 to 32.0 per cent of that base, with the first half of
2026 at 2.3 per cent. **The collapse is in 2025 and the quota takes effect on
2026-01-01, so the quota did not cause it.** The plant registrations that let US
beef establishments ship to China expired in March 2025 and were not renewed;
the same customs system renewed dairy, pork and poultry on 15 and 17 March.

**This is a registration point in the sense the framework uses**: the point is
there, the edge is there; the point expires, the edge is gone, and no price
mechanism intervenes anywhere in between.

The 2026 unit value is not a price series. Six months of it climb 80 per cent
from $4.77 to $8.61 while the annual figure sat at $8.1 to $9.5 for five years,
on 2 per cent of normal volume. That is composition, not price, and the minimum
volume floor is what catches it.

### B36: two axes, and the cause is pinned to one pair of countries

Neither axis alone identifies anything. Changing the destination while holding
product and origin fixed rules out a contraction in US supply; changing the
origin while holding product and destination fixed rules out China cutting every
source. Both bands were fixed before either was read, at the same 1.5-factor
convention used throughout.

| axis | reading | verdict |
|---|---|---|
| US beef to destinations other than China, 2025 against the 2021-24 mean | **0.8975** | holds, band was 0.75 |
| Brazilian beef to China, same window | **1.4718**, an all-time high | holds |
| US beef to China, same window | 0.2964 | the collapse |

**The US supply story is not zero and it is not nothing: non-China fell 10.3 per
cent, which is roughly what a multi-decade low in the cattle herd would do. It
cannot account for the other sixty points.** Nor was the volume resold: US beef
exports fell 20.4 per cent overall, so that meat was not sold, it did not change
buyer. China's share of US beef exports went from a stable 16.0-18.1 per cent to
6.3 per cent.

The monthly series adds a different instrument to the same conclusion. March 2025
is entirely normal and April is a cliff: fresh-chilled falls 95.7 per cent in one
month and is zero for most of the following fourteen. **A cattle herd is a
variable measured in years and cannot produce a one-month step.**

### B36: three meats, one registration system, two different tariffs

Pork and poultry are meat. Same customs order, same expiry, same tariff
announcement; the only systematic difference is whether that category's plants
were renewed. The statistic is a three-month-over-three-month ratio and the
read-outs were registered before any of the three series was seen. Gate six ran
first, on a log scale after the raw scale compressed all three into the same
0.8 (a ruler-shape artefact, recorded as such): 1.513, 1.131 and 1.463 standard
deviations, all three clear.

| meat | registration | tariff | step month | lowest ratio | after the April step |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| pork | renewed | +10% | 2025-04 | 0.558 | **0.728** |
| poultry | renewed | +15% | 2025-04 | 0.310 | 0.307 |
| beef | **not renewed** | +10% | 2025-04 | **0.182** | **0.051** |

**The answer is not one cause but two, with two different dates.** All three
steps land in April, and only the tariff reaches pork and poultry, so the step is
the tariff. The floor is the registration: pork and beef carry the identical
+10%, imposed the same day and removed the same day, and pork recovers to 0.728
while beef sits at 0.051. Fourteen times. **Poultry recovered no better than beef
despite renewed registrations, and this station does not explain that**; its
tariff is higher and it has its own avian influenza suspension history, neither
of which was checked. Recorded as residue.

### B36: the switch was thrown twice more, in another country, with no tariff anywhere

Brazil suspended its own beef exports to China twice on atypical BSE findings,
2021-09-04 to 2021-12-15 and 2023-02-23 to 2023-03-23. Dates come from documents,
and four predictions were written before the monthly series was seen. **All four
hold.**

| suspension | months closed | months below half | trough, against the pre-suspension mean |
|---|---|---|---|
| Brazil, 2023 | 1.0 | 2 | 0.478 |
| Brazil, 2021 | 3.5 | 3 | **0.0051** |
| United States, 2025 | 14 | 14 | 0.043 |

**The length of the hole follows the length of the closure, across three events,
two countries and three unrelated proximate causes.** The one-month closure
leaves a two-month hole because the pipeline takes about a month to drain, and
the same lag is visible inside the 2021 event, which is also why the US step
lands in April rather than March. A purely administrative switch, with no tariff
moving at all, produces the same shape as the US episode, so the tariff is not
necessary to it. The switch also has an opening: a nationwide self-suspension
bottoms at 0.005 against 0.043 for a partial loss of plant eligibility, eight
times deeper.

### B36: a registered prediction was refuted, and the instrument was measuring a leg rather than a loop

The framework separates a rate instrument, which moves a weight on an edge, from
a quantity instrument, which decides whether the edge conducts at all. If that
split is real, one shock should leave two marks whose durations follow their own
causes. **The two durations are documented and they differ by six months**: the
+10% tariff ran 2025-03-10 to 2025-11-10, eight months; the registrations were
down from March 2025 to 2026-05-15, fourteen months.

The registered prediction was that the unit-value wedge would track the tariff
window. It does not.

| window | n | log wedge | sd |
|---|---|---|---|
| before, 2024-01 to 2025-02 | 14 | **+0.1125** | 0.0333 |
| tariff on, registrations down | 7 | -0.2573 | 0.3782 |
| **tariff off, registrations still down** | 6 | **-0.7254** | 0.0315 |
| both restored, 2026-06 | 1 | -0.1457 | — |

**Verdict in the words it was registered in: not separate on this carrier.** The
wedge does not move when the tariff is removed and it moves the month the
registrations return, recovering 69 per cent of the distance in one month.

The shape is worth more than the verdict. Two windows have almost identical
standard deviations, 0.0333 and 0.0315, with the transition between them eleven
times noisier. **The wedge is not drifting; it switches between two tight
plateaus, and it switches on the registration dates.**

The registered control settles what that means. Pork carries the identical
tariff, imposed and removed on the same days, and its registrations were renewed,
so its seller set did not change. **Pork's wedge is flat**: a monotone drift of
0.065 over two years against beef's 0.838 step, a factor of 12.9, with a standard
deviation of 0.032 that shows the instrument is not blunt. So the beef step is
not the tariff and not anything common to all US meat.

**Why the tariff moves nothing here has a one-line answer that the project's own
first theorem already gave**: the +10% is levied by the importer on the landed
price, and the wedge is computed on the US free-on-board price, before it. A
wedge is a quantity on a loop, not on one leg, and looking at one leg cannot see
it. The refuted prediction was a badly shaped criterion, not a failed claim, and
the correction is checkable: the theorem is one of the oldest documents here.
**One real reading falls out of it**: if exporters had absorbed the whole +10%
the wedge would fall 0.0953, and pork's fell 0.0192, so full absorption by the
exporter is excluded and most of the wedge is not in the US price. The 20 per
cent point estimate has a margin of roughly nineteen points and is not claimed.

### B36: two customs systems, and the offset between them is the voyage

The Brazilian quota cell is 1,106,000 tonnes for 2026 out of a 2,688,000 tonne
total, taken from the annex table the official HTML does not carry (a research
source, not an official one, and that is recorded wherever the figure is used).
The unit was checked rather than copied: the source rendered it as million tonnes
and two figures already on disk, the US cell and the total, both land on ten
thousand tonnes.

China announced Brazil reached 50 per cent of its cell on 2026-05-09. Aligning
that against Brazilian shipment data gave a lag of minus nine days, which is
impossible, and **the impossible sign is what caught the definition**: the quota
counts customs clearance in China, and January clearances left Brazil the
previous November. Solving for the lag rather than guessing it gives **52 days,
with 50 and 52 bracketing the target at 0.9953 and 1.0046**, one day of shift
moving 0.47 per cent of the target. The six covered headings on one side map
exactly onto the ten eight-digit codes on the other, so the definitional gap is
zero rather than small.

**Two customs systems built by different countries for unrelated purposes, and
the offset between them lands on the sailing time of the ship, 51 days give or
take one.**

### B36-7: both halves of the criterion fired, in opposite directions, in one year

The criterion was registered as either-or: a collapse as the quota is approached,
**or** a rush to ship before it binds, either one counts.

```
January to June 2026 against 2025      1.0844      the rush
July 2026 against July 2025            0.522       the collapse
same month, control destinations       about 1.51
```

Chile and Egypt rose about fifty per cent in the same month from the same source
and the same codes, so July was not an incomplete publication. Against this
lane's own ten-year seasonality, July over June runs 0.683 to 1.336 since the
lane had scale, median 1.122, and 2026 reads **0.522**, below every one of them.
July is normally this lane's strongest month-on-month step of the year.

**And the turn does not sit on the quota line, it sits on the quota line minus a
voyage.** A full quota's worth of beef had left Brazil by 2026-07-23, clearing
around 2026-09-13. Ships leaving in July clear from 2026-08-22, which is to say
July cargo is exactly the cargo at risk of arriving after the ceiling and paying
55 per cent. **The lag used to place that date was solved independently, two
sections earlier, and not chosen for this explanation.**

### B36 criterion table — the station is open

Registered read-outs, their verdicts, and the ones with no verdict yet.

| criterion | verdict | reading |
|---|---|---|
| B36-0 does the quota bind on the US leg | **degenerate, and the reason is dated** | 2026 half-year 2.3 per cent of the cell, 4.7 per cent annualised; the line sits twenty-one times above the flow. The collapse predates the quota by a year |
| B36-1 the quota's own footprint | **both halves fired, on the Brazilian leg** | rush 1.0844 for January to June, collapse 0.522 in July, controls about 1.51 the same month |
| B36-2 the quota is written on a coordinate the exporter cannot change | **PASS** | share of July 2021 to June 2024; 2023 and 2024 sit at 101.3 and 95.9 per cent of the resulting cell |
| B36-3 anti-circumvention text | **not fetched** | |
| B36-4 pork and poultry as a same-system control, annual | **not identified, and the criterion was missing a branch** | beef 0.296, pork 0.480, poultry **0.115**. Poultry fell further than beef and the registered three-way read-out had no cell for that. All three fell in 2025, and a common retaliatory tariff explains that as easily as expiry does |
| B36-5 change the destination | **PASS** | non-China 0.8975 against a 0.75 band |
| B36-6 change the origin | **holds** | Brazil to China 1.4718, an all-time high, and 1.2462 against 2024 alone |
| B36-7 the quota on the leg where it is inside the flow | **both halves, see B36-1** | Brazil 2025 at 1.49 times its cell, 2026 annualised at 1.33 |
| B36-8 read the two documents rather than cutting the series again | **read** | pork 365 and poultry 210 plants renewed 15-17 March 2025; 386 of 654 beef plants overdue; beef and pork +10%, chicken +15%; 425 beef plants renewed 2026-05-15 |
| B36-9 three meats, one system, two tariffs | **two causes, two dates** | steps all in 2025-04, so the step is the tariff; pork and beef share the tariff exactly and end at 0.728 against 0.051, so the floor is the registration |
| B36-10 a second cycle, in another country, with no tariff | **four predictions of four** | hole length tracks closure length across 1, 3.5 and 14 months; trough 0.0051 against 0.043 |
| B36-11 do the two graphs leave marks of different lengths | **not separate on this carrier** | the wedge ignores the tariff's removal and moves on the registration date; recorded in the words it was registered in |
| B36-12 the pork control on the same wedge | **flat, and it settles B36-11's reading** | beef steps 0.838 between two tight plateaus, pork drifts 0.065 with no step, ratio 12.9 |
| B36-13 does reopening speed measure what a closed edge left behind | **not run** | the 2017 reopening after fourteen years is on disk; the 2026 reopening after fourteen months recovered 69 per cent in one month |
| registered prediction: August 2026 | **registered, source has not published** | mechanism puts August below the 72,417 to 102,327 tonne seasonal band, because every August sailing clears after the ceiling |
| registered prediction: US beef, second half of 2026 | **registered, not yet readable** | if eligibility was the binding constraint, monthly volume should keep rising above June's 1,152 tonnes |

**Not claimed by this station.** Which of expiry and tariff caused the April step
was undecidable on the monthly series alone and is answered only by the
cross-meat design; poultry's failure to recover is unexplained; the Brazilian
quota cell rests on a research source rather than an official one; the control
destinations were pulled for 2026 only.

**One candidate for the wrong-answer cell was registered and did not survive its
own control.** B36-11's refutation was registered as entering that cell if the
pork control failed to hold. It held, and the reason the prediction failed is
that the instrument measured a leg where the theory says the quantity lives on a
loop. The criterion's shape was wrong, not the claim under test, and both figures
stay on the record for a reader who wants to judge that for themselves.


## B33 — the five classes a benefit scheme writes, and the clause vectors they receive

Arm one of station B33 asks whether the partition a published scheme writes over
its positions equals the partition its full clause vectors induce. The object
compared is the whole vector, not one scalar component of it.

Carrier: Singapore, Central Provident Fund (Revised Workfare Income Supplement
Scheme) (Amendment No. 2) Regulations 2025, S 156/2025, made 5 March 2025, first
published in the Government Gazette, Electronic Edition, on 5 March 2025.
Thirty-three pages, transcribed in full; the coverage table sits in the record.
Script `experiments/b33_wis_schedules.py`, record `results/b33_wis_schedules.json`.
Exact rational arithmetic throughout, no floating point. Criteria are written in
the script that produces the record, the record carries their text, and every
quantity this run produced is reported.

The instrument writes five classes for a relevant month, and draws the mutual
exclusion into each definition: an eligible employee `worked as an employee (and not
also as a platform worker)`, an eligible Group A worker `being a Group A worker,
worked as a platform worker (and not also as an employee)`, an eligible Group B
worker likewise, and an eligible employee-platform worker `worked as an employee,
and also as a platform worker`. A fifth class, the eligible self-employed person,
is assessed over a relevant year rather than a month, and the instrument writes
the rule joining the two grains: that eligibility is `assessed after the member's
eligibility for each relevant month in that year under regulation 8AA, 8AB, 8AC or
8AD`.

The five dimensions read for each class are the qualifying quantity, the
small-sum exclusion, the top-up payable on the waiver path, the cash proportion
of the benefit, and the schedule that gives the benefit amount.

| criterion | reading | |
|---|---|---|
| **B33-1** every coefficient of the Thirteenth Schedule is exactly two-thirds of the corresponding coefficient of the Twelfth | **48 coefficients compared over seven bands and four age columns, slopes and intercepts alike; the set of distinct ratios has one element, `2/3`; zero anomalies** | PASS |
| **B33-2** the Fourteenth Schedule is cell for cell identical to the Twelfth, only the variable read against differs | **56 cells compared, 0 differ** | PASS |
| **B33-3** no two of the clause vectors coincide on all five dimensions | 5 written classes carrying 6 clause vectors, 0 colliding pairs | PASS |
| **B33-4** every page of the instrument was opened, and the coverage table names what each batch carried | 33 of 33 | PASS |
| **B33-5** where the read partition is finer than the written one, the extra line is drawn by the instrument itself and its provisions are named | 1 of 5 written classes carries more than one vector, and two provisions draw that line | PASS |
| **B33-26** *(rival)* the rival's scalar generates one set of terms at one position, so the two classes standing there, 8AB and 8AC, must receive identical clause vectors in every period pairing | **2 period pairings, each differing on 4 of the 5 dimensions.** The one that does not differ is the qualifying quantity, aggregate platform earnings for both | PASS |

**Read the kinds before the count.** B33-1, B33-2, B33-3 and B33-5 are this frame's own readings of the instrument, B33-4 is bookkeeping, and B33-26 is a named rival's point prediction, registered so that passing means the rival is wrong. A failure in one of these says something quite different from a failure in another, so they are not added up.

**What makes the last one available, and it had to be fetched.** The rival's entailment bites only if the two classes stand at one position, and the instrument does not say what separates a Group A worker from a Group B worker. It sends the definition to paragraph 1(1) of the Fourth Schedule to the Central Provident Fund Act 1953, which sends it on to paragraphs 5 and 8 of that Schedule: Group A is a platform worker born on or after 1 January 1995, or born before that date and having opted in; Group B is the rest. The eligibility sentences of 8AB and 8AC are then the same word for word but for the group name, so what the member did is identical while the terms are not.

**Both schedules are banded by age, so a reading that the terms are a function of age has to be answered, and the option answers it.** Paragraph 4(3) says an option cannot be withdrawn, and it runs from B to A only, with no route to Group B for anyone born on or after 1 January 1995. A worker born before 1995 who has exercised it is Group A while a worker of the same age in the same month who has not is Group B. The class index is a label the Board records rather than a function of any position variable.

The read partition equals the written one, so the arm passes on this carrier. The
pass is not a narrow one: every pair of classes is separated on at least two
dimensions, and by numbers rather than by a single non-scalar side right. The two
platform classes are separated by a small-sum exclusion of `$50` against `$500`
from any one platform operator, and by a waiver top-up that is a five-step age
table for one and a two-dimensional schedule for the other.

Two readings fell out of the run and bear on nothing the criteria scored.

**Three written benefit tables carry two functions.** The Thirteenth Schedule is
`(2/3)` times the Twelfth on every one of 48 coefficients, and the Fourteenth is
the Twelfth cell for cell. A published scheme pointing at three tables is reading
off two. This is the same object the tariff-block corpus measured on national
electricity schedules, where 53 schedules drew 179 blocks and wrote 156 distinct
values; there the collisions were bounded by the survey's rounding to two decimal
places, and that limit was recorded with them. Here the collision is exact and
carries no resolution limit, which makes it the first one in this repository read
off a published price table without one.

**One class carries two vectors, and the instrument dates the change.** For an
eligible Group A worker the cash proportion moves from one-tenth to two-fifths at
applicable year 2029 (reg 13B(1)(b)(ii)), and the benefit table moves from the
Thirteenth to the Twelfth Schedule at the same year (reg 13C(2)(b)). After that
year the class is separated from the eligible employee on three dimensions rather
than five. The Income Tax Act 1947 carries a matching date: the additional
deduction at section 39(2)(hb) runs for years of assessment 2026 to 2029 only.
Two instruments end the same class's transitional treatment at the same point.
Registered as a prediction, not as a reading.

**What this station does not claim.** It does not claim the two platform classes
are objects of the counting law in the Income Tax Act 1947: there `Group A worker`
qualifies income and contributions rather than persons, and `Group B worker` does
not appear in any operative provision. It does not claim a Group B worker
receives nothing under the tax statute; those workers carry mandatory MediSave
contributions and are reached by the provisions already written for self-employed
persons. It does not claim the arm has been scored in more than one jurisdiction:
one carrier, one piece of subsidiary legislation. And it does not claim the
Fifteenth Schedule has been checked cell by cell; it belongs to one class alone
and has no counterpart table to compare against.


## B48 — a reference number whose input is removed in three steps, and the channel carrying it never stops

The Old Mutual Implied Rate is the ratio of one share's price in Harare against
its price in London or Johannesburg, computed and posted every trading day by a
third party. Its Harare leg was removed in three steps, each with a date and each
with a document. The question is what the posted number does at each step.

Carrier: 287 daily market posts, 22 July 2019 to 23 July 2021, plus 20 live
readings recovered from the sidebars of those pages. `data/fetch_zw_rates.py`
captures the pages and `data/build_zw_daily.py` builds the working panel from
them; the pages themselves and the panel are data and stay on the machine that
fetched them, and rerunning the first script rebuilds them. Criteria are written
to be read off the act of publishing and off the content published, with no
threshold on any level.

| criterion | date and what was removed | reading | |
|---|---|---|---|
| **B48-1** the transfer edge is cut while both prices still exist | 15 March 2020, Exchange Control (Suspension of Fungibility of Certain Shares) Order 2020, GN 583/2020, in force to 12 March 2021 | the number goes on being computed and posted, **and moves faster**: `60.77` on 13 March to `75.20` on 23 March, `+24%` in a week | PASS |
| **B48-2** the Harare price itself stops being produced | announced 26 June 2020, trading halted from 29 June; **no statutory instrument was ever promulgated**, and a legal analysis service recorded that the halt `was not done in terms of any law` | **frozen**: `122.22` reprinted on 17 consecutive posts from 10 July to 4 August, and that value is by construction the last close before the halt | PASS |
| **B48-3** the Harare leg is removed permanently | 3 August 2020, trading resumes without the counter | **empty**: `0.00` from 5 August, 146 posts unbroken to the end of the series on 23 July 2021 | PASS |
| **B48-4** each of the three dates points at a document | — | all three do, and one of them is the recorded fact that no statutory instrument exists | PASS |

The publisher never stopped. It posted on every trading day through the month the
exchange was shut and through the 146 posts that carried `0.00`. So this station
reads the cell where the transfer graph is cut and the information graph is
whole, at three depths rather than two.

**Two of the three states had no name before this.** A stale copy reprinted
verbatim seventeen times is one; a channel that runs on schedule and delivers a
sentinel meaning `this number does not exist` is the other. Silence is the
absence of a message; this is a message whose content is the absence of the
quantity. Both occur with the information edge intact, so both describe the state
of the object carried rather than the state of the edge carrying it.

**Alongside the criteria, four readings the run produced.** The leave-one-out
log-linear interpolation floor, binned by gap length, is `0.0137` median at one
to three days and `0.0176` at four to seven, against a headline move of about
`0.9` log points. Four post dates carried the previous year in their titles and
were corrected from each page's own `article:published_time` and JSON-LD, all 287
pages checked with no false positives; what found them was two outlying
leave-one-out points at `1.5` log points. Sweeping the sidebars of all 287 pages
returned 324 date-value pairs, 38 of them on days absent from the panel and 20
carrying a live value, seven of those around the 15 March 2020 cut. Of 733
calendar days, 287 carry a post; the publisher posts on trading days, so 102 of
104 Saturdays and 102 of 104 Sundays are absent by design, 20 of the 21 weekday
public holidays are absent, and only 13 isolated single weekdays are missing.

**What this station does not claim.** It does not claim the cell where both edges
are cut: the information edge here was never cut. It does not claim `122.22` was
independently confirmed; the exchange's own 2020 closing prices could not be
obtained, its daily price files covering only August 2016 to January 2018. It
does not claim its own series fixes the last trading day, which is bounded by the
external dates instead, and the series carries an 18-working-day hole from 16
June to 9 July 2020 with no archive capture in that month. And the registered
cross-publisher dispersion criterion is **not decidable on this carrier**: the
orbits do not cross the window, and the one leg present throughout is an
administratively pegged rate in one window and an auction rate in the other,
which are two objects.

**A permanent limit on the source.** The publisher's domain no longer resolves as
of September 2026, so the 287 captured pages held here are the only copy of that
series known to this project. They are treated as non-reproducible.


## B49 — the two energy carriers that cannot be resold, and a square sum that is never zero

Station documents: [`b49_prereg.md`](docs/b49_prereg.md) and [`b49_results.md`](docs/b49_results.md).

A class differential can only be read off two prices when the holder of the
cheaper one cannot resell it to the holder of the dearer one. Electricity and
piped natural gas arrive over a fixed network and the connection point is the
class definition, so nothing moves past the meter. Kerosene, LPG, fuel oil and
coal all travel in drums, bottles and wagons, so a gap between two buyer classes
there is carriage and handling. Gasoline and diesel do not even have two classes
in this source: they exist in the transport sector only, one price, and their
paired-cell counts are zero rather than small. Positions are therefore
electricity and gas, classes are residential and industrial, and the square sum
read here is the first of the three terms,

    w_resid(elec, gas) - w_ind(elec, gas)
      = log(P_resid_elec / P_resid_gas) - log(P_ind_elec / P_ind_gas)

Carrier: the public read endpoint of the IEA End-use Energy Prices data set, CC
BY 4.0, annual prices by sector. The locked panel is every country carrying all
four series in all three published years, 13 countries by 3 years by 4 series,
156 prices, every one of them in the record. `experiments/b49_energy_class_square.py`
fetches and scores; responses are cached under `data/cache/iea/` so a rerun goes
to the network zero times. All four prices are on one basis, VAT included: the
database documentation states that the World Energy Prices series includes VAT
for the industry and electricity-generation sectors as well, to keep countries
comparable, and it is that series and not the OECD-only one that this endpoint
returns, which is read off the country list rather than assumed, since Algeria is
in the locked panel and is not an OECD member. Criteria are written into the
script that produces the record, the record carries their wording, and every
quantity this run produced is reported.

| criterion | reading | |
|---|---|---|
| **B49-1** the locked panel is complete, all four series in all three years | 13 countries, 39 cells, 156 prices | PASS · `instrument` |
| **B49-2** the country list is never shorter than the records it names, reported per product | all eight products return list and records equal to the digit; the sparsity is in the years, not in the list | PASS · `bookkeeping` |
| **B49-3** the square sum does not move when the four prices are quoted in another currency | median gap `9.19e-09` over 39 of 39 cells, worst `2.471e-03` at Netherlands 2000 | PASS · `instrument` |
| **B49-4** every square sum stands above that measured floor | 39 of 39, smallest `7.4x` the floor, median `56x`, none at or below | PASS · `instrument` |
| **B49-5** no cell matches the rival's point prediction of exactly zero | 0 of 39 | PASS · `rival` |

The rival here is a scalar price field over positions: if the terms facing every
class were the gradient of one potential, every square sum would be exactly zero
whatever the level of prices. This is a point prediction of zero, so it carries
no band, and what it is read against is a measured floor rather than an
interval. The floor is not declared. One exchange rate per country and year
cancels in the log difference, so quoting the four prices in national currency
must return the same square sum, and the largest departure over the 39 cells is
what the instrument cannot resolve. That check is an implementation check and not
an independent confirmation: the cancellation is forced by the construction, and
only a coding error can break it. Its worth is exactly one code check, and the
floor it hands over is the part that is used.

What the reading does not cover. The square sum has three terms and the two
transfer wedges are not observed, because moving between the residential and the
industrial class is what the connection rules forbid. For the full sum to vanish,
the difference of those two wedges would have to cancel the measured term in
every one of the 39 cells.

Counting the independent loops. The four vertices are the position-class pairs
and the four edges are two within-class position edges and two agent edges, so
`b1 = 4 - 4 + 1 = 1`. There is one independent loop, and the 39 cells are that
one loop read once in each country-year rather than 39 independent loops. Any
power claim multiplying by 39 would be counting the same circuit repeatedly.

Sign and level, reported without a line drawn on either. `|square sum|` runs from
`0.0183` at Spain in 2000 to `0.8526` at New Zealand in 2025, median `0.1383`. By
year the sign splits 5 positive against 8 negative in 2000, 2 against 11 in 2010,
1 against 12 in 2025, with medians `-0.0472`, `-0.1610` and `-0.2302`. Hungary is
the one country running the other way, `-0.062` then `+0.041` then `+0.107`, and
the reason is visible in its four prices: in 2025 its residential electricity is
`125.595` against `232.128` for industry and its residential gas is `35.625`
against `73.314`, both roughly half. Slovakia inverts on electricity in 2025 as
well but not on gas, so its square sum stays negative.

Which products can carry this square at all, counted before anything was read.
The columns are the number of countries with a price in each sector, then the
country list, the records, the countries carrying all three years, and the cells
where one country-year holds two or more sectors.

| product | ELGEN | IND | RESID | TRANS | list | records | 3 years | paired cells |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| electricity | 0 | 88 | 110 | 0 | 111 | 111 | 38 | **179** |
| natural gas | 19 | 56 | 58 | 15 | 69 | 69 | 28 | **102** |
| light fuel oil | 0 | 66 | 99 | 0 | 103 | 103 | 32 | 122 |
| LPG | 0 | 7 | 89 | 42 | 96 | 96 | 15 | 48 |
| fuel oil | 15 | 71 | 0 | 0 | 73 | 73 | 19 | 17 |
| steam coal | 18 | 21 | 22 | 0 | 38 | 38 | 13 | 22 |
| gasoline | 0 | 0 | 0 | 138 | 138 | 138 | 44 | **0** |
| automotive diesel | 0 | 0 | 0 | 137 | 137 | 137 | 46 | **0** |

Light fuel oil has more paired cells than LPG and is still the wrong object,
because a drum can be carried. The count is larger and the thing being counted is
not a class differential, which is the reason this table prints the object beside
the count.

A third class is visible in this table and is not read here. Natural gas carries
26 cells pairing electricity generation against industry and 23 pairing it
against residential, and coal carries 16 of the first kind. That is the same
molecule with a third class defined by what it is burned for. Whether that
division is imposed or chosen has to come from the rules granting it, not from
the prices, so it is registered and left.


## B50 — a statute that caps one leg, and why a ceiling is not an equality

Station documents: [`b50_prereg.md`](docs/b50_prereg.md) and [`b50_results.md`](docs/b50_results.md).

B49 read the square sum on electricity against piped gas, residential against
industrial, and found it nonzero in every cell. This station asked whether that
quantity moves when a published rule changes one leg and leaves the other alone.
Hungary wrote such a rule: Act LIV of 2013 caps what a household may be charged
at 90 per cent of a named reference tariff, covers household universal service
only with industry outside it, fixes the sizes itself and delegates nothing.

Carrier: Eurostat bi-annual energy prices, `geo=HU`, 37 semesters from 2007-S2
to 2025-S2, four legs at the standard reference bands Eurostat itself uses, in
all three of its tax bases. `experiments/b50_hungary_class_square.py` fetches and
scores; responses are cached under `data/cache/eurostat/` so a rerun goes to the
network zero times. Criteria are written into the script that produces the
record, the record carries their wording, and every quantity this run produced is
reported, including the two windows registered in advance as unlikely to read.

Two arithmetic screens, both computable before any data is fetched, cut the five
rounds of the programme down to one window. The square sum is a difference of
log ratios, so a round cutting both carriers in the same proportion does not move
its first term at all, and two of the five rounds are of that kind. A Eurostat
semester price is an average over six months rather than a price on a date, so a
round taking effect inside a semester is diluted in proportion to the months it
covers, and only one round begins on the first day of a semester.

| criterion | reading | |
|---|---|---|
| **B50-1** the panel is complete, four legs in every semester and every tax base | 37 semesters, 37 of them in all three bases | PASS · `instrument` |
| **B50-2** the reading uses the per-band series, not the total band | bands carry 37 semesters against the total band's 10, 10, 1 and 6 | PASS · `instrument` |
| **B50-3** the square sum does not move with the currency the prices are quoted in | floor `7.404e-04` over 37 comparisons in euro, worst at 2018-S2; the purchasing-power unit is reported separately at `5.190e-02` and excluded, since it is not one scalar per country-semester and so cannot bound the instrument | PASS · `instrument` |
| **B50-4** the point prediction over the surviving window, in four states | **premise does not hold, so there is no point prediction here to judge** | not judged · `own_reading` |
| **B50-5** the premise: both household carriers moved in the same proportion | household electricity `-0.1025`, household gas `-0.1342`, difference `0.0318` against a floor of `7.404e-04` | **FAIL** · `premise` |
| **B50-6** the cut reached the price and not only the tax | tax-excluded `-0.1060` and tax-included `-0.1025`, same sign | PASS · `premise` |

**What went into the design and did not survive contact with the statute.** The
screens assumed the law required equal proportional cuts. It sets a ceiling: not
more than 90 per cent of the reference tariff. A ceiling does not imply equality,
gas fell 13.4 per cent against electricity's 10.2, that is fully lawful, and the
first term of the square is therefore not constant by construction. The window
the two screens left is not a clean point prediction after all, which is why
B50-4 is recorded as not judged rather than as a pass or a failure.

**Where the movement in that window actually came from.** The square sum moved
`-0.0483`. Splitting it: the two household legs contribute `+0.0317` between
them, and the two industrial legs contribute `-0.0801`, because industrial gas
fell 7.3 per cent in the same semester while industrial electricity was flat at
`+0.0075`. **The industrial half is two and a half times the household half, and
the statute does not reach industry at all.** Wholesale gas was falling in early
2013. So this window cannot separate a shared procedure from a shared
environment, because the environment moved on its own.

**Two yardsticks, and one of them is not the floor.** `0.0483` stands at 65 times
the measured floor, so it is visible. Against this quantity's own movement it is
ordinary: over the 36 semester-to-semester transitions the median absolute change
is `0.0969`, and this one ranks 28th, at the 22nd percentile. A resolution floor
says whether a number can be seen. It does not say whether the number stands out,
and that needs the series' own distribution, taken from the distribution rather
than from a constant chosen here.

**The other two windows, reported as they came.** The 2014 rounds fall five
months apart and semester averaging cannot separate them, so they were registered
in advance as a single change of about `+0.0085`, likely below anything readable.
The reading is `-0.1230`: readable, opposite in sign, and fourteen times the size.
The reason is the same one as above, industrial gas fell 23.1 per cent over that
span. The 2022 window was downgraded in advance because the industrial leg moves
in the same semester for reasons outside the statute; it reads `+0.6552` with
industrial gas at `+1.0772`, and the downgrade was right.

**What the station leaves for the next one of its kind.** Two requirements, both
bought here. A carrier's statute has to write an equality rather than a ceiling,
or the two legs' actual movements have to be independently checkable as equal.
And "the other leg does not move" has to be written down as an explicit
assumption and checked on the spot, rather than living inside the arithmetic of
the prediction, which is where it was here in all three windows.


## B51 — the screen that decides where a class difference can be read, written out and checked against a count

Station documents: [`b51_prereg.md`](docs/b51_prereg.md) and [`b51_results.md`](docs/b51_results.md).

B49 counted how many of eight energy products can carry a class difference and
