Across a hundredfold range of amounts the financial layer's median goes from `0.7423` to `0.7421`,
and across the three floors from `0.7423` to `0.7420`. The class that receives the injection keeps
slightly more of it, in each of 45 runs for each of the financial layer, the intermediate block and
the wage earners: `+0.0047`, `+0.0033` and `+0.0003` (medians, against the same class's share when
the injection goes elsewhere). **Where new claims enter, and how many, barely moves where they end
up.** Of what is injected, `0.9998` stays in holdings at `4` a round and `1.0000` at `40`. The
remainder is the carrier's own small issuance, which any injection displaces: on all 150 runs the
four classes' gain equals the injected total less the issuance it displaced, to the record's
precision. The stock rises and the effective number of receivers falls in `150` of `150` runs, to
`0.9927` of the control at about 1.1 times its stock, `0.9187` at 11 times and `0.9108` at 100 times
(medians).

**Free credit removes the part of the ranking that capital made and leaves the part that the number
of attempts makes.** Wage earners' plays per round against the financial layer's at equal caps,
median over seeds, floors and chances:

| attempts a round | stake | no line | one stake | four stakes | no limit |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `0.005` | `0.605` | `1.000` | `1.000` | `1.000` |
| 1 | `0.25` | `0` | `0.730` | `1.002` | `1.000` |
| 10 | `0.09` | `0` | `0.489` | `0.950` | `1.000` |
| 10 | `0.25` | `0` | `0.429` | `0.892` | `1.000` |

At equal caps, per-node net result ranks the financial layer above the wage earners in `179`, `160`,
`122` and `84` of `180` cells as the line goes from none to no limit, and the count term's share of
the gap falls from `1.00` to `0.00` (medians). With the financial layer's cap ten times the others it
ranks above them in `180` of `180` cells at every line, the count term is `0.99` of the gap under no
limit, and the wage earners' plays sit at the cap ratio, a median of `0.100`. The price term is
exactly zero everywhere.

**One stake of credit makes what reaches the non-bettors worse than no credit, and four stakes or no
limit make it milder.** Cells where the wage shortfall averages above the control, at chance `0.51`
and stake `0.25`: `57`, `57`, `47` and `42` of 60, with median uplifts of `+0.029`, `+0.034`,
`+0.013` and `+0.011`. With a floor at that chance and stake, one stake has the highest median
uplift in all four cap settings, and four stakes and no limit are below no line in all four. The
wage earners are cleared in `1`, `5`, `0` and `0` of 360 cells, and intermediate nodes leave above
the control by `41`, `116`, `48` and `43`. In the ten cells at floor `0.06`, chance `0.51`, stake
`0.25` and ten attempts, 17 to 30 of the 30 wage payers went below zero after a settlement under one
stake, against 10 to 19 under four stakes; in the five cleared cells the line stopped them `0.16` to
`1.88` times per node per round, against `0.01` to `0.05` in the same cells under four stakes. A
payer below zero pays no wages. **One stake lets a payer put its last partial stake on the table and
then holds it below zero until inflows refill it; with a deeper line it keeps playing.** In the
cleared cells the numbers after the first earner's exit belong to the exit mode of the floor, as in
the first block, and the reading there is the clearing and its round.

**The class with no in-edges borrows, its winnings flow out and its losses stay.** Without a floor,
all 75 of its nodes end in debt in every cell with a finite line, each close to the line (median
debt `0.96` of the line at one stake and `0.98` at four), and a median of 62 under no limit. Its
holdings gain is negative in `360` of `360` cells without a floor, while its net result on the
ticket is positive in `300` of them; under no limit at `0.55` the medians are `+311` on the ticket and
`−22.9` in holdings. Its negative share is what moves the other classes' shares off the injection
column. The financial layer's share of what the financial layer and the intermediate block gain
together does not move: `0.7450` in the first block, `0.7440` under injection, and `0.7446`, `0.7446`
and `0.7445` under the three lines.

**Total up, receiving set down.** The stock rises and the effective number of receivers falls in
`1080` of `1080` cells. On the positive part of holdings the top-10 share moves by a median of
`−0.0049` and the Gini by `+0.0004`, against `−0.0043` and `+0.0003` in the first block under the
same rule.

**Counted by kind: six `instrument` criteria hold, and the second block registers no `rival` and no
`own_reading` criterion.** The readings above are printed without a registered verdict.

## A44: where new claims end up, read off the carrier's rules

**RUN: 2026-09-16. Script `experiments/a44_occupation_operator.py`, record
`results/a44_occupation.json`, carrying the configuration it ran under. The carrier, its four classes
and the injection are A41's, imported. The readout against A41's injection record reads
`results/a41_inject.json` and runs no new injection. Nothing fetched.**

**What is built.** One round of the carrier moves a marginal claim by a linear map, and the station
builds that map from the network object's own routes, spending bands, payroll sets and history, in
three versions. The **path tangent** follows the control run: its propensity draws, which payers hold
less than their share of the wage bill in each round, each round's membership and the carrier's own
issuance response. The **path tangent without issuance** sets that response to zero, the tangent at
an injection large enough to displace the carrier's issuance. The **mean field** is one fixed matrix:
each propensity at the midpoint of its band, each payer short in the share of rounds it was short in
the control, the control's closing membership, no issuance response. Applied round after round to
new claims, the mean field moves them towards its stationary vector; over `T` rounds a class's share
is its stationary share plus the deviation matrix's term divided by `T`, less a tail that shrinks
with the second eigenvalue's modulus to the power `T`.

| | criterion | reading |
|---|---|---|
| PASS | A44-0 `instrument` **recording the propensity draws touches nothing** (run by `--gate`, not in the record) | With the recording proxy in place, every history field of the control is bitwise the plain network on three floors and two seeds, and every random generator the network holds ends in the same state. Two planted faults, one extra draw a round and one read after the last draw, are each reported by the half meant to see them |
| PASS | A44-1 `instrument` **the path tangent is the carrier's rule** | On 50 cells, five seeds by three floors by each target class, its four class shares of the end-of-run gain match a finite difference of the whole model with `1e-07` claims added a round, to within `1e-05`; the largest difference measured is `5.6e-10`. Four planted faults are reported, the least by `1.1e-2`: the wage bill not answering spending, the derivative at a zero holding taken from the left, the issuance response removed, and short payers paying their share of the marginal bill |
| PASS | A44-2 `instrument` **the mean-field map conserves claims, has one stationary split and closes the finite sum** | On 65 carriers, the 15 defaults and 50 variants of them: every column conserves claims to within `1e-12`, exactly one eigenvalue lies within `1e-09` of 1, and for each target the sum over 250 rounds equals 250 times the stationary vector plus the deviation matrix's term less its tail, to `1e-10` relative. Four planted faults are each reported by the clause meant to see them: routes into departed nodes removed without rescaling the rest, the pass-on to wage earners divided by the payers' count, two trading nodes that spend nothing, and the deviation matrix with the stationary term left in |

**The split is the map's stationary vector.** On the 15 default carriers, beside A41's injection arm:

| class | stationary share | A41 injection, 150 runs |
|---|---|---|
| financial layer | **`0.7456` (`0.7415` to `0.7518`)** | `0.742` (`0.734` to `0.753`) |
| intermediate block | **`0.2522` (`0.2461` to `0.2564`)** | `0.255` (`0.245` to `0.263`) |
| wage earners | **`0.0021` (`0.0021` to `0.0023`)** | `0.0023` (`0.0019` to `0.0031`) |
| no in-edges | **exactly `0`** | `0.0000` (`0.0000` to `0.0003`) |

The ratio A41 read under the ticket, the injection and three credit lines, the financial layer's
share of what it and the intermediate block gain together, is `0.7472` (`0.7431` to `0.7534`) on
the stationary vector, and the ten variants below move it from `0.666` to `0.858`. **It is this
carrier's stationary ratio.** The map has negative entries, where a payer pays more of a larger bill;
the stationary vector has no negative entry on any of the 65 carriers.

**Against A41's injection record.** At `4` and `40` a round every class share from the path tangent
without issuance is within `0.00097` of the record, and from the mean field within `0.0021`; the

## A45: how long new claims stay ahead where they enter, and which parts of the carrier set the split

**RUN: 2026-09-16. Script `experiments/a45_duration_levers.py`, record
`results/a45_duration_levers.json`, carrying the configuration it ran under. The carrier, its classes,
its control paths, its variants and its mean field are A44's, imported, and the mean field is rebuilt
here from its parts. Nothing fetched.**

**What is built.** A44 read the split of new claims off one round's linear map on this carrier and
found that the class the claims enter keeps a fixed amount more, so its advantage in share falls as
`1/T`. This station rebuilds that map from its parts (routes, spending bands, payroll sets, the payers'
short shares, the bill slope), so that one part can move at a time, and reads three objects. The
**entry term** `K` comes off the deviation matrix, a class's term when the claims enter it less the
median of its term when they enter each of the other two home classes, the same comparison on every
floor. The **class chain** is the map aggregated into its four classes and the spending state, each
class's nodes weighted by stationary mass; for its second eigenvalue `λ`, `λ/(1−λ)` counts the rounds
a deviation between classes takes to wash out, summed. The **derivative of the stationary split** with
respect to eleven parts of the map is `Z (dB/dθ) π`.

| | criterion | reading |
|---|---|---|
| PASS | A45-0 `instrument` **the rebuilt map is A44's mean field** | On 65 carriers, the 15 defaults and A44's 50 variants, the matrix assembled from the mean field's parts is bitwise A44's; 58 of them have short payers, where the pass-on lines matter. Two planted faults are reported: the pass-on to wage earners divided by the payers' count, and the spending state's row taken before the wage step |
| PASS | A45-1 `instrument` **the derivative of the stationary split is `Z (dB/dθ) π`** | On 165 pairs of 15 carriers and 11 levers it matches the central difference of the re-solved split to within `1e-6`; the largest difference measured is `7.9e-9`. Four planted faults are reported, the least by `1.2e-3`: a pseudo-inverse in place of the fundamental matrix, the map transposed, the spending state dropped, and the pass-on lever scaling payers that have left the market |
| PASS | A45-2 `instrument` **the class chain keeps the stationary split** | On 235 maps, the 15 carriers and 220 sweep points, every column conserves claims (`4.4e-16`), the chain returns the stationary class sums (`1.7e-14`), and the sums over the classes that hold claims add to one (`1.6e-14`), all within `1e-12`. Two planted faults, nodes weighted by count and the spending state counted as mass, are each reported by the clause meant to see them. The selftest also holds a class with no stationary mass to node-count weights, and reports a test that reads the mass off the class's sum |
| PASS | A45-3 `instrument` **every lever moves what it names** | On 165 pairs, an edge lever changes only the routes out of its source class and raises the share they send into its destination; a propensity lever changes only its class's spending rates; the elasticity lever raises the bill slope; the pass-on lever scales only the short shares of payers still trading. Two planted faults, an edge lever with source and destination swapped and one that reweights the edges into its destination from every source, are reported |

**How long the entry advantage lasts follows the mixing between classes.** On the 15 default carriers
the financial layer's `K` is `1.165` (`1.127` to `1.232`) against summed rounds of `1.207` (`1.165` to
`1.236`). Scaling the three kinds of edge that couple the financial layer to the rest (financial to
intermediate, intermediate to financial, households to financial) by `s`, on five seeds without a
floor, medians:

| `s` | financial `K` | chain's summed rounds | financial stationary share | intermediate `K` |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `1.175` | `1.205` | `0.7456` | `0.801` |
| 0.5 | `2.612` | `2.708` | `0.7593` | `1.599` |
| 0.2 | `6.991` | `7.161` | `0.7722` | `3.904` |
| 0.1 | `14.342` | `14.549` | `0.7776` | `7.622` |
| 0.05 | `29.077` | `29.308` | `0.7804` | `14.994` |
| 0.02 | `73.318` | `73.565` | `0.7822` | `36.963` |

**How long the advantage lasts and where the claims end up are set by different parts of the map**: at
a fiftieth of the coupling the entry term is sixty times longer and the financial layer's share moves by
`0.037`. On the medians of the 19 points of three sweeps (the coupling, the weight of the financial
layer's internal edges, its propensity), `K` is within `7%` of the summed rounds at every point; seed
by seed, 19 of 235 maps differ by more than `7%`, at most `8.0%`, all at the two ends of the
internal-edge sweep. A class's own propensity alone, `(1−p)/p`, reads the wage earners, who spend
nothing within their class (`0.067` against `0.070`), and falls twelve times short for the intermediate
block, which does (`0.067` against `0.801`).

**Against the whole model.** Four carriers from the default to thin coupling, five seeds, injections
of `25`, `75` and `250` rounds at `4` a round into each home class: 180 runs. `T` times the entry term,
whole model against the mean field with its tail, differs by at most `0.027` for the financial layer,
`0.070` for the intermediate block and `0.015` for the wage earners. On the thinnest carrier `K` is
`6.604`; at `T = 25` the whole model reads `6.321` and the mean field `6.322`, the tail not yet gone at a
chain eigenvalue of `0.88`, and at `T = 250` they read `6.602` and `6.604`.

**The split: a class holds its inflow over its out-rate.** A 5 by 5 grid of the financial layer's
propensity and internal edge weight gives the same split wherever the out-rate, the share of the class's
claims that leave it in a round, is the same: seed by seed, 20 pairs of points with out-rates within `3%`
of each other and different propensities differ in the financial share by at most `0.0036`. The
derivative makes this exact. The financial layer neither pays nor receives wages, its claims leave only
by spending, and claims reach it after its own spending; its share's elasticity to its propensity is
`−(1−π)` and every other class's `+π`, to within `3.3e-11` on the 15 carriers. The wage earners receive
their wages before they spend, so they hold `(1−p)/p` times their wages: elasticity `−(1−π)/(1−p)`,
about `−16`, and `+π/(1−p)` for the others, to within `5.1e-10`. The intermediate block misses the same
form by `0.101` in its own share and `0.041` in the others'. It holds every payer: before it spends, each
payer pays its share of a marginal bill that follows the layer-two spending its own spending is part of,
and a short payer passes its marginal claims to the earners. With the bill slope at zero the gap in its
own share falls from `0.097` to `0.009` (medians); with the pass-on removed as well, both gaps are below
`1.1e-11`.

**The largest elasticities**, median over the 15 carriers, financial / intermediate / earners: the
financial propensity `−0.254` / `+0.746` / `+0.746`; the intermediate propensity `+0.220` / `−0.651` /
`+0.217`; the weight of the financial layer's internal edges `+0.195` / `−0.569` / `−0.572`, and of its
edges into the intermediate block the exact negatives, since each class routes to two classes only and
only the ratio of the two weights counts. The households' propensity moves the wage earners alone
(`−15.966`, the others `+0.034`); the wage elasticity gives the earners `+0.862`; the pass-on strength at
most `+0.068`.

**First-order predictions of eight of A44's variants, split into their steps.** Each variant is matched
to the levers that move the default carrier toward it, and the stationary financial share is read four
ways: to first order from the default's derivative; on the default's map with the levers moved; on that
map with the variant's own control run put in, its payers' short shares and its bill slope; and on the
variant's own map, which matches A44's record to ten places on all 40 carriers. Medians of five seeds;
the default is `0.7456`.

| variant | first order | levers moved | plus the variant's control run | variant's own map |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| financial propensity 0.3 | `0.8215` | `0.8301` | `0.8301` | `0.8301` |
| financial propensity 0.7 | `0.6698` | `0.6768` | `0.6765` | `0.6765` |
| production propensity 0.55 to 0.65 | `0.6773` | `0.6523` | `0.6574` | `0.6574` |
| wage elasticity 0 | `0.7383` | `0.7381` | `0.7381` | `0.7381` |
| wage elasticity 1 | `0.7526` | `0.7523` | `0.7523` | `0.7523` |
| upward out-degree 4 | `0.7617` | `0.7564` | `0.7592` | `0.7573` |
| 10 financial-to-intermediate edges | `0.8420` | `0.8808` | `0.8835` | `0.8571` |
| 60 financial-to-intermediate edges | `0.6010` | `0.6442` | `0.6442` | `0.6638` |

On the five variants that keep the default's graph and nodes, the last step is exactly zero. The
linearization accounts for up to `0.043` on the two edge-count variants and `0.025` on the production
propensity. The control run accounts for `0.0100` of the wage earners' share on the production
propensity, where the variant's bill slope is `0.207` against `0.132` and one or two payers' short
shares change. **Reweighting edges moves the split further than changing how many there are**, on all
three variants that change edges: from the default, `+0.138` against `+0.112` at 10
financial-to-intermediate edges, `−0.101` against `−0.082` at 60, and `+0.014` against `+0.012` at an
upward out-degree of 4.

## B101 — is the share-mix slope a technology parameter, or an average over who staffs the industry

**RUN: 2026-09-16.** Script `experiments/b101_mixture_slope.py`, record
`results/b101_mixture_slope.json`, the growth accounts joined to the labour accounts on
(industry, country). Nothing retrieved; the fitting routine is imported from the arm that
registered it rather than written twice.

**Why the arm exists.** B101-11 records that the rival's restriction holds on this panel and is
deliberately not scored, because a slope of a factor share on a factor ratio is not this frame's
object. That leaves a sharper question. If the price a class is paid at a position is
class-dependent, and B106 measures exactly that on these economies, the labour share at a position
is a composition-weighted average rather than a scalar property of the position, and the fitted
slope is a functional of the class mixture: bounded by the class-specific slopes, placed inside
that range by the mixture. **So the frame's answer is not that there is no slope and not that the
slope is arbitrary. It is that the slope is not a primitive: there is a range, and where a country
sits inside it is set by a state that moves slowly.** The labour accounts put a number on how
slowly: composition correlates +0.95 with itself a year on, +0.68 ten years on.

**What that predicts, and what came out.** Across the countries of one industry the spread of the
fitted slope should be wider where the countries staff that industry with more different mixtures.
The rival's slope carries no such term, so under it the relation is flat.

| criterion | reading | |
|---|---|---|
| **B101-36** *(instrument)* the two files join and every industry carries the minimum countries on both sides, matched count printed per industry | 19 industries joined, fewest matched countries in any of them 20 | PASS |
| **B101-37** *(own reading)* the relation between how differently the countries of an industry staff it and how far apart their fitted slopes are, printed against the rank correlation's own scale, no line drawn | **rank correlation −0.4456 across 19 industries, its own scale about 0.236** | PASS |
| **B101-38** *(bookkeeping)* every industry named with both axes and both floors | 19 carried in full | PASS |

**The sign is the opposite of the one the step predicts, and that is the reading.** Leaving each
industry out in turn keeps it negative every time, from −0.37 to −0.52, so it is not one industry.
Nineteen industries put the scale at 0.236, so the reading sits near twice it and settles nothing
decisively either way.

**Both confounds I can name push the other way.** An industry whose composition is stable within
countries gets a large composition ratio through a small floor, and a stable composition is also
one on which the slope is better determined, which enlarges the slope ratio too; an industry noisy
on both axes shrinks both. Each couples the axes positively and the measurement is negative against
them.

**One scope error was caught before anything was read, and it is the kind that prints.** The first
version built the slope's floor over every country in the industry while the spread ran on the
matched ones, which puts two sides of one ratio on two populations. The ratio still printed. Fixed,
the reading moved from −0.37 to −0.45.

**Registered and not done.** The spread relation is a consequence of the step, not the step itself.
The direct test compares a slope fitted on the actual mixture against one fitted on a mixture held
fixed, and the class-level wage shares it needs are in the same labour file.

## B106 — a labelled two-index price field, and the square its labels make possible

**RUN: 2026-09-15. Scripts `experiments/b106_labour_classes.py` (read and describe),
`b106_separability.py`, `b106_absorption.py` and `b106_caliber.py`; records
`results/b106_separability.json`, `results/b106_absorption.json` and
`results/b106_caliber.json`, each carrying the configuration it ran under. EU KLEMS &
INTANProd labour accounts, joined to the other three modules for the position
characteristics. Renumbered from B105 on the day it was opened, because another station
took that number the same afternoon and its number carries a sequence while this one's
does not.**

B2A reads dispersion at a position: two loans in the same cell at different rates, a
within-cell share of `0.7831`. That is an `H0` statement, and it is all that carrier can
give, because its borrowers have no labels and so there is no "the same class at another
position" to compare against. A square needs two positions and two classes.

This module labels them. At every position (country, industry, year) it reports, for each of
3 education by 3 age by 2 gender cells, that cell's share of employment and its share of the
wage bill. Their ratio is the class's pay relative to that position's average, and both
shares sum to 100 at every position, so the position's own level is normalised away by
construction and what is left is the ladder. It is a survey reading, not an imputation,
which is what set the employee and self-employed split aside in B101-34.

**Additive separability is not an analogy for the field being a gradient, it is the same
statement.** The additive subspace of a `J` by `K` table is the image of the coboundary on
the complete bipartite graph, so what is left carries `(J-1)(K-1)` independent cycles, each
a difference in differences of log relative pay across two positions and two classes. At 19
industries and 18 classes that is 306 cycles per country-year.

**What the field is measured in was settled from the panel, not from a document.** The
published methods note says only "the shares of employment and labour compensation by type
of worker", and the module's naming points one way while the construction the release is
built on points the other. The labour accounts exist to build the labour services index
published in the growth accounts, which is a Tornqvist over these same classes, so putting
the total at hours and then at persons and asking which reproduces that index decides it
against a series this station did not construct: hours, by a factor of thirty in root mean
square error. The field is relative hourly pay, and part-time composition is therefore not
an alternative for any part of the leftover.

Above the floor 139,811 (`74.3%`), above twice it 101,142 (`53.8%`), median `2.22` times it. Floor by lag, where a longer lag carries more real drift and so bounds the noise from above: 1 year `0.1766` clears `74.3%`, 2 years `0.2346` clears `66.9%`, 5 years `0.3470` clears `54.4%` |
| PASS | B106-17 `rival` `grid B` **the position-scalar reading puts every square at exactly zero** | 139,811 of 188,054 squares stand above the measured floor and 101,142 above twice it. The same reading B106-4 scores, on the object itself rather than on whether the leftover repeats |

**Reported as a square, so this station reads beside the ones that report a loop sum.**
The floor's construction bends both ways and both are stated: treating a square as fixed
makes real drift count as noise and raises the floor, while survey error correlated between
adjacent years would lower it. Against a floor that has absorbed five years of drift, more
than half the squares still clear it.

**Where in the class structure it lives, and one alternative it closes.** All three single
attributes sit above their own floor and all four of their crossings sit below: the
position-specific part of the ladder moves along one attribute at a time rather than along
combinations. Education is the largest at `1.78` times its floor, which is the component the
skill-premium literature already works on, and by rule 0b that is a cell both accounts read
the same way rather than a win for either. Age and gender sit above their floors too and
repeat just as strongly, and that literature does not organise them as one object with
education; this framework predicts an obstruction without naming an attribute, so the three
are read together. It does not predict that education premia vary by position, and should
not be written as though it did.

Education and age are each compressed to three levels, so part of the leftover could be
composition inside a coarse class differing by position rather than pay differing by
position. Gender is not compressed: two levels, with nothing inside them to shift. Its
component sits above its floor and repeats at `+0.9578`, so compression is not the source.

**Both halves of the reading belong in any statement about it.** The additive part is the
larger one: a common ladder accounts for about six tenths. And what it is measured against
is not that the interaction is small, it is that the interaction is identically zero, so
four tenths is a point prediction missing rather than a matter of degree. The leftover
repeats at `+0.95` a year later and `+0.67` a decade later, does not shrink the way sampling
error would, and four position characteristics given their own loading per class account for
about a tenth of it and two per cent when the loadings must be shared.

## B105: what cutting a relation rewrites, read before the cut

**RUN: 2026-09-15; Corollary 43.5 and B105-3 2026-09-16; Corollary 43.6, B105-4 and B105-5 2026-09-16. Statement and proof in `docs/b105_cutting_relations.md`. Checks in
`experiments/b105_cutting_relations.py`, record `results/b105_cutting_relations.json`, which
carries the configuration it ran under. Paper station: zero data. The projection and the graph
helpers are imported from B103.**

B103 reads an action that adds a relation, from the world before it. This station reads the
action that removes one, from the world that still holds it. **What a cut will rewrite is set by
the relation's leverage `h_e = w_e R`, a number the fit already carries for every relation.**

**Theorem 43.** `G` is connected; for `e = (i → j)`, `u = L⁺(e_j − e_i)`, `R` is the effective
resistance and `r_e` the residual the fit leaves on `e`; for a package `F`,
`H_F = W_F^{1/2} B_F L⁺ B_F' W_F^{1/2}`. (1) `0 < h_e ≤ 1`, with `h_e = 1` exactly at a bridge; the
leverages add to `n − 1`, and `h_e` is the probability that a weighted random spanning tree
contains `e`. (2) Cutting a relation that is not a bridge leaves its pair at `ω_e − r_e/(1 − h_e)`,
moves every potential by `−(w_e r_e/(1 − h_e)) u` and lowers `ρ²` by `w_e r_e²/(1 − h_e)`. (3) A
bridge carries no residual, and cutting it moves no level on either side and frees the `|S| · |T|`
levels across it. (4) `det(I − H_F) = τ(G − F)/τ(G)`, the probability that the random spanning tree
avoids `F`, so `I − H_F` is singular exactly when cutting `F` disconnects `G`. (5) Otherwise the
gaps the package leaves are `W_F^{−1/2} (I − H_F)^{−1} W_F^{1/2} r_F`, every potential moves by
`−L⁺ B_F' W_F` times them, and `ρ²` falls by `r_F' W_F` times them, never less than what the
members carried. **Corollary 43.1**: with `D_e` the discrepancy from the graph without `e`,
`r_e = (1 − h_e) D_e` and the cut moves the pair by `−h_e D_e`; read before the action, an addition
rewrites the share `h_e < 1` of what it sees, and a cut rewrites `h_e/(1 − h_e)` times what it sees,
without bound. **Corollary 43.2**: a member's own multiplier in a package is `1/(1 − h'_f)`, with
`h'_f` its leverage after the other members are cut, never below `1/(1 − h_f)`. **Corollary 43.3**:
the rewrite stays inside the blocks that hold the cut relations. **Corollary 43.4**: if the action happens with probability `π`, no single quoted level
beats an expected squared miss of `π(1 − π)` times the square of its rewrite, and only the
probability-weighted middle, a level of neither world, reaches it. **Corollary 43.5**: weakening a
relation to `(1 − κ) w_e` leaves its pair at `ω_e − r_e/(1 − κh_e)`, moves every potential by
`−(κ w_e r_e/(1 − κh_e)) u` and lowers `ρ²` by `κ w_e r_e²/(1 − κh_e)`; the pair moves by less than
`κ/(1 − κ)` times the residual whatever the leverage, so only closing a relation removes the bound. **Corollary 43.6**: moving a relation's term by `Δ`
moves its pair by `h_e Δ`, its residual by `(1 − h_e) Δ`, every potential by `w_e Δ u` and no pair by
more than `h_e |Δ|`; a package's levels move by `W_F^{−1/2} H_F W_F^{1/2} Δ_F`; the share and the move
`m` of a later cut return the residual as `−m (1 − h_e)/h_e`; after a weakening the share is
`(1 − κ)h_e/(1 − κh_e)`. A published change of a term reads the leverage before anything is cut.

**Every criterion passes** at `--seed 105`, on every connected labelled graph on 2 to 6
vertices and on 200 sparse random connected graphs of each of 16, 32 and 64 vertices, B105-3 on the
enumeration and on the random graphs of 16 and 32 vertices. Each closed form is compared with a
second fit after the cut or the weakening, with the error divided by the amplification or by the
norm of `(I − H_F)^{−1}`. B105-4 moves the term of every relation B105-1 cuts, and B105-5 the terms
of every package B105-2 cuts and the share of every relation B105-3 weakens; a moved term changes no
weight, so their closed forms are compared with the tolerance itself, except the residual recovered
from a share and a cut, read divided by the larger of `1/h_e` and `1/(1 − h_e)`.

| | criterion | reading |
|---|---|---|
| PASS | B105-1 `own_reading` one cut | `218,494` cuts in the enumeration (`28,907` bridges) and `37,354` on the random graphs (`2,863`); the leverage calls the bridges with no mismatch; on the other cuts the level, the shift and the fall in `ρ²` match to `1.30e-13` and `7.02e-14` after dividing by the amplification, against a floor of `3.69e-14` and `3.81e-14`; the amplification has median `2.41` and `2.27` and reaches `661` and `459` |
| PASS | B105-2 `own_reading` a package | `798,279` pairs and `14,657` triples in the enumeration and `3,000` packages of 2 to 4 relations on the random graphs; the determinant calls the `208,517` and `785` disconnecting packages with no mismatch; on the `604,419` and `2,215` that leave the graph connected the closed forms match to `1.59e-13` and `4.36e-14` after dividing by the norm, against a floor of `2.75e-14` and `3.13e-14`, and the smallest determinant among them is `3.1e-5` and `4.4e-5` |
| PASS | B105-3 `own_reading` a weakening | `436,988` weakenings in the enumeration (`57,814` of bridges) and `30,938` on the random graphs of 16 and 32 vertices (`2,664`), at `κ = 0.3` and `0.8`; the level, the shift and the fall in `ρ²` match to `1.04e-13` and `4.74e-14` after dividing by `1/(1 − κh_e)`, against a floor of `2.69e-14` and `2.44e-14`; off the bridges the amplification reaches `4.97` and `4.85`, below `1/(1 − κ) = 5` |
| PASS | B105-4 `own_reading` a term moved | `218,494` term moves in the enumeration (`28,907` of bridges) and `37,354` on the random graphs (`2,863`); the level, the residual, the potentials and `ρ²` match to `2.07e-13` and `3.50e-13`, and no pair moves further than `h_e\|Δ\|`, against a floor of `1.74e-14` and `2.52e-14`; on the `189,587` and `34,491` relations that are not bridges the share and the cut return the residual to `2.94e-14` and `2.19e-14` after dividing by the larger of `1/h_e` and `1/(1 − h_e)` |
| PASS | B105-5 `own_reading` package terms and a weakened share | `812,936` packages in the enumeration and `3,000` on the random graphs, terms moved by `0.7` with alternating signs; the members' levels match to `8.18e-14` and `1.32e-14`, and `666,004` and `2,793` packages have interacting members; `436,988` and `30,938` weakened shares match `(1 − κ)h_e/(1 − κh_e)` to `9.19e-14` and `3.93e-14` |

**Every criterion has seeded failures in `--selftest`**, and each seed is asserted to have landed.

**Two things the checks found that the statement did not contain.** Most relations hide more than
they show: `60.7%` of the relations that are not bridges in the enumeration and `57.9%` on the
random graphs have leverage above one half, because the leverages add to `n − 1` and both families
carry fewer than `2(n − 1)` relations on average. And a package is rarely the sum of its members:
`97.7%` and `99.7%` of the packages that leave the graph connected have members that interact, and
`34.7%` and `10.4%` of the disconnecting packages consist only of relations that each have a route
around them.

**Placement.** A: the leverage, the deleted residual and group deletion through `(I − H)^{−1}` are
regression diagnostics (Cook 1977; Belsley, Kuh and Welsch 1980; Cook and Weisberg 1982); the
spanning-tree reading and the matrix-tree theorem are Kirchhoff's (1847), the sum of the leverages
is Foster's theorem (Foster 1949), and the determinant is the avoidance case of the transfer current
theorem (Burton and Pemantle 1993); the same single and group corrections, applied to power flows, are the line outage distribution factors of transmission contingency analysis, singular when outages island the network (Guler, Gross and Liu 2007); changing an observation's weight instead of deleting it is a case-weight perturbation (Cook 1986), and a finite change of weight is again a rank-one update; moving an observation's value moves its own fitted value by its leverage, the hat matrix read as the influence of each observed value on each fitted value (Hoaglin and Welsch 1978). D: that in a price graph a relation's leverage is the share of
weighted backbones through it, one exactly at a bridge, whose cut removes the comparison itself;
that a relation in place shows only the share `1 − h_e` of its discrepancy, so that, read before the
action, a cut rewrites `h_e/(1 − h_e)` times what it can see while an addition rewrites less than
what it can see; that a package disconnects exactly when no weighted backbone avoids it, including
packages of relations that each have a route around them, and otherwise releases its residuals
through `(I − H_F)^{−1}`, each member's own residual weighted as in the last cut of a sequence; that a relation weakened in place rewrites through the same leverage by less than `κ/(1 − κ)` times the residual it shows; that a change of a relation's term passes to its pair's price in the share `h_e`, so that a published change reads the leverage before anything is cut; that before an action that may not happen no single price beats an expected squared miss of
`π(1 − π)` times the square of the rewrite; and
that the rewrite stays inside the blocks that hold the cut relations. **C is empty**, and this
station cannot produce it: it reads no data.

## B111: the 2026 Black Sea cuts on both sides, printed week by week against Theorem 43

Novorossiysk loadings. On each side the interior, the cut port and the route that stayed open sit

interior's weekly change next to the same week of 2025 (Theorem 43 (2)); a fifth object, `e`, is

sources, a broker's weekly report and the grain exchange's daily purchase price page, each with its
own floor. A reading is not read when an end is missing or quoted as nominal, when a Ukrainian port

## B112: where newly created euro area reserves stay, and which rule keeps them in the country they enter

**RUN: 2026-09-16. Scripts `experiments/b112_fetch.py` (ECB Data Portal, 77 requests) and
`experiments/b112_object.py`, record `results/b112_object.json`, which carries the configuration it
ran under. Data `data/b112/raw/`, described in `data/SOURCES.md`.**

The classes are the national components of the Eurosystem. Minimum reserves "shall be held on
reserve accounts, denominated in euro, with the relevant NCBs in each euro area Member State in
which they are established" (Regulation (EU) 2021/378, Article 3(1)(b)), so a unit of reserves sits
in the class whose central bank books it, and a longer-term refinancing dose enters exactly there.
From end-of-month central bank balance sheets, 2016-06 to 2026-07, the station prints each
country's share of euro area reserves around the dated rules that change what holding reserves
pays, and the same-month share of each refinancing dose that stays in the borrowing country. From
annual TARGET payments, 2019 to 2021, it prints how many days of payments to other national
components, and of payments inside the home component, a country's average reserves come to.

| no verdict | `B112-2` `known_answer` the directions ECB Occasional Paper 302 (p. 15) states for the start of the two-tier system read the same way from September to November 2019 | shares: Italy +2.92 pp (z +3.0) and Greece +0.32 pp (z +3.3) as stated, Portugal +0.22 and Slovakia −0.02 within noise; TARGET claims, monthly averages: Germany −42.3, France −15.6, Netherlands −9.5, Belgium −13.9 bn, each in the stated direction and within its two-month noise |
| PASS | `B112-3` `own_reading` the same-month share of a refinancing dose that stays in the borrowing country is higher while holding it pays (TLTRO III special rate period, from 2020-06-24) than under the first TLTRO III terms | median 1.05 over 14 cells against 0.39 over 3; the order is the same at all nine points of the two declared knobs (noise multiple 2, 3, 4; quiet-month cut 10, 20, 40 bn) |
| PASS | `B112-4` `bookkeeping` every rule date and regime boundary names the dated ECB text it was copied from | 11 dates |

`B112-2` reads a country as stated or opposite only at three times its own two-month noise; any
opposite country fails it, one as-stated country per statement passes it, and anything else carries
no verdict. `B112-3` counts a country-month when its dose is at least three times that country's
month-to-month noise in months with little net refinancing, December and January left out.

**Retention of a refinancing dose, by the terms in force at month end.**

| Terms | Cells | Share kept at home (median) | Share out through TARGET (median) |
|---|---|---|---|
| TLTRO II: MRO rate at allotment, as low as the deposit facility rate for banks meeting the lending benchmark (2016-03-10) | 1 | 0.54 | 0.52 |
| TLTRO III as first set: average MRO rate + 10 bp, as low as the average deposit facility rate + 10 bp (2019-06-06); bridge LTROs at the average deposit facility rate from 2020-03-17 (2020-03-12) | 3 | 0.39 | 1.06 |
| Special rate period from 2020-06-24: as low as 50 bp below the average deposit facility rate (2020-04-30), extended to 2022-06-23 (2020-12-10) | 14 | 1.05 | 0.12 |
| Indexed to the average key rates from 2022-11-23, with added repayment dates (2022-10-27) | 18 | 0.78 | 0.15 |

While holding borrowed reserves paid, the dose stayed in the borrowing country: Germany 159.1 bn in
June 2020 with retention 1.08, France 105.3 bn with 1.08, Spain 78.1 bn with 1.38. After the terms
were indexed, repayments came out of the same country's reserves: Italy −145.3 bn in June 2023 with
0.94, France −116.7 bn with 0.98. Under the first TLTRO III terms most of a dose left the borrowing
country within the month (France March 2020 0.79, Greece April 2020 0.08, Greece May 2020 0.39).
The long-run split of reserves across classes follows each class's out-rate, and these terms set
the out-rate of the borrowed units.

**Speed.** When the two-tier system started, Italy's share of euro area reserves went from 4.30% to
7.21% in one month and stayed at 7.22%; Greece's went 0.10%, 0.23%, 0.42%, 0.39%, 0.62% over four
months. Month-to-month noise in a share is 0.94 pp for Germany, 0.93 for France, 0.87 for the
Netherlands and 0.67 for Italy, larger over December and January, and 0.07 to 0.14 pp for Greece,
Portugal and Ireland. For the large classes the adjustment completes inside one month-end
interval, and so does what the payment clocks give: in 2019 Italy's average reserves came to 3.6
days of its payments to other components and 5.1 days of its payments at home. At end-of-month
sampling this carrier bounds the duration from above for those classes.

**Two clocks, 2021** (days of payments to other components against days of payments at home):
Belgium 3.2 and 53.5, Luxembourg 4.7 and 40.6, Estonia 23.5 and 105.6, Germany 5.5 and 3.2, France
7.6 and 7.7, Netherlands 11.1 and 3.6, Italy 16.5 and 22.8, Spain 16.6 and 13.9, Ireland 38.0 and
8.1, Greece 48.3 and 18.8, Cyprus 125.1 and 268.9. The countries where the two clocks disagree are
the ones that would separate a class's cross-border coupling from its own turnover; under terms that
paid nothing for holding, two of their doses clear three times the noise, both Greek (April and May
2020).

No `rival` is registered. On the split, the corridor attribution in ECB Occasional Paper 196 and
the tiering flows in Occasional Paper 302 point the same way as this reading; on the duration of
reserves across national components, no point prediction in the opposite direction is on record.

## B113: the discount window edge, and where banks with and without it pay for overnight fed funds against the posted rate

**RUN: 2026-09-16. Scripts `experiments/b113_dw_loans.py` (the Federal Reserve's discount window loan
files, 56 quarterly workbooks from 2010Q3 to 2024Q2, fetched by `scripts/fetch_dw_lending.py`) and
`experiments/b113_discount_window.py`, records `results/b113_discount_window.json` (the criteria and the
readings behind them) and `results/b113_after_2020.json` (the years after 2020Q1 in stretches and year by
year, under each filter), each carrying the configuration it ran under. Sources in `data/SOURCES.md`.**

The position is overnight borrowing by a depository institution, and its price is the size arm's
RC-K reading: the quarter's expense on fed funds purchased over their quarterly average, with repo
absent at both quarter ends. The posted price is the primary credit rate, which 12 CFR 201.4(a)
extends "as a backup source of funding to a depository institution that is in generally sound
financial condition in the judgment of the Reserve Bank". The class is read from the loans. A loan
names its borrower by ABA routing number and each quarter's panel of reporters carries every filer's
number, so a loan joins to a filer through the panel of the quarter it was made in. Two writings of
the class are read together: ever, a primary credit loan between 2010Q3 and 2024Q2, and near, one
within four quarters either side of the quarter read.

Inside each size band and quarter the filers are cut by the rank of their assets into 1, 2 and 4
pieces. In each piece the station takes the share paying above the quarter's mean primary credit
rate outside the class minus inside it, weights the piece by 1/(1/n outside + 1/n inside), and pools
the three bands below $10 billion. The same difference is read in log odds, each count moved by a
half (Haldane 1956; Anscombe 1956), which is not capped the way a share is. Standard errors
resample filers whole, 4,000 draws under each of two seeds. From 2010Q1 to 2019Q4 a verdict on the
rival rests on all twelve readings at once (two writings, three cuts, two scales): every one past two
of its own standard errors, every one past minus two, or neither. From 2020Q2 to 2024Q2 the rival is
read in three stretches, one criterion each (2020Q2 to 2021Q4, 2022, 2023Q1 to 2024Q2), on the
members that had used the window by the quarter read and on the readings the instrument decides, and
a verdict rests on the six readings of a stretch (three cuts, two scales). Both terms are set out
below the table.

| | Criterion | Reading |
|---|---|---|
| PASS | `B113-1` `instrument` every loan in the parsed files is counted once, joined to a filer or not joined under one named reason | 68,454 loans, 52,389 joined; not joined: credit unions by name 14,212, numbers that name a filer only in another quarter's panel 392, numbers in no panel 1,461 |
| PASS | `B113-2` `known_answer` every primary credit loan carries the primary credit rate of its day, or of a day within two calendar days where a Reserve Bank's effective date differs from New York's | 57,524 on the day, 11 within two days, 0 neither |
| PASS | `B113-3` `rival` 2010Q1 to 2019Q4, banks below $10 billion: outside minus inside the class, the share paying above the posted rate is not zero | twelve readings from 3.36 to 4.17 se, all positive; grid B |
| no verdict | `B113-4a` `rival` 2020Q2 to 2021Q4, banks below $10 billion: outside the class minus its members that had used the window by the quarter read, on the readings the instrument decides, the share paying above the posted rate is not zero | six readings from −0.09 to +0.64 se; 63 filer-quarters outside the class remain |
| no verdict | `B113-4b` `rival` 2022, the same | six readings from +0.54 to +0.89 se |
| PASS | `B113-4c` `rival` 2023Q1 to 2024Q2, the same | six readings from 2.49 to 3.00 se, all positive; grid B |
| no verdict | `B113-5` `own_reading` the class difference moves with the rate: at the height over the effective federal funds rate where the rate stood from 2011Q3 to 2019Q4, and at the height where it stood from 2023Q1 to 2024Q2, the difference is larger in the span when the rate stood there | twelve readings from −1.11 to +0.56 se |
| PASS | `B113-6` `instrument` each seed's standard errors alone put `B113-3`, `B113-4a` to `B113-4c` and `B113-5` in the same state | above; no verdict, no verdict, above; no verdict under both seeds |

`instrument` 2 pass · `known_answer` 1 pass · `rival` 2 pass 2 no verdict · `own_reading` 1 no verdict

The rival is one price at the position with the posted rate as its cap for every sound institution.
Under it no sound bank pays more than the rate except through the instrument's own noise, and that
noise does not depend on whether the bank has borrowed at the window, so the difference is zero. The
framework reads the cap as holding along the edge that exists, so the difference is positive.

**The readings, pooled below $10 billion, finest cut.**

| writing | 2010Q1 to 2019Q4 | 2020Q2 to 2024Q2 |
|---|---|---|
| ever, share | +0.068 (3.71 se) | +0.035 (1.90 se) |
| ever, log odds | +0.289 (3.68 se) | +0.180 (1.99 se) |
| near, share | +0.073 (3.46 se) | +0.055 (2.24 se) |
| near, log odds | +0.317 (3.36 se) | +0.301 (2.54 se) |

Inside the class the share above the rate is 0.473 (ever) and 0.406 (near)
in the first span and 0.686 and 0.673 in the second: the instrument's floor rises as the
cap comes down, which is why every reading is also taken in log odds.

**Printed next to the verdict, on the same readings (share and log odds, finest cut, in se).**

| instrument | ever, first span | near, first span | ever, second span | near, second span |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| fed funds held at both quarter ends (4,950 filer-quarters in the first span) | 2.02 and 1.94 | 1.91 and 0.89 | 0.69 and 0.87 | 0.00 and 0.25 |
| filer-quarters within four quarters of a secondary credit loan left out | 3.77 and 3.74 | 3.43 and 3.32 | 1.79 and 1.91 | 2.19 and 2.49 |
| 2014Q1 to 2019Q4 only | 3.44 and 3.41 | 3.79 and 3.65 | | |

Secondary credit goes to institutions not eligible for primary credit, so the second row reads the
first span and the second with those institutions away; the third reads the years after the FDIC's list
of problem institutions had fallen to a fraction of its 2010 length.

**After 2020Q1, in stretches.** The years after the rate came down to the top of the target range
read differently from each other. Three objects, two of the instrument and one of the class, set them
apart.

1. *The instrument's step.* The arm admits a quarter only with a positive expense, and expense is filed
   in thousands, so where one thousand dollars of expense on a filer's average balance already exceeds
   the rate, the filer reads above it whatever it paid. With the rate at 0.25 percent, from 2020Q2 to
   2021Q4, that holds for 76.6 percent of the filer-quarters outside the class and 37.6 percent inside
   it. The readings the instrument decides leave 63 filer-quarters outside.
2. *The rounding.* A quarter's expense after the first is the difference of two year-to-date figures,
   each filed in whole thousands, and the average is filed the same way. A reading is decided where
   every price those bounds allow lies on one side of the rate. From 2024Q3 to 2026Q2, where average
   balances are the smallest in the sample, 59 percent of the readings outside the class and 48
   percent inside are undecided.
3. *Members counted before their first loan.* Under ever, a bank that first borrowed in 2023 is in
   the class in 2022. Those banks paid above the rate more often than banks that never borrowed:
   outside minus them reads −0.119 (−3.04 se) in 2022, against +0.025 (1.00 se) from 2015 to 2019.
   The stretches count a member from its first primary credit loan on.

| stretch | criterion | share, cuts 1, 2, 4 (se) | log odds, cuts 1, 2, 4 (se) | filer-quarters outside / inside |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2020Q2 to 2021Q4 | `B113-4a` | +0.093, +0.031, −0.014 (0.64, 0.20, −0.09) | +0.355, +0.176, +0.053 (0.62, 0.32, 0.10) | 63 / 248 |
| 2022 | `B113-4b` | +0.043, +0.040, +0.029 (0.86, 0.76, 0.54) | +0.207, +0.197, +0.140 (0.89, 0.82, 0.57) | 403 / 362 |
| 2023Q1 to 2024Q2 | `B113-4c` | +0.093, +0.086, +0.089 (3.00, 2.73, 2.79) | +0.405, +0.380, +0.381 (2.89, 2.64, 2.49) | 1,202 / 994 |

On the same terms, at the finest cut, 2015 to 2019 reads +0.127 (4.68 se) and 2011Q3 to 2014 reads
+0.079 (1.60 se). Past the end of the loan data, where a first loan cannot be seen, 2024Q3 to 2026Q2
reads +0.075 (1.72 se) under ever on the readings the instrument decides. Within 2022, the rate
moved inside every quarter; keeping only prices above the quarter's highest rate or at or below its
lowest leaves the stretch flat as well (+0.025, 0.59 se).

The numbers in this subsection outside the table are in `results/b113_after_2020.json`, with the
objects behind them, the same readings year by year, and every filter read on the arm of every row
and on the arm whose two quarter-end balances sit near the quarterly average.

**The difference at the rate's two heights.** From 2011Q3 to 2019Q4 the primary credit rate stood,
in quarter means, 62.1 basis points over the effective federal funds rate; from 2023Q1 to 2024Q2 it
stood 17.0 over it, a shift of 45.1 basis points. `B113-5` reads the class difference at both heights
in both spans, on the members that had used the window by the quarter read and on the readings the
instrument decides at each height. In the span where the rate stood at a height, that height is the
quarter's own mean rate; in the other span it is that rate moved by the shift. A difference made by the
rate standing at a height is larger there in the span when it stood there.

| height over the effective rate | 2011Q3 to 2019Q4 | 2023Q1 to 2024Q2 | the span the rate stood there minus the other |
|---|---|---|---|
| 17.0 bp, where the rate stood from 2023Q1 | +0.125 (3.00 se) | +0.089 (2.81 se) | −0.037 (−0.73 se) |
| 62.1 bp, where the rate stood to 2019Q4 | +0.113 (4.27 se) | +0.107 (3.36 se) | +0.006 (0.16 se) |

Finest cut, share of prices above the height. The twelve readings `B113-5` rests on run from −1.11 to
+0.56 se. The class difference holds at both heights in both spans, from 2.81 to 4.27 se, at nearly the
same size whether the rate stood there or 45 basis points away: the banks that had used the window
paid less along the whole range read, and the height of the posted rate does not add to that at this
resolution. The readings are in the `crossed` block of `results/b113_discount_window.json`.

**What a loan at the window looks like.** The amount that recurs most among the 41,890 joined
primary credit loans is 1,000 dollars (7,880 loans, 94 percent of them overnight).
712 of the 2,885 class members never borrowed more, and 632 of those had pledged collateral
worth at least a thousandth of their assets. Outside minus the half of the class that borrowed more
reads 3.58 to 4.07 se in the first span and 2.25 to 2.96 in the second; outside minus the
half never above 1,000 dollars reads 1.66 to 2.19 and 0.13 to 0.83. The difference sits
with the banks that used the edge.

**The band at $10 billion and over** has 0 filers outside the class in its thinnest quarter
(2015Q4) and one filer outside it from 2020Q2 on. It is printed and does not enter the pooled cell.

## B114: how long new money stays in the area it enters, and which clock sets it

**RUN: 2026-09-16. Script `experiments/b114_sarafu.py`, record `results/b114_sarafu.json`, which carries
the configuration it ran under. Data: the Sarafu transaction archive, UK Data Service ReShare record
855142, described in `data/SOURCES.md`.**

Sarafu was a digital community currency used in Kenya from January 2020 to June 2021 (Mattsson,
Criscione and Ruddick, Scientific Data 9, 426, 2022). Every transfer is on file with a timestamp, new
currency is marked as a disbursement, and every account carries an area. The station follows each
month's disbursements into each area through every later transfer, with each wallet's balance treated
as well mixed, and reads the share still in the entry area among that money still in circulation, week
by week. Beside it run two class chains built from the same end-of-day balances and quarterly spending
rates: in the network chain each area's payments land where they did, and in the one-pool chain each
payment lands across areas in proportion to what each area receives. Each area also has two clocks:
days of balance against all its transfers out, and against its transfers to other areas.

| | Criterion | Reading |
|---|---|---|
| PASS | `B114-1` `instrument` the archive passes its reading checks, the tag pass conserves value, and the demurrage and cash-out totals the data descriptor states come back from the transfers to the Sarafu | demurrage reclaimed 2021-02-01 to 2021-02-03, 352,834.00 against 352,834; cash-out, 6,172,074.95 against 6,172,075; tagged value conserved to 1.4e-07. Printed without a verdict: the balance of all accounts except admin accounts, 19,414,222.25 against 19,419,736; balances rebuilt from the flows match the users table for 54,883 wallets and differ for 83, by at most 1,000 |
| PASS | `B114-2` `rival` the one-pool chain misses the range of the observed entry-area share across monthly cohorts, area by area and age by age, at every setting of the station's knobs | 55 cells: the one-pool chain outside the range at all 18 settings in 41; inside it with the network chain outside in 0; both inside in 1 (Kilifi at 0 weeks); not read in 13. Placed in the grid: A 1, B 1, both_unmet 22 |
| PASS | `B114-3` `own_reading` the observed share sits nearer the network chain than the one-pool chain, the whole cohort range on one side of their midpoint | 55 cells: nearer the network chain 37, nearer the one-pool chain 0, moving with a knob 15, across the midpoint 3 |
| PASS | `B114-4` `rival` the rival's strongest chain, every wallet at its own spending speed with payments landing across wallets by what each receives, misses the range of the observed entry-area share across monthly cohorts, area by area and age by age, at every setting of the station's knobs; ours is the wallet chain on each wallet's own payees | 55 cells: the rival's wallet chain outside the range at all 18 settings in 43; inside it with ours outside in 0; both inside in 0; not read in 12. Placed in the grid: B 38; in 5 more the rival misses while our wallet chain moves with a knob (Kisauni Mombasa, 0 to 8 weeks, where the cohort range is 0.4 to 0.7 points wide) |

A cell is an area at an age that at least three monthly cohorts reach; a cohort is at least 10,000
Sarafu disbursed into one area in one month, and the label `other`, which the users table gives
accounts with no area, is not read. Each cell is read at 18 settings of three knobs: the smallest
cohort (5,000, 10,000 or 20,000), the day the chains start (the entry month's first day, 15 days before
its end, or its end), and the window their rates come from (a quarter or a half-year). Each chain's
position against the range is settled over the 18 settings on its own, and a position that differs
between settings is not read. `B114-2` counts a cell toward PASS when the one-pool chain is outside the
range, and toward FAIL when the one-pool chain is inside and the network chain outside (grid C); it
passes when every counted cell counts toward PASS, fails when every counted cell is C, and otherwise
carries no verdict. A cell enters the grid only where both chains are settled. The rival, as scored: a
sum of money that leaves its holder leaves the group the holder is in, and how long it stays is set by
how fast the holder spends; so new money's excess share in its entry area decays at the holding period,
and the one-pool chain built from each area's own balance and turnover is that trajectory.

**Two clocks, whole period.**

| Area | Wallets | Days of balance, all transfers out | Days of balance, transfers to other areas | Paid within the area | Share of all transfer value received |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Mukuru Nairobi | 10,107 | 11.1 | 120.2 | 90.8% | 60.2% |
| Kinango Kwale | 23,668 | 37.7 | 612.4 | 93.8% | 31.7% |
| Misc Nairobi | 5,257 | 35.6 | 52.4 | 31.9% | 6.9% |
| Nyanza | 641 | 49.0 | 272.6 | 82.0% | 0.6% |
| Kilifi | 908 | 89.0 | 173.9 | 48.8% | 0.3% |
| Kisauni Mombasa | 6,119 | 114.7 | 1,905.8 | 94.0% | 0.2% |

Holding periods measured on the same data by unit-level tracing (Mattsson, Luedtke and Takes 2022,
arXiv 2209.01512, Table 1) are shorter: Nairobi 0.66 weeks, Kinango Kwale 2.74, Kilifi 2.57, Mombasa
3.54. The balance clocks here count balances that do not move.

**Retention.** Share of new money still in its entry area, among that money still in circulation.

| Area | Cohorts | 13 weeks | 52 weeks (lowest to highest cohort) | Network chain, 52 weeks | One-pool chain, 52 weeks |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Kinango Kwale | 18 | 99.5% | 98.2% (97.1 to 99.2) | 93.5% | 53.3% |
| Mukuru Nairobi | 17 | 93.8% | 91.8% (79.1 to 93.0) | 66.8% | 32.3% |
| Misc Nairobi | 16 | 75.3% | 62.9% (45.8 to 91.4) | 18.9% | 9.3% |
| Nyanza | 13 | 95.2% | 77.8% (73.8 to 81.7) | 15.6% | 1.7% |
| Kilifi | 12 | 93.5% | 57.1% (44.6 to 77.3) | 10.6% | 1.9% |

Of the new money in Kinango Kwale, 97.3% has been paid on at least once by 52 weeks, 5.0 times on
average, and 98.1% of that money is still in Kinango Kwale; in Mukuru Nairobi, 92.5%, 18.8 times, and
91.1%. Where one payment lands in an area in proportion to what the area receives, those shares would
be 31.7% and 60.2%. The network chain treats an area's balances as one pool leaving at the area's
average rate to other areas; new money leaves more slowly than that, most of all in the small areas.

**Where money that leaves lands first, and whether the first stop passes it on.** In the first week
after the entry month, of the money that has left Misc Nairobi, 93.5% is in Mukuru Nairobi and 4.5% in
Kinango Kwale (network chain 95.1% and 2.6%, one-pool chain 47.3% and 51.1%); of the money that has left
Mukuru Nairobi, 94.6% is in Misc Nairobi and 3.4% in Kinango Kwale (90.8% and 4.7%; 21.8% and 75.8%).
Kinango Kwale's share of that money grows to 15.4% and 11.7% after a year. Mukuru Nairobi, which spends
in 11 days and pays 90.8% within itself, takes 97.7% of what Misc Nairobi pays other areas. The share of
Misc Nairobi's new money that has gone beyond Mukuru Nairobi to a third area:

| Weeks | Observed (lowest to highest cohort) | Network chain | Entry area as it paid, every other area as one pool | One-pool chain |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 4 | 1.7% | 3.8% | 30.9% | 42.8% |
| 13 | 1.9% (0.2 to 6.0) | 6.3% | 45.9% | 54.0% |
| 52 | 7.2% (2.3 to 10.2) | 14.1% | 54.7% | 58.2% |

For Nyanza, whose first stop is also Mukuru Nairobi, the same shares at 13 weeks are 1.7% (0.1 to 11.8),
9.1%, 19.3% and 59.0%.

**Rules.** The 2% monthly demurrage reads in the data: in February, April and May 2021 the five main
areas lost 1.9% to 2.2% of their balance in the month, charged on the first to third day; the March
charge was 130,703 Sarafu, a third of April's or May's. The October 2020 reclamation from long-inactive
accounts took 20% (Nyanza) to 76% (Kilifi) of that month's balance. After the demurrage began, spending
did not speed up: the spending clock of Kinango Kwale went from 18.6 days in October 2020 to 87.8 in
February 2021 and 249 in March, Mukuru Nairobi's from 7.8 to 51.0 and 77.8. Across entry months the two
clocks mostly move together; in Nyanza they separate. For the cohorts that entered from April to December
2020, the spending clock over the 13 weeks after entry stays between 32 and 43 days (60 in October),
the clock to other areas goes from 54 days to between 1,183 and 1,755, the share still in Nyanza at 13
weeks goes from between 64.7% and 89.0% (April to August) to between 98.7% and 99.0% (September to
December), and the one-pool chain stays between 5.5% and 9.7%.

**The chains wallet by wallet.** The same chains run over the 54,957 wallets in circulation, with each
wallet's spending speed taken from itself or from its area, and its payees taken from its own
counterparties, from its area's mix of destinations (landing on wallets by what each receives inside
the area), or from the whole network by what each wallet receives. The two chains with the area's speed
and the area's or the network's destinations are block 5's chains by construction; run, they differ from
them by at most 2.5e-14 and 4.5e-14. Share still in the entry area at 52 weeks, in percent:

| Area | Observed | Own speed, own payees | Own speed, area mix | Area speed, own payees | Area speed, area mix (network chain) | Own speed, by receipts | Area speed, by receipts (one-pool chain) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Kinango Kwale | 98.2 | 98.3 | 93.7 | 97.9 | 93.5 | 55.5 | 53.3 |
| Mukuru Nairobi | 91.8 | 90.4 | 69.0 | 70.6 | 66.8 | 37.6 | 32.3 |
| Misc Nairobi | 62.9 | 58.4 | 26.3 | 28.0 | 18.9 | 17.4 | 9.3 |
| Nyanza | 77.8 | 77.5 | 35.7 | 47.3 | 15.6 | 19.5 | 1.7 |
| Kilifi | 57.1 | 56.3 | 29.8 | 18.0 | 10.6 | 17.7 | 1.9 |

The tagging follows the same well-mixed rule wallet by wallet with exact timing, so the first chain
column says that quarterly wallet rates are enough. In Kinango Kwale the wallets' own payees alone bring
the network chain to the observed share; in the other four areas neither half does and both together do:
the wallets that receive new money spend more slowly than their area and pay nearer counterparties,
and their coupling to the wallets that pay outside the area is thin. With each holder at its own
spending speed and payments landing by receipts, the chain rises 2 to 18 points above the one-pool
chain and stays 39 to 58 points below the observed share.

## B110: A-share placements, the edge they open to one class, what crosses it, and what the price leaves over the most a lock can be worth

**RUN: 2026-09-16; offerings priced in advance split 2026-09-17. Scripts `experiments/b110_fetch.py` (offering, unlock-batch and holder tables, and daily bars) and
`experiments/b110_placements.py`, record `results/b110_placements.json`, which carries the configuration it ran under.
Data `data/raw/b110/`, described in `data/SOURCES.md`.**

A company listed in Shanghai or Shenzhen can sell new shares to at most 35 investors of its choosing: a private
placement, from 2023 an issue to specific objects. The edge into those shares at the issue price is open to that class
only. The rules in force on the bid day T set the rest. From 2020-02-14 the price is at least 80% of the average price
over the 20 trading days before the base date, and the shares are locked for 6 months, or for 18 when the holder is one
the rules name (a controlling shareholder or a party it controls, an investor who gains control through the issue, a
strategic investor the board brings in); from 2017-02-15 to 2020-02-13 the figures are 90%, 12 months and 36. The
station reads the 2,925 offerings in the offering table with T on or after 2017-02-15: 1,771 priced by bids
(`网下询价配售`), for most of which the base date is the first day of the offering period, two trading days before T;
1,136 priced in advance (`网下定价发行`), which hold both cash placements at a price fixed on a resolution date and issues paying for assets with new shares; and 18 mergers. To each it joins the holder rows of the unlock
batches, whose lock month is the class the rules gave the holder, and the stock's daily bars. With P the issue price, Pm
the close on T, H the day's high, n the shares issued and N the shares before the issue, the issue hands its new holders
n N (Pm − P) / (N + n), the discount is d = 1 − P / Pm, and Longstaff's bound LB(σ, ℓ) (Journal of Finance 50, 1995,
1767-1774) is the most a lock of ℓ years can be worth to a holder who could time a sale perfectly, with ℓ from T to the unlock.

`B110-1` takes the states in order and stops at the first that holds: the smallest k from 0 to 10 with
P ≥ floor × VWAP20(T−k) − 0.01; a split between T and listing; a base date the pricing text writes; the one-day
average; the last yuan price the text prints, as it stands and less the cash dividends of the year before T. An
offering none of these explains is unclassified and fails the criterion; one without a price or volume carries no
verdict. VWAP20 as of a day is the amount over the volume of the 20 days the stock traded before it, each day taken in
the price basis of T through the exchange's adjustment factors, since the rules price a day before a split or dividend
at its adjusted price. Before 2017-02-15 only the table is read: 922 offerings print a floor, 853 are at or above it and
69 below it, with no verdict. `B110-3` joins a batch to the offering whose listing date plus the lock month lands from 3
days before to 20 days after the unlock, does not choose between two offerings that fit equally, and moves groups or
rows between offerings only where the shares add up exactly in one way with no split in between. `B110-5` reads a cell
only where the sign of d − LB is the same under the four volatilities. `B110-4` puts an offering priced in advance
in the table when its pricing text reads as a cash placement and the offering table prints net proceeds below gross.
An issue paying for assets prices its shares under the reorganisation rules (a market reference price, a counterparty,
the assets bought) and matching funds are raised in cash. Each set of words turns up in the other's text, so the word
that comes first decides, and a text naming the asset part first and the matching funds after prices both parts
without saying which one its row is. Net below gross is an issuance cost taken out of cash: 1,769 of the 1,771 bid
offerings print it, and 565 of the 587 texts that read as an issue paying for assets print net equal to gross. The record carries every number to six
significant digits, and the tables below are computed from it.

## B115: China's 2018 tariff on US soybeans, and the share of the step that reached Dalian against the Gulf

**RUN: 2026-09-17. Station document `docs/b115_soy_tariff.md`. Scripts `experiments/b115_soy_fetch.py`,
`experiments/b115_soy_describe.py` and `experiments/b115_soy_step.py`; records
`results/b115_soy_describe.json` and `results/b115_soy_step.json`, which carry the configuration they ran
under. Sources and caliber in `data/SOURCES.md`.**

On 2018-07-06 China's additional tariff on US yellow soybeans went from nothing to 25% over a 3% rate, a
term move of Δ = ln(1.28/1.03) = 0.2173 on the relation from the Gulf to Dalian. Corollary 43.6
(`docs/b105_cutting_relations.md`) gives Dalian against the Gulf the share `h_e` of it, and by Theorem 42
Paranaguá's move against the Gulf lies between 0 and that share. The station averages the Gulf bid, the
Dalian No. 2 soybean settlement on traded days, the Paranaguá indicator and the yuan over a plateau
before the step and one after it, in four settings, and sets each move against the median move over
window pairs of the same shape in 2016 to 2020 that span no dated soybean tariff document. The yuan
moved in the same weeks, so Dalian is read at the market rate and at the pre-plateau rate, and the
tariff's part of each leg is read as an interval.

| | Criterion | Reading |
|---|---|---|
| PASS | `B115-1` `instrument` every week of both plateaus, in every setting, has a Gulf bid, a Paranaguá day, a yuan day and a day the chosen No. 2 soybean contract traded | four settings, b1809, no week missing |
| PASS | `B115-2` `instrument` no placebo window pair spans a dated soybean tariff document, and every setting has placebo pairs for both legs | 131, 131, 182 and 182 pairs kept |
| PASS | `B115-3` `own_reading` the six moves are printed in every setting against their placebo floors | Paranaguá against the Gulf +0.1376 (floor 0.0406), Dalian against the Gulf +0.1030 at the market rate and +0.1592 at the pre-plateau rate, Dalian against Paranaguá −0.0346 and +0.0216, the yuan +0.0541, setting A |
| PASS | `B115-4` `own_reading` the tariff moved Paranaguá up against the Gulf | matches in all four settings: [+0.138, +0.192], [+0.117, +0.162], [+0.137, +0.188], [+0.116, +0.158] against floors 0.041, 0.042, 0.022, 0.020 |
| no verdict | `B115-5` `own_reading` the tariff's part of Dalian against Paranaguá is at least 0 | within the floor in all four settings |
| PASS | `B115-6` `own_reading` the interval for `h_e` | 0.633 to 0.733, 0.539 to 0.695, 0.630 to 0.745, 0.536 to 0.708 |
| PASS | `B115-7` `known_answer` Paranaguá minus the Gulf, late June to late November 2018, against Adjemian, Smith and He (2021)'s +1.71 $/bu | +1.591 $/bu, ratio 0.93 |

The low end of `h_e` comes from Paranaguá in every setting, the leg that does not pass through the yuan.
The floors of settings A and B rest on five separate stretches of 2016 to 2020, those of C and D on
sixteen. The tariff steps of 2019-09-01 (+0.0383) and 2020-02-14 (−0.0190) carry no reading here: their
largest effect is the size of the narrowest floors. The station's sorghum branch is read in the next section.

## B115: China's 2018 deposit on US sorghum and its end, read against Gulf corn

**RUN: 2026-09-17. Station document `docs/b115_sorghum_deposit.md`. Script `experiments/b115_sorghum_step.py`;
record `results/b115_sorghum_step.json`, which carries the configuration it ran under; the transcribed
tables in `data/b115_sorghum_fob.json`, with sources and caliber in `data/SOURCES.md`.**

From 2018-04-18 importers of US sorghum paid a deposit of 178.6%, and on 2018-05-18 China ended the
investigations and refunded the deposits. Both steps touch only the relation from US sorghum to China, so
by Theorem 42 and Corollary 43.6 (`docs/b105_cutting_relations.md`) sorghum falls against every other
position at the deposit and rises back at its end. The plateau before the deposit lies inside the
investigation opened on 2018-02-04, where a forward quote can already carry part of the deposit, so the
two steps together are at least 0 (Corollary 43.1). The station reads NOLA and Texas sorghum against Gulf
corn in the US Grains Council's weekly FOB tables, chaining the levels over the delivery months two issues
share, over plateaus in four settings, and sets each move against the median move over windows of the
same shape from 2016 to January 2018.

## B117: how coarse the classes of a payment chain can be and still read how long new money stays in its area

**RUN: 2026-09-17. Script `experiments/b117_partition_grain.py`, which imports `experiments/b114_sarafu.py`; record
`results/b117_partition_grain.json`, which carries the configuration it ran under. Data: the Sarafu archive read by
B114, described in `data/SOURCES.md`.**

B114 follows each month's new Sarafu into the area it entered and reads the share still there, week by week. A chain
run wallet by wallet, each wallet at its own quarterly spending speed and paying its own counterparties, reads that
share back; the same chain run on whole areas reads it low, at 52 weeks by up to 62 points. This station runs the
chain on classes between those two ends. The state stays wallet by wallet, and a wallet's spending speed and the
landing of its payments come from its class: what a class pays lands across classes in the class's mix of destination
classes, and inside a class by what each wallet receives. With areas as the classes the chain is B114's area chain;
with single wallets it is B114's wallet chain.

| | Criterion | Reading |
|---|---|---|
| PASS | `B117-1` `instrument` classes = areas and classes = single wallets give B114's recorded area and wallet chains on its cells, the chain on class balances equals the wallet chain summed into classes, every partition stays inside its areas and every random partition keeps its reference's class sizes, and the tag pass conserves value | largest difference from B114's record, which prints nine significant figures: 5.0e-10, at three settings that between them take every value of every knob; class balances against wallets, 4.1e-15; tagged value conserved to 1.4e-07 |
| PASS | `B117-2` `rival` the chain on area x business type cells misses the range of the observed entry-area share across monthly cohorts, area by area and age by age, at every setting of the station's knobs; ours is the chain on the circles of payments inside each area | 55 cells: the area x business type chain outside the range at all 18 settings in 20; inside it with the circle chain outside in 0; both inside in 6 (Kilifi from 0 to 8 weeks, Mukuru Nairobi at 1 week); not read in 29. Placed in the grid: A 6, B 17, both_unmet 1 (Kisauni Mombasa at 8 weeks, where the cohort range is 0.6 points wide). The circle chain is inside the range at every setting and seed in 41 cells |
| PASS | `B117-3` `own_reading` the observed share sits nearer the chain on the circles than the chain on random classes with the circles' sizes, the whole cohort range on one side of their midpoint, at every setting and seed | 55 cells: nearer the circles 5, nearer the random classes 0, across the midpoint 31, moving with a knob or a seed 19 |

The cells and knobs are B114's: an area at an age that at least three monthly cohorts of 10,000 Sarafu or more reach,
read at 18 settings of the smallest cohort, the day the chains start and the window their rates come from. `B117-2`
and `B117-3` read the circles at Louvain resolution 10 with seeds 0, 1 and 2, and each seed against random classes
with that seed's class sizes, so each cell is read 54 times; a position that differs between readings is not read.
`B117-2` counts a cell toward PASS when the area x business type chain is outside the range, and toward FAIL when it
is inside and the circle chain outside; it passes when every counted cell counts toward PASS. The rival, as scored:
inside one area the wallets of one business type are interchangeable, each spending at the speed of its area and
business type together and paying across area-and-business-type cells in that cell's mix of destinations; so the chain
on those cells gives the entry area's share of new money week by week.

In the three large areas the business types read the share about as well as random classes of the same sizes, and the

Cutting each circle into its slower and faster half moves the three large areas by -8 to +7 points.

## B120: the locked placement price as an option one class holds, read against the price path from the resolution date to the end

**RUN: 2026-09-17. Scripts `experiments/b120_fetch.py` (the announcement census, the agreement and adjustment PDFs, the
placement filings), `experiments/b120_plans.py` (the documents read, and the announcements joined into plans and ends),
`experiments/b120_bars.py` (each plan's window of daily bars, added to the B110 store) and
`experiments/b120_readings.py`, record `results/b120_readings.json`, which carries the configuration it ran under.
Data `data/raw/b120/` and `data/raw/b110/daily_baostock/stock/`, described in `data/SOURCES.md`.**

B110 reads the edge a private placement opens to at most 35 investors of the company's choosing. This station reads
one class of that edge along time. From 2020-02-14 a company whose board fixes every subscriber in advance, all of them
of the three kinds the rules name, may take the board or shareholder resolution day as the base date, so the price is
set there and the shares are issued months or years later, at a price no lower than 80% of the average price over the
20 days the stock traded before that day. B110 treated the lock as a forward, its gain or loss the price path's own; if
the named subscriber can leave when the stock falls below it, the lock is instead a call option written to that class
alone, and B110-4's column counts the ones exercised. The station reads every locked plan from 2020-02-14 to the data
end 2026-09-16 and every end each plan reached: issued, ended, moved to first-day pricing, re-locked, still pending, or
the stock delisted under it. With P the locked price carried through the dividends and splits after the base date by
the agreements' own formula, Pm the close of the last day the stock traded before the end, M = Pm / P, n the shares the
plan's own documents cap it at and N the shares before the issue, a plan that did not issue would have handed its
subscriber n N (Pm - P) / (N + n), the same transfer B110-4 reads on the issues that did happen.

| | Criterion | Reading |
