**Arm B: did a TAF auction clear above the discount window's posted rate?** RUN 2026-09-22, script
`experiments/b121_b_taf_cap.py`, record `results/b121_b_taf_cap.json`. The TAF and the window are two edges
from one lender to one set of borrowers against one collateral pool: the TAF was open only to institutions
eligible for primary credit. One price at the position bounds every auction's stop-out rate by the primary
credit rate, since an eligible bank can borrow at that rate on demand. The reading is a count and a list. A
window term loan floats with the posted rate ("the new rate will apply on and after the effective date of the
change") and a TAF loan is fixed for its term, so two of the declared bounds allow for that: the posted rate
plus the whole three-month expected rise (three-month OIS minus the target, from the rival's workbook, to
2008-08-08), and the posted rate averaged over the loan's term.

| | Criterion | Reading |
|---|---|---|
| PASS | `B121-24` `instrument` the loan file groups into 60 auctions with one rate each, and each has a posted rate under every bound | 60 auctions, 2007-12-20 to 2010-03-11 |
| PASS | `B121-25` `rival` at least one auction cleared above the posted rate, under every declared bound | settle 15, bid 15, highest 15, expected rise 9, realised 19; grid B |

Above every bound: 2008-03-27 (`+11.5` bp), 2008-04-10 (`+32.0`), 2008-04-24 (`+37.0`), the 84-day auction of
2008-08-14 (`+46.5` over the expected-rise bound) and 2008-09-25 (`+150.0`; `+176.8` over the realised
average). The June and July 2008 auctions sit `+0.4` to `+4.8` bp over the expected-rise bound, and one of
them (2008-06-19) `-5.0` under it. What this reads against is one price at the position, as `B113` does; an
account that adds a cost of using the window as a friction is separated from this framework only by the ratio
of Corollary 6.1 of `docs/b4_directed_edges.md`, which this arm does not read.

Cell three: was the Term Auction Facility big enough to reach the marginal borrower
(`experiments/b121_taf_cover.py`, `results/b121_taf_cover.json`). The Board's results release for each of the
60 auctions prints the offering, total bids, accepted bids, bid/cover and the stop-out; each announcement prints
the per-institution maximum award (10% of the offering) and the minimum bid rate. `B121-26` (instrument) PASS:
all 60 parse and every printed bid/cover equals bids over offering. `B121-27` (own reading) PASS. All 19 auctions
to 2008-08-08 were oversubscribed, and each of the five capacity increases followed a full auction, with $15.6 to
$38.3 billion of bids left unfilled. From December 2007 to April 2008 ($20 to $50 billion per auction), 3 to 5
banks took the maximum award every time (30% to 50% of the offering) and the auction's own price over OIS (25 to
85 bp) tracked LIBOR-OIS, leaving `-11.0` to `+29.1` bp between them. From May to July 2008 ($75 billion), 0 to 3
banks were at the cap, the auction price fell to 12.3 to 29.8 bp over OIS, and LIBOR-OIS stayed at 65.3 to 78.2
bp: a gap of 41.7 to 57.7 bp between two prices at one position that held for three months. Around the capacity
increase of 2008-05-02 the auction price moved `-61.7` bp and LIBOR-OIS `-11.8`. The terms are not matched
(28-day loans against three-month rates), so the gap is printed and not graded.

The crossing cost in the closed form. A bank that takes auction funds and lends them on at LIBOR carries the
borrower's default risk, so LIBOR-OIS can fall no lower than the auction price plus that cost, and the narrowing
the facility can buy is at most the gap left over in the previous paragraph: no more than 29.1 bp per auction
from December 2007 to April 2008 (no more than 10 bp from February to April) and 41.7 to 57.7 bp from May to July
2008. Pricing the cost with the median CDS of fifteen LIBOR banks from the replication workbook (column
`CDSMEDIAN2`; the package does not print its tenor), scaled by a tenor factor `k`, gives zero narrowing on all 19
auctions at `k = 1` (`B121-28`), and the largest `k` at which any auction allows a narrowing is 0.953. The workbook's
own regression shape (LIBOR-OIS on the lagged CDS median and a TAF dummy) gives `k` of 0.570, 0.093 and 0.044 on
three windows ending 2008-08-08, which allow a narrowing on 4, 12 and 16 of the 19 auctions. The sign of the
narrowing turns on `k`, so that part is unread; the upper bound does not depend on it.

The default part of that cost, from a published decomposition (`experiments/b121_ft_default.py`,
`results/b121_ft_default.json`). Filipovic and Trolle (Journal of Financial Economics 109(3), 2013, Figure 4
Panel A) split the three-month USD LIBOR-OIS spread into a default and a non-default component; the figure is
vector graphics and both outlines are read from the PDF's drawing paths. `B121-29` (instrument) PASS: ticks even to
within one point (about 2.6 bp); the paper's fitted spread differs from this station's LIBOR-OIS by at most
16.6 bp, which is the floor of this reading. `B121-30` (own reading) PASS. From May to July 2008 the default
component is 8.0 to 15.4 bp, which puts `k` at 0.095 to 0.185, below every auction's turning point. The room the
closed form leaves for LIBOR-OIS to narrow is then zero on every auction from late January to April 2008 and 29.0
to 49.1 bp on every auction from May to July, each above the floor. LIBOR-OIS moved `-11.8` bp around the capacity
increase of 2008-05-02 and then held at 65 to 78 bp, inside that bound. With the default component taken out,
29 to 49 bp stayed between the auction price and LIBOR for three months: two prices at one position, net of the
borrower's default risk. What fills that gap is the non-default component, which has no measurement apart from the
spread itself, so the bound is not narrowed to a point.

The rate-dose rows (`B121-3`, `B121-8`) test a zero that holds on edges whose wedge does not scale with the rate
level; on an edge whose wedge does, a cut moves the loop. Read from its rules, the unsecured term edge does not scale
within the main window: the reserve ratio on Eurocurrency liabilities has been zero since 1990-12-27, the primary
credit rate sat a fixed number of basis points over the target (100, then 50 from 2007-08-17, then 25 from
2008-03-17) while the target fell from 5.25 to 2.00, and the zero bound was not reached until 2008-12-16. The zero
therefore applies on this edge; `B121-3` records that the cuts moved the wedge while the cuts themselves followed the
wedge's spikes, so the instrument does not separate the two. The readings stand as recorded.

## B128: euro area bank rates, a square of two countries by two products against ECB rate changes

Design and results are kept with the station; scripts `scripts/fetch_b128.py`, `experiments/b128_a_rate_dose.py`,
`experiments/b128_a_long_difference.py`; records `results/b128_a_rate_dose.json`, `results/b128_a_long_difference.json`.
The object is the country-by-product interaction of new-business rates (row and column means removed each month),
which is zero exactly when every square is. Rates are published on a 0.01 grid (53,407 values, no exception).

First instrument (monthly dose regression, floor from shifting the dose round the window): `B128-1` (instrument)
PASS; `B128-2` (known answer) FAIL, it sees the level pass-through of loan rates in 6 of 16 settings, so its
interaction readings are not used. Second instrument (long differences against every window of the same length
with no rate change): `B128-4` (known answer) PASS, loan rate levels move 2.4 to 3.8 points across the hikes of
2022-07 to 2023-09 against at most 0.85 in dose-free windows. `B128-5` (own reading) PASS. The rival's linear
pass-through predicts that each cell's change across the cuts of 2024-06 to 2025-06 is -0.44 times its change
across the hikes.

| products | countries | cells | interaction change, hikes | dose-free max | cut on hike: correlation | slope |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| loans | 13 | 78 | 1.039 | 0.902 | +0.503 | +0.397 |
| deposits | 16 | 64 | 0.424 | 0.204 | -0.796 | -0.393 |
| all ten | 11 | 110 | 0.604 | 0.798 | -0.439 | -0.297 |

On loans the cuts moved the interaction the same way as the hikes, the opposite sign to the rival's prediction and
above 98% of 822 dose-free pairs. On deposits the cuts undid the hikes in proportion, slope -0.39 against -0.44,
more negative than every dose-free pair, in every leave-one-country-out run and in term and overnight deposits
taken alone. The framework says a square does not move with the rate on an edge whose wedge does not scale with the
rate level and moves with it on an edge whose wedge does; which of the two each edge is gets read from rules and
contracts, not from these rows, and is pending.

Split at the zero floor (`experiments/b128_a_split.py`, `results/b128_a_split.json`). An ECB speech of
2016-07-28 says retail deposit rates have a zero lower bound and that cuts pass more strongly to loan rates; on that
ruling the deposit edge breathes and the loan edge does not. The hike window is cut where the floor lets go: part
one to the boundary (-0.50 to 2.00), part two to 2023-12 (2.00 to 4.00); the boundary month is a knob. The rival's
linear pass-through gives part two about +0.80 times part one in every group. Registered before these halves were
read, the framework's shape was: deposits above the dose-free floor in part one and inside it in part two, loans
inside it in both. Across loans, deposits, household deposits and corporate deposits and all three boundaries, the
correlation of part two on part one runs from -0.32 to +0.01, inside the dose-free range every time, so the +0.80
is absent; and deposits move above the floor in both parts (part two 0.29 to 0.34 against about 0.20), loans in
part two (0.82 to 0.95 against about 0.79), so the registered shape does not hold either. `B128-6` to `B128-9`
(rival) are recorded as both sides read and neither held. What was read, both parts moving and in unrelated
directions, is what a floor that lets go at a different rate level in each country gives; that is a lead, to be
tested on data not yet read once the level at which each country's deposit rates left zero is taken from its
own statistics.

Return to the floor (`experiments/b128_floor_return.py`, `results/b128_floor_return.json`). Household
overnight deposit rates mostly reached zero near a deposit facility rate of -0.40 on the way down and left it at +2
to +4 on the way up. Compared within each country from 2022 to 2026, when no country entered or left an assistance
programme or capital controls: of the countries that left zero at a policy rate of 2.50 or more, 2 of 7 returned
below 0.05 while the rate sat at 2.00 (BE, FR) and the rest came down to 0.06 to 0.31; of those that left earlier,
none returned. `B128-10` (own reading) gives no verdict, since neither registered reading (all late leavers return;
none returns) holds at either zero line. Late leavers fell lower than early ones, which is the direction of a lag
with a floor.

Arm B, TLTRO (`experiments/b128_b_tltro.py`, `results/b128_b_tltro.json`). The eligible-loan definition in ECB
Decision 2014/34 leaves out loans for house purchase, so the tool splits by product as well as by country take-up.
Registered before the 2020-21 data were read: where more TLTRO III was taken (the increase in longer-term
refinancing from 2020-02 over the 2019-02 eligible loan stock), the eligible-minus-house-purchase rate gap falls more.
Across 15 to 16 countries the correlation is positive in all 12 settings (+0.16 to +0.51), above the dose-free
floor in 8; `B128-11` (own reading) gives no verdict because the window's end moves it across the floor. The rule's
boundary sets which lending counts toward the allowance and the rate discount, while the funds themselves can
finance any loan, and the national state-guaranteed loan schemes of 2020 fell on corporate loans in amounts that
differ by country and move with take-up; this arm does not separate them.

Second dose, the national guarantee schemes (`experiments/b128_b_guarantees.py`,
`results/b128_b_guarantees.json`). Each sovereign's COVID-19 guarantee envelope (ECB Occasional Paper 257, tables
A.3 and A.4) over its 2019-12 corporate loan stock enters the same cross-country regression as TLTRO take-up; the two
doses correlate +0.14 to +0.37. On the eligible-minus-house gap the guarantee coefficient sits inside the dose-free
floor in all six settings. On the corporate-minus-house gap it sits above the floor in all six (+0.14 to +0.33),
and it falls back inside when Germany or Slovenia is left out, since Germany's own 2017-19 path sets that floor.
`B128-12` (own reading) gives no verdict; neither dose shows a reliable effect on the squares in this window, and
the TLTRO association of the previous paragraph falls inside the floor on the corporate gap once the guarantee dose
is in the regression.

With take-up in place of the envelopes (`--takeup`, `results/b128_b_takeup.json`): the EBA risk dashboard's
statistical annex reports newly originated loans under public guarantee schemes by country (2021-06: Italy 110.7,
France 118.9, Spain 106.8, Germany 12.7 billion euros), parsed from its text tables with the page of every figure
kept. On the eligible-minus-house gap the guarantee coefficient sits above the floor in all six settings and in
every leave-one-country-out run; on the corporate-minus-house gap, the product the guarantees touch, it does not
hold up when single countries are left out. The consumer-minus-house gap carries the pattern (+0.56 to +4.22, above
the floor in every window): consumer credit rates fell by one point or more where take-up was small and stayed flat
where it was large, and consumer credit is outside the schemes. `B128-13` (own reading) gives no verdict. Across the
three readings of arm B, none lands on the product boundary the tools' rules draw; in this window the instrument
does not separate the tools from what each country did at the same time.

The deposit backstop as a feature (`experiments/b128_backstop.py`, `results/b128_backstop.json`). Deposits are
backed by each country's deposit guarantee scheme, paid from that sovereign's means; loans are not. A square pairing
two products with the same cover cancels the backstop between two countries. Arm A's loan group and household-deposit
group are such squares; the mixed deposit group is not. Of the fifteen squares per carrier read in B97 (Cyprus and
Greece against the euro area), three pair products with the same cover (household overnight and term deposits,
corporate overnight and term deposits, house-purchase and corporate loans). `B128-14` (known answer) reproduces B97's
counts digit for digit with B97's comparison as coded; under B97's stated rule, which counts a square of exactly 0.02
as rounding, they are 2,343 of 2,395 and 3,173 of 3,240. `B128-15`: the three same-cover pairs stand above the floor
in 461 of 467 months for Cyprus and 625 of 648 for Greece, up to 114 to 186 times the floor, so a country premium plus
a separate deposit backstop premium, which would make these three zero, does not hold.

## B122: one input, two deduction ratios, and the square the statute writes

`experiments/b122_vat_input_square.py` · `results/b122_vat_input_square.json` · 2026-09-22

A value added tax writes two numbers into every purchase between businesses, and a statute
prints both. The rate is written per input: what is sold decides it. The share of that tax the
buyer may take back is written per class: who buys decides it, or, in the Japanese arm, which
class the seller belongs to. A buyer of class `a` who pays `p` for input `j` carries
`p (1 + v_j (1 - r_a))` after the deduction, and the logarithm of the second factor does not
split into a part in `j` plus a part in `a`. Two inputs and two classes make a square whose sum
is fixed by four printed numbers. The price `p` cancels from it, and so does any discount a
seller gives that depends on the class alone. Cross-multiplied, the two products differ by exactly
`(v_1 - v_2)(r_b - r_a)`, so where the cost factors are positive a square vanishes if and only if
the two rates are equal or the two deduction ratios are equal, and its sign is the sign of that
product; the identity is checked on every square read here.

**The square is a loop.** Both statutes let a buyer cross between classes, and the crossing
applies to every input at once: a small-scale taxpayer may register for the general method
(China's VAT Law, article 9, second paragraph), and a Japanese exempt business may register as
an invoice issuer. The cost of the crossing is the same at both positions of a square, so it
cancels, and what is left is the difference of the statutory terms.

**Everything is rational and the test is exact.** Rates and ratios are printed as
percentages, so a square vanishes if and only if a product of four rationals equals one, which
the script decides in `fractions.Fraction` with no tolerance. The printed values are the legal
values themselves, so there is no rounding behind them and no floor to measure. Logarithms are
printed beside the ratios for reading and decide nothing.

Two rivals are scored separately. The bare rival puts one cost on one input whoever buys it.
The separable rival lets the class enter the cost as a factor provided it is the same factor on
every input; every symmetric class-level friction, every class markup and every published
class-only conversion constant has that form, and it closes every square. A criterion of this
kind passes when the rival is wrong.

**China, VAT Law in force from 2026-01-01.** Inputs at `13%`, `9%` and `6%` (article 10);
buyers who deduct in full (article 14), buyers on the simplified method who deduct nothing
(article 8, second paragraph, and article 22, first item), and advanced manufacturers who add
`5%` to their deductible input tax through 2027 (Announcement No. 43 of 2023). Nine squares,
four independent, all non-zero. Goods against services, full deduction against simplified,
is `106/113`, `-0.0639` in log; simplified against advanced manufacturing on the same pair of
inputs is `+0.0675`. The advanced-manufacturing row holds where the firm's tax payable absorbs
the additional deduction.

**Japan, the invoice system's transitional measure, read as a dose.** Inputs at `10%` and
`8%`; purchases from invoice issuers deduct in full, purchases from other sellers deduct a
share that the tax agency's Q&A (question 130, revised April 2026) prints period by period.
The one square moves with that share:

| period | share deductible from a non-issuer | square, log |
|---|---|---|
| 2023-10-01 to 2026-09-30 | 80% | `-0.003929` |
| 2026-10-01 to 2028-09-30 | 70% | `-0.005842` |
| 2028-10-01 to 2030-09-30 | 50% | `-0.009569` |
| 2030-10-01 to 2031-09-30 | 30% | `-0.013170` |
| from 2031-10-01 | 0% | `-0.018349` |

The schedule has four steps, so it is reported as a dose on one loop and not as five loops or
as a single step. The first step falls on 2026-10-01.

The known-answer check reads the agency's own printed coefficients back from this table:
`7.8/110` for the standard rate and `6.24/108` for the reduced rate must equal `v/(1+v)` times
the national share `78/100`, and they do on all ten Japanese rows.

The self-test seeds the shape the separable rival describes, a class-only factor on every
input, and the separable criterion flips as it should; it seeds equal rates, and the bare rival
stays refuted while the separable one is right; it seeds equal ratios, and both rivals are
right. Seven deliberate faults in the implementation were each caught by the self-test.

The edge between buyer and seller runs one way, so the two-orientation decomposition is not
reported here.

| | criterion | detail |
|---|---|---|
| PASS | B122-1 `instrument` every statutory value sourced, every square on two paths | no unsourced value; 14 of 14 squares agree between the four-cell ratio and the written-out closed form, which share no helper |
| PASS | B122-2 `premise` rates per input, ratios per class, class edge present and position-free | no provision names the other's index; both carriers record a class crossing that applies to every input |
| PASS | B122-3 `known_answer` the agency's printed coefficients read back | `7.8/110` and `6.24/108` equal `v/(1+v) x 78/100` on 10 of 10 rows |
| PASS | B122-4 `own_reading` the statutory term does not separate | China 9 of 9 squares non-zero, 4 independent; Japan one loop, non-zero at every dose |
| PASS | B122-5 `rival` bare: one cost per input | 16 of 16 class gaps non-zero; largest `0.122218` in log, simplified against full deduction on goods |
| PASS | B122-6 `rival` separable: one class factor on every input | 14 of 14 squares differ from one, in exact rational arithmetic |
| PASS | B122-7 `bookkeeping` law, rates, ratios and class edge printed with their provisions | six carriers, none missing a field |

## B123: two networks' interchange schedules, and whether the card's class factors out

`experiments/b123_interchange_square.py` · `experiments/b123_fetch.py` · `results/b123_interchange_square.json` · 2026-09-22

A card network prints, for every fee program (a merchant category, a way of taking the card)
and every class of card, the share of a sale that the merchant's bank pays the cardholder's
bank. The schedule has two indices. If the logarithm of `1 + rate` split into a program term
plus a class term, one scalar on programs and one factor per class would reproduce the whole
schedule. That is the separable rival: it covers any class markup or symmetric friction that is
the same on every program, and under it every square of two programs and two classes sums to
zero.

Two class lines are read apart. **The statutory line:** an issuer with ten billion dollars of
assets or more is regulated (12 CFR 235.5), and its fee is capped at 0.05 per cent of the sale
plus 21 cents (12 CFR 235.3), one cent more for an issuer that meets the fraud-prevention
standards (12 CFR 235.4). The merchant can neither see nor choose which side of the line a
card's issuer is on. **The product line:** the networks' own card products, drawn by the
networks.

**Sources.** Visa USA Interchange Reimbursement Fees, effective 18 April 2026; Mastercard
2026-2027 U.S. Region Interchange Programs and Rates, effective 17 April 2026, and the
2025-2026 edition, effective 11 April 2025; and the Board's table of average interchange fee by
payment card network under Regulation II. Every file is in the fetch manifest with its SHA-256,
and the record checks the bytes on disk against it. Mastercard's server refuses a scripted
request, so its two files were saved from a browser and imported through the same integrity
check as a fetch. Visa prints ruled tables. Mastercard prints positioned text, and its rows are
rebuilt from word positions.

**The test is exact.** At a fixed ticket every cell's fee is rational, so a square vanishes if
and only if a product of four rationals equals one, which `fractions.Fraction` decides with no
tolerance. Printed caps and minimums apply at each ticket. Each square is read across six
tickets from $10 to $1,000, two transforms (`log(1 + r)` and `-log(1 - r)`, the merchant's
gross-up, defined only where every cell's fee is below the ticket, so a setting where one is not
is not counted for it) and the fraud cent. A square non-zero on every setting its cells apply to is read; one
zero on every setting is zero; one zero on some settings and not on others is left unread.
Whether a read square also holds one sign is printed beside it. On the statutory tables two
exempt programs, one flat and one ad valorem, change places as the ticket grows, so their square
changes sign without ever being zero.

| | squares read | of them one sign throughout | zero | unread |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Visa, statutory line, 7 tables | 237 | 152 | 69 | 21 |
| Mastercard, statutory line, 2 tables | 431 | 281 | 15 | 16 |
| Visa, card products, 5 tables | 4,209 | 4,041 | 1,385 | 16 |
| Mastercard, card products, 4 tables | 2,156 | 1,827 | 818 | 40 |

Two networks drew these schedules separately, and neither factors on either line.

**Where a square is zero, two printed prices coincide.** On the statutory line every zero square
pairs two programs whose exempt rate is printed the same (on Mastercard's debit table, Full
UCAF, Key-Entered, Merchant UCAF and Merit I all at `1.65% + 0.15`). Among products, Mastercard
prints World High Value and World Elite at the same rate on every consumer credit program, so
all 325 squares between those two are zero: two product names, one price. Visa's small merchant
table does the same with two pairs of its products.

Mastercard prints the regulated purchase rate once, for every program, under "Purchases,
Purchases with Cash-back and Unique", and calls exempt issuers "Unregulated". Its statutory
tables pair each unregulated program with that one printed rate.

**Known answers.** Every regulated cell must be the statutory cap: 83 of 83 are, 63 on Visa's
schedule (starred for the fraud cent) and 20 on Mastercard's two editions (the fraud cent as a
row of its own, one cent above the base row). The Board's covered average fee must not exceed
the cap at the covered average ticket, plus half a cent for the printed rounding: 220 of 220
network-years hold.

**Mastercard's two editions.** Every table read here is printed the same in 2025-2026 and
2026-2027, row for row and cell for cell, so the squares are the same in both years.

The CPD fit on `log(1 + r)` at a $100 ticket is printed per table (largest absolute residual
`0.0006` to `0.0063`, and `0.1166` on Visa's business and purchasing prepaid table). It decides
nothing.

**Scope.** 46 rows are set aside, each with its reason in the record: Small Ticket and Large
Ticket rows, whose ticket threshold is not printed for the row or is printed as $5 and below,
under the grid;
merged cells holding two rates; incentive adjustments; and, on Mastercard's schedule, refunds,
payment transactions and rebates, which are not fees on a sale.

The self-test plants a fault for every criterion and for the Mastercard reader (no room for a
continued line, class columns started too far left, a misplaced word, a regulated row off the
cap, a fraud row a cent off, file bytes that do not match the manifest, every table factoring at once,
a fixed fee at or above the ticket, a Large Ticket row read): 27 checks. Twenty deliberate faults in
the implementation were each caught, and the unchanged script passes.

| | criterion | detail |
|---|---|---|
| PASS | B123-1 `instrument` class names found in each table's own header; hand-checked cells; Mastercard rows rebuilt whole | no header word missing; 11 of 11 hand-checked cells match (4 Visa, 7 Mastercard, one of them a printed N/A read as absent); 119 Mastercard rows rebuilt, 0 cells that are neither one rate nor N/A |
| PASS | B123-2 `premise` the class index is the card's or its issuer's | every statutory table has exactly one regulated column; product columns are card products |
| PASS | B123-3 `known_answer` regulated cells are the cap; the Board's covered averages sit under it | 83 of 83 cells; 220 of 220 network-years |
| PASS | B123-4 `own_reading` the printed schedules do not factor | statutory line 668 squares read, product line 6,365 read |
| PASS | B123-5 `rival` separable, on the networks' card products | 6,365 of 8,624 squares with four present cells read non-zero on every setting (Visa 4,209, Mastercard 2,156); 2,203 exactly zero; 56 unread |
| PASS | B123-6 `rival` separable, on the statutory line | 668 of 789 read (Visa 237, Mastercard 431); 84 zero; 37 unread |

## B124: Kleinrock's conservation law on the directed square

`experiments/b124_kleinrock_square.py` · `results/b124_kleinrock_square.json` · 2026-09-23

A paper station, no measurement. The directed square of `b4` section 5.1 takes a position edge
`(i, j)`, two classes `a` and `b`, and the two orientations `S = w_a(i,j) + w_b(j,i)` and
`S' = w_b(i,j) + w_a(j,i)`; `S + S'` is the two classes' round-trip friction and `S - S'` the
index part. Put a queue on it: the positions are two service places, an early one with wait `T_e`
and a late one with wait `T_l`, and a member of class `p` who moves from place `u` to place `v`
has edge weight `-w_p (T_v - T_u)` in money, where `w_p` is the money value of the class's time.
The square is the two classes exchanging places.

In time units every such square is zero: waiting is the difference of one scalar on places.
That is the content of Kleinrock's conservation law, which the script reads back from Cobham's
non-preemptive priority formulas against first come first served on five parameter sets, exactly:
the work-weighted wait `sum_p rho_p W_p` does not move. In money units the index part is
`S - S' = 2 (w_b - w_a)(T_l - T_e)`, a holder attribute times a place attribute, and on the queue
the money dissipation rate moves between the two rules by
`dC = rho_a dW_a (w_a/x_a - w_b/x_b)`, zero exactly where the two classes' value per unit of
service is equal (one of the five sets is built that way, and its `dC` is zero). A pure
reallocation has no symmetric part, so the ratio `rho` is `0/0` there: its denominator is a
friction on trading places. With no such friction one orientation of the square is a positive
directed cycle, a gain from exchanging places; an allocation that stands needs
`-(S + S') >= |S - S'|`.

The self-test seeds a priority formula that breaks conservation, a square that drops one class's
time value, a symmetric part on a pure swap, the two classes costed at each other's values, and a
rule that moves no waiting; each flips the criterion it should. Seven deliberate faults in the
implementation each made the self-test fail.

| | criterion | detail |
|---|---|---|
| PASS | B124-K1 `known_answer` Kleinrock's law read back from Cobham's formulas | work-weighted wait equal under both rules on 5 of 5 parameter sets, exactly |
| PASS | B124-K2 `own_reading` the two-place square | index part `2 (w_b - w_a)(T_l - T_e)` on 4 of 4 swaps; symmetric part zero on every pure swap; time-unit square zero; 2 of 4 swaps carry a positive directed cycle |
| PASS | B124-K3 `own_reading` the money dissipation moves with the rule | `dC` matches the formula on 5 of 5; the rule moves waiting in every case; the one zero `dC` has equal value per unit of service |

## B125: the island resident air fare discount, and the square its base rule writes

`experiments/b125_resident_square.py` · `experiments/b125_fetch.py` · `results/b125_resident_square.json` · 2026-09-23

Residents of the Canary and Balearic Islands, Ceuta and Melilla pay a discounted fare on
domestic scheduled flights. Ley 17/2012, additional provision 13, section Three, sets the
discount at 75% of the fare and deducts from that fare the three public charges of letters d),
e) and f) of article 68.2 of Ley 21/2003, whether or not they were passed on to the passenger:
the security charge, the passenger charge and the charge for passengers with reduced mobility.
The airport operator sets all three per departure airport. A one-way ticket from airport `r` at
airline fare `f` then costs a non-resident `f + U_r` and a resident `f + U_r - alpha f`, and the
resident's factor on the price, `1 - alpha f/(f + U_r)`, depends on the airport. Real Decreto
1316/2001, article 2.4, names only the first two charges; the law names three and governs.

Two departure airports and two classes make a square, `log k_R(r1) - log k_R(r2)`. It is zero
exactly when `U_r1/f1 = U_r2/f2`. The charges are read from Aena's tariff guide, August 2026
edition, section 2.2, for 22 departure cells: six Peninsula airports under the EEE column, six
island, Ceuta or Melilla airports on flights to the Peninsula, six on inter-island flights, and a
November-to-March cell for Palma and Ibiza on each of the last two tables, where the guide prints
a 20% reduction of the passenger and security charges. The guide prints charges to the cent, and
the arithmetic is exact rational arithmetic.

At `alpha = 3/4` and one fare on both segments, on a grid of 40, 80, 150 and 300 euro, 908 of 924
(square, fare) cells are non-zero. The 16 zeros all fall where two cells carry the same charges
in the same table, which is where the base rule says they should. Against a Madrid departure at
80 euro the square is `0.015` for Barcelona, `0.150` to `0.232` for the other Peninsula airports,
`0.186` to `0.261` for island departures to the Peninsula and `0.363` to `0.398` for inter-island
departures. At `alpha = 1/2`, the share in force before July 2018, the same squares are about 60%
smaller. With two different fares a square closes on one fare ratio only, and that ratio is
printed per square.

The smallest non-zero square, `0.000019`, is La Palma inter-island (`U = 1.930`) against Ibiza
inter-island in winter (`U = 1.932` after the 20% reduction). It rests on a fifth of a cent that
the reduction produces below the guide's printed precision, and it would close if the operator
rounds to the cent. Only pairs with nearly equal charges are affected.

The discount's history is on record in the Official State Gazette: 33% in Real Decreto
1316/2001, 38% in Real Decreto 207/2005, 50% in Ley 17/2012, and 75% from July 2018 under Ley
6/2018 and Real Decreto 949/2018. Before the 2007 amendment the regulation defined the fare as
the fare the airline registered, without taxes or airport charges, so the base then left out
every charge; the amendment widened it to leave out only the named ones. The square is non-zero
on both sides of that date.

The rise to 75% came in two steps, and between them the share itself differed by route. Ley
17/2012 as enacted set 50% for journeys to the rest of the national territory and for
inter-island journeys alike. Ley 3/2017, in force from 2017-06-29, raised inter-island journeys
to 75% and left the others at 50%; the Council of Ministers agreement of 2018-07-13 raised the
others to 75% from Monday 2018-07-16. (For Canary residents the Constitutional Court annulled
the 2013 provision in October 2014 for want of the Canary Parliament's prior report, deferring
the nullity a year; Ley 40/2015 re-enacted it from 2015-10-03 with effect back to 2013-01-01, so
the share runs unbroken. The re-enacted text dropped a ministerial power to cap the subsidised
fare per route, a power the Official State Gazette shows was never used.) In the year between, an
inter-island segment against a
segment to the Peninsula carries a square that alpha writes alone, with the airport charges set
aside: `log(0.25/0.5) = -0.693`. It is zero before and after. The script prints the three
periods; the 2026 tariff guide is not paired with the earlier shares.

**Where the fare is published.** On the Canary Islands inter-island routes under public service
obligations the state sets a reference fare per route, and the declaration defines it as the
lowest fare without conditions, which is how the regulation words the basic fare. Thirteen
routes, both directions, 26 positions, each at its reference fare (84 to 136 euro, from
2026-08-01) with the departure airport's inter-island charges: 320 of 325 squares are non-zero,
and the five zeros fall where fare and charges coincide. A flexible fare may be priced up to 130%
of the reference fare. The regulation's annex on the airlines' monthly filings says what the
cap on higher fares is in practice: the basic-fares file is there to check the maximum subsidy on
each coupon, and an airline with no basic fares files its highest fares instead. So the subsidy on
any coupon stops at `alpha` times the registered basic fare, whatever the product is called. With
the basic fare read as the reference fare on these routes, the square of reference fare against
flexible fare, resident against non-resident, is `0.474` to `0.504` in log, non-zero on all 26
route-directions and different from the uncapped figure on every one; with no airport charges it
is `(1 + m - alpha)/((1 + m)(1 - alpha))`, written by the cap alone. The uncapped figure, `-0.018`
to `-0.008`, is printed beside it and decides nothing. The airlines' filed basic fares are not
public, so reading them as the reference fares rests on the two definitions' wording.

**A second class axis, age.** Both declarations oblige the airlines to offer social fares at a
minimum discount off the reference fare: in the Balearic Islands 20% for residents under 24 or
over 65, and residents only; in the Canary Islands 10% for passengers under 22 or over 65, with no
residence condition. The resident subsidy is taken on the fare charged, the social fare. At one
route-direction the four classes, age by residence, close a loop of their own, and the separable
rival (a route term plus an age term plus a residence term in logs) makes it zero. It is non-zero
on all 32 route-directions at the published reference fares and the statutory minimum discounts,
and the two archipelagos write it differently. With the airport charges set to zero the Balearic
square is still `log 0.8 = -0.223`, because the age discount is written for residents only; the
Canary square is exactly zero, two class-only discounts that multiply, and it opens only through
the airport charges, which neither discount touches (`+0.004` to `+0.008` with them; the Balearic
figure with them is `-0.209` to `-0.202`). The statutes fix a floor on the discount, and the
airlines may go further; the floor is what is read here.

The ministry's own answer to residents says the same thing as the main reading in plain words:
the discount is 75% of the fare and does not cover airport charges, so on a low fare it can look
small and still be right.

Two rivals are scored separately, as in B122. The bare rival puts one price on one seat whoever
buys it. The separable rival lets the class enter as one proportion on every segment, which is
what a discount on the whole ticket would be, and it closes every square. A criterion of this
kind passes when the rival is wrong.

The self-test seeds equal charges everywhere, a discount on the whole ticket, a zero discount,
and a factor that puts the reduced-mobility charge back into the base on a pair of cells built so
that its zeros are ones the statute does not explain, and reference fares drawn in proportion to
the charges, a flexible fare equal to the reference fare, a Balearic social fare opened to
non-residents, and no social discount; each flips the criterion it should. Seventeen deliberate
faults in the implementation each made the self-test fail.

square is against the format its inputs are printed in is a separate question, and where a number
is printed in a fixed published format the printed digit is the floor. Each printed input of a

## B126: how far an auction price moves at each sale, against how often the wine sells

`experiments/b126_fetch.py` · `experiments/b126_parse.py` · `experiments/b126_readings.py` · `experiments/b126_retail.py` · `results/b126_auction_jump.json` · `results/b126_retail.json` · 2026-09-23

One unit is a wine and a vintage from Sauternes and Barsac, on the public auction-result pages of
wineauction.ai: 505 vintage pages of 32 wines from 1985 on, 29 of them read (a dry white twice and
a merchant's own label are excluded by name). A unit's density is the site's own lot count over
the years since the later of the site's first recorded sale and three years after the vintage;
the page's table shows only the most recent part of the history on 89 of 505 pages, so rows are
not counted. An event is one house on one day; its price is the median log price per 750 ml of
that house's lots of the unit that day. A jump is the absolute log change between adjacent events
of a unit, and a unit's statistic is its median jump. Units are the observations.

Each reading is taken at 36 settings: bottle size (750 ml only, or all sizes with the price per
750 ml), the lag before a vintage enters the window (2, 3, 4 years), the fewest pairs a unit needs
(3, 5), and a cleaning rule (none, 3x, 2x) that drops a lot priced more than c times, or under 1/c
times, the median of other houses' lots of the same unit and size within a year either side. The
rule exists because some lots on the pages carry a bottle count of one for a multi-bottle lot or a
currency left unconverted, and neither is visible in the row itself. A reading is read where its
sign does not move across the 36 settings.

Three kinds of pair are read apart. **Across houses**, each event price is taken net of its
house's price level, fitted as house plus unit-year effects: the density rank-correlates with the
median jump at -0.179 to -0.367 at every one of the 36 settings, over 60 to 142 units. The sign
holds in every interval bin and every age bin whose own sign is steady across the settings. The
first run read 22 wines (-0.217 to -0.469, one-sided permutation p 0.0005 to 0.036 at five
representative settings); the seven wines added afterwards, read on their own, give a negative
sign at 11 of 12 settings over 15 to 46 units. **Within one house** (its consecutive sales of a
unit): -0.142 to +0.036, the sign moving with the settings. **All adjacent pairs together**, the
registered reading: -0.169 to +0.015, the sign moving. The median jump is 2.0 to 5.8 times the
same-day spread between one house's lots of a unit, at every setting.

A sale between two houses rewrites the price further the thinner the wine trades, and a sale
within one house does not depend on how thin the wine is.

| | criterion | detail |
|---|---|---|
| PASS | B126-1 `instrument` own price per 750 ml agrees with the site's; every HTML/structured-data disagreement is a tagged size conflict | 0 gaps over $1 in 5,051 rows; 117 disagreements, all size conflicts, kept out |
| — | B126-2 `own_reading` all adjacent pairs, thinner units jump further | sign moves across the 36 settings: -0.169 to +0.015 |
| PASS | B126-3 `instrument` median jump clears the same-day same-house spread | 2.0 to 5.8 times, every setting, every pair kind |
| — | B126-4 `own_reading` B126-2 inside interval bins | no main sign to hold |
| — | B126-6 `own_reading` B126-2 inside age bins | no main sign to hold |
| PASS | B126-7 `own_reading` cross-house pairs net of house level, thinner units jump further | negative at 36 of 36 settings, -0.367 to -0.179 |
| PASS | B126-7a `own_reading` B126-7 inside interval bins | every bin with a steady sign is negative |
| PASS | B126-7b `own_reading` B126-7 inside age bins | every bin with a steady sign is negative |
| — | B126-8 `own_reading` same-house pairs, thinner units jump further | sign moves: -0.142 to +0.036 |
| PASS | B126-5 `bookkeeping` units are the observations; pairs per unit printed | default setting 145 units, median 10 pairs |

**Retail listings.** A unit that has not sold for a while still carries a retail listing. Along one
wine's chain of vintages, with the vintages sold in the last year as fixed values, the harmonic
value of an unsold vintage is the linear interpolation between the nearest sold vintage below and
above. On a unit that sold recently the harmonic value and the unit's own price coincide, so the
cells that separate "the listing holds the unit's own last price" from "the listing is set from
its neighbours" are the units whose own last sale is a year old or more. Listings priced in US
dollars only, at the site's per-750 ml figure, net of the retail markup (+0.33 to +0.41 in log).
The unit's own price is the median of its events in a window of the same length as an anchor's,
ending at its last sale. Eight settings: size (bottle or all), anchor window (one or two years),
auction-side cleaning (off, 3x).

On units that sold recently, the own price is as close to the listing as the interpolation at all
eight settings (median error 0.15 to 0.20 against 0.19 to 0.24). On units whose last sale is a year
old or more, 42 to 58 per setting, the interpolation is closer on 23 to 36, more than half at every
setting, one-sided sign p 0.043 to 0.322. That majority comes from the first 22 wines; on the stale
units of the seven wines added afterwards the interpolation is closer on 7 of 16 and 10 of 20.

| | criterion | detail |
|---|---|---|
| — | B126-9 `own_reading` stale units: the neighbours' interpolation is closer to the listing than the own price | median-error sign moves across the settings |
| PASS | B126-9k `known_answer` units that sold recently: own price at least as close as the interpolation | median error 0.15 to 0.20 against 0.19 to 0.24 |
| — | B126-10 `own_reading` stale units: listing inside the anchors' range more often than the own price | at least as often in 15 of 16 cells, strictly more in 11 |

**Squares** (`experiments/b126_squares.py` · `results/b126_squares.json`). The rival: a lot's
price is the wine's value plus one level per house, so for two vintages u, v and two houses A, B
in one quarter the square S = [p(u,A) - p(u,B)] - [p(v,A) - p(v,B)] is zero. Each cell's price is
one lot drawn at random. The floor is the same statistic on pseudo-squares whose two houses are
one house: two different lots drawn from one cell. The ratio of median |S| to the floor's gets its
own band from 500 resamples of whole quarters, and a setting reads above the floor when the band's
5th percentile clears 1. Independent loops (b1 of each quarter's unit-house graph) are counted
beside the squares: 186 to 427 loops in 18 to 23 quarters over all wines.

| two vintages of one wine | 220 to 1,008 | 1.19 to 1.30 | above 1 at three of four settings |
| two different wines | 321 to 1,197 | 1.63 to 2.46 | above 1 at all four |
| Yquem alone, 750 ml | 200 to 201 | 1.00 to 1.08 | holds 1 |

Across two wines, a unit's median |S| rank-correlates with its density at -0.165 to -0.236
(permutation p 0.031 to 0.048), while the same statistic on the pseudo-squares runs +0.11 to
+0.27. Inside one wine it moves with the settings.

**The dry white.** Y d'Yquem, excluded from the carrier as a dry white, read on its own with the

## B129: the Berlin rent cap, twelve class values on one kind of dwelling, and an index cut at 1948

`experiments/b129_fetch.py` · `experiments/b129_readings.py` · `results/b129_readings.json` · 2026-09-23

Berlin's rent cap law (MietenWoG Bln, in force 2020-02-23, rents above the cap cut from 2020-11-23, void
from the Federal Constitutional Court's ruling published 2021-04-15) writes a table of rents per square
metre by the year a dwelling was first ready and its equipment. Dwellings first ready from 2014-01-01 are
exempt. Every number below is read off the statute, the bill, the Berlin statistical office's rent index,
the 2019 Mietspiegel, or a published paper, and the files are in `data/b129/raw` with their sources in
`data/SOURCES.md`.

**The statute writes twelve values for one position.** The §6 table has twelve rows and no two share a value,
3.92 to 9.80 EUR/m2. With the two surcharges of §6 (ten percent in buildings of at most two dwellings, one
euro for modern equipment) there are 48; with the three location adjustments of §5 there are 129 distinct
values among 144 combinations, 3.64 to 12.52. The bill's reasoning (Drucksache 18/2347, p. 34) derives
every row as the row's 2013 Mietspiegel median times 1.134, the real wage index carried from 2012 to 2019;
all twelve rows match to the cent. §6(5) would have re-indexed the table to real wages every two years.

**Two statutes write a third class.** The federal rent brake exempts dwellings first used and let after
2014-10-01 (BGB §556f); the cap exempts those first ready from 2014-01-01. Dwellings first ready between
the two dates are outside the cap and inside the brake.

**The square.** Hahn, Kholodilin, Waltl and Fongoni (2023, Management Science, doi:10.1287/mnsc.2023.4775),
on 74,657 asking-rent ads with hedonic controls and exact location, report the regulated-minus-exempt gap
before and after enactment: Treatment x Post-E `-0.113` (s.e. 0.019), and `-0.170` in March 2020. A scalar
potential on positions fixes the gap between two classes by their quality, so between two dates at which no
dwelling changed the square sums to zero. The floor is the largest absolute monthly coefficient the same
regression printed before the announcement, `0.040` over sixteen months; the reading is 2.83 times it.

**The index sees the reduction only because it happens to fall on its own older class.** The statistical
office's Nettokaltmieten index splits Berlin's rents at 1948, not at 2014, so the exempt class sits inside
"built from 1949" and cannot be read. The freeze shows as a slope: mean monthly change +0.204 (pre-1948)
and +0.154 (from 1949) before the announcement, +0.000 in both while the freeze was in force. The cut of
2020-11-23 appears in February 2021 in the pre-1948 class, -1.9 points against a pre-announcement monthly
maximum of 0.7, with no step in the later class; after the ruling the pre-1948 class climbs back, +0.9 in
May and +1.0 in June 2021.

**Which class falls more was predicted from the statute and the 2019 Mietspiegel before the index was read.**
The cut acts only on rents above 120 % of the cap, so the statistic is the upper end of each Mietspiegel
cell's 3/4 range. In all four declared readings (mean ratio or share above the line, the 2003-2017 column
with or without) the pre-1948 cells sit further above the line: mean ratio 1.236 against 1.070 to 1.077,
share above 0.917 against 0.607 to 0.646. From January to March 2021 the pre-1948 class fell 1.84 % and
the later class 0.37 %. The cell median, which the cut does not act on, reads 0.921 against 0.903 to 0.906
as a mean ratio and 0.208 against 0.286 to 0.292 as a share above the line.

| | criterion | reading |
|---|---|---|
| PASS | B129-1 `instrument` the §6 table as transcribed is the enacted text | 12/12 rows, in order; the bill and the paper's Table 1 agree |
| PASS | B129-1b `instrument` every cap is its 2013 median times 1.134 | 12/12, to the cent |
| PASS | B129-2 `own_reading` class values the statute writes | 12, 48, 129 |
| PASS | B129-3 `rival` the regulated/exempt square is zero (pass: it is not) | -0.113, 2.83 x floor; grid B |
| PASS | B129-4 `own_reading` when the index moves | freeze: slope to 0.000; cut: 2021-02, -1.9; ruling: 2021-05, +0.9 |
| PASS | B129-5 `own_reading` the older class falls more, as the statute predicts | -1.84 % against -0.37 % |
| PASS | B129-6 `own_reading` a third class between the two exemption dates | present in both texts |

## A47: ownership tied to residence, public rental housing, and rent caps on the asset carrier

**RUN: 2026-09-23. Model `src/monetary_topology/housing_rules.py` (a subclass of A3's model; `asset.py`
unchanged), scripts `experiments/a47_block1.py` to `a47_block5.py`, records `results/a47_block1.json` to
`results/a47_block5.json`. Nothing fetched.**

**What is built.** Rules for the housing market A3 already runs, each a switch that defaults off.
*Residence binding*: a node holds at most one unit and lives in it, so no node collects rent; a resident
who moves must sell, at the market price or at cost (opening price times the wage index), and the
landlord buys what no household does. *Who holds the rental stock*, by behaviour and by where the money
goes: a public pool outside the graph, or a listed company owned by the financial layer that pays part of
its rent out as cash dividends to owners outside the graph (0.271 and 0.421 of rental earnings, the cash
and total dividend over rental Adjusted EBITDA in Vonovia's fiscal 2024 accounts). *Tenancy by unit*:
a renter occupies a rental unit and pays rent on that unit's tier price to its owner. *New building*,
flagged new. *Rent caps* from a set round: 30 % of the median wage plus maintenance at cost (0.30 is
HUD's rent-burden line; maintenance 0.0093 of value, Vonovia 2024), or the rent at the start carried
forward by the wage index, the form of Berlin's 2020 law (B129). *Public housing that keeps itself*:
rent pays upkeep, a surplus stays with the project and pays for building, and a gap is met out of the
levy. *A price floor* at cost.

**The carrier.** On A3's registered network the production layer's share of net worth falls to zero in
every arm, so no housing rule can move the distribution there. The runs use A9's transfer levy at 0.20,
the one configuration on record that keeps a share in the households (31 % to 33 % of claims at round
299 with A3's asset layer on top), with 1.1 dwellings per node and unsold opening stock kept by its prior
owner (A3b's registered values).

| | criterion | reading |
|---|---|---|
| PASS | A47-1 `instrument` **every rule off is A3** | 5 seeds x 300 rounds, 11 fields each, bit for bit; rerun after every block |
| PASS | A47-1b `instrument` **each block leaves the earlier blocks' readings where they were** | every stored preview of blocks 1 to 3 reproduces field for field on the final model |
| PASS | A47-2 `instrument` **claims are conserved** | holdings plus the public pool plus what has left the graph, asserted every round in every arm; under residence binding nobody holds two units and units close |
| PASS | A47-3 `instrument` **tenancy** | no housed renter owns a unit, tenants never exceed rental units in a tier, housed plus unhoused equals renters, read at the moment of matching |
| PASS | A47-4 `instrument` **building** | units in nodes plus the landlord plus unowned stock equal the opening supply plus what was built; new flags never exceed units and sum to what was built |
| PASS | A47-5 `instrument` **the carrier is A9's** | the levy with the housing market closed is A6's model bit for bit, 5 seeds x 300 rounds |
| PASS | A47-6 `instrument` **the cap binds and nothing before it moves** | regulated rent paid never exceeds the caps or the uncapped rent; every round before the cap is the uncapped run's bit for bit |
| PASS | A47-7 `instrument` **the floor** | every tier's price is at or above its cost price every round |
| PASS | A47-8 `instrument` **public housing's books** | units close with public building counted; the pool is never negative; the state's top-up never exceeds the levy |

Each check has a planted error in its script's `--selftest`, and each planted error is reported.

**Readings.** Grid: regime x public building {0, 0.002, 0.005} x private building {0, 0.002, 0.005}
x cap {none, wage}, five seeds, 240 runs; every run is in the record. The cap wage share, the
maintenance rate and the levy were each moved to two other values (270 runs), and a comparison is read
only where its sign held at every value in every seed.

| | reading, production layer's share of net worth, five seeds | knob sweep |
|---|---|---|
| K1 `own_reading` residence binding with a public landlord, minus no binding | +0.377 to +0.390 (0.417 against 0.032, both cells with building at 0.002); top decile 0.60 against 0.97; the price stays at cost against a rise of 3.3 times | read |
| K2 `own_reading` public landlord minus listed landlord, both bound | +0.217 to +0.227 (0.417 against 0.194); a dividend exit of 0.421 in place of 0.271 gives 0.192 | read |
| K3 `own_reading` public building at 0.002 without binding, minus none | +0.008 to +0.011; the price rise falls from 3.3 to 1.9 times | read |
| K4 `own_reading` regulated rent paid under the wage cap, over uncapped | 0.360 to 0.469 | read |
| K5a `own_reading` new rent over regulated rent, after the cap less before (log) | +0.78 to +1.10 | read |
| K5b `own_reading` sale price under the cap over uncapped, round 199 | +0.11 % to +1.08 %; negative at one levy value | direction not read, size within 1.1 % |

Residence binding carries most of the effect: with it the price no longer follows the claims of
those who already own, which is where A3's rise came from. Where the rent goes carries much of the rest:
the same binding with a listed landlord keeps about two fifths of it (0.194 against 0.417, from 0.032), and whether 27 % or 42 % of that
landlord's rent leaves the graph hardly matters beside the rent reaching the financial layer at all.
Building concentrates wealth when the listed landlord builds (0.217 to 0.155) and spreads it when the
public landlord does (0.385 to 0.422). Without binding, public housing and caps move the distribution
little and in a stable direction; once public housing or new building is present the wage cap no longer
binds. Two readings line up with Berlin (B129): the cap opens the gap between new and regulated rents,
and it leaves sale prices within about one percent, as Sagner and Voigtländer (2023) found. The model has
no location, no subsistence floor on this carrier and no choice to stay, so these are the rules'
mechanism and not a city's magnitudes.

## A48: a core location under residence binding, who stays put, and who ends up with the premium

**RUN: 2026-09-23. Model `src/monetary_topology/housing_rules.py` (A47's, two switches added, both off by
default), scripts `experiments/a48_block1.py`, `experiments/a48_grid.py`, records `results/a48_block1.json`,
`results/a48_grid.json`. Nothing fetched.**

**What is built.** On A47's bound carrier (levy 0.20, 1.1 dwellings per node, tenancy by unit, cost
floor, public or listed landlord), the top tier is made a core location: after every other rule has set
its price, the price is multiplied by `R0 (1+g)^t`, and nothing new is built there. `R0 = 1.16` is the
median ratio of good-location to simple-location rents in Berlin's 2019 Mietspiegel, same age and size
band, over 29 pairs of cells (range 0.79 to 1.52); `1.45` is its upper end; `g` is a knob. A3's turnover
of 0.04 is split into moves that must happen and moves that may. A core owner drawn for a move that may
happen sells only if it could come back: the gap between buying the core again after the holding period
at the premium's path, and what selling the core and buying a low-tier unit leaves, must not exceed its
claims. A budget, not a preference. Someone who does come back later buys as anyone else does; the model
keeps no record of who lived where.

| | criterion | reading |
|---|---|---|
| PASS | A48-1 `instrument` **both switches off is A47** | A47's stored grid rows, three regimes, five seeds, reproduce field for field |
| PASS | A48-2 `instrument` **the premium is applied exactly** | the core price is the other rules' price times `R0 (1+g)^t` every round to `1e-12`; nothing is built in the core |
| PASS | A48-3 `instrument` **every optional move in the core is a move or a lock** | a lock only where the gap exceeds the owner's claims; with no optional moves nothing is optional |
| — | A48-4 `known_answer` **no premium** | lock rate 0.077 in one seed: an owner who cannot pay for a low-tier unit stays even without a premium |

Each check has a planted error in `--selftest`, and each is reported.

**Readings.** Grid: landlord {public, listed} x `R0` {1.00, 1.16, 1.45} x `g` {0, 0.005, 0.01, 0.02}
x optional moves {none, 0.01, 0.02, 0.03}, five seeds, 480 runs; levy and maintenance moved to two other
values each on one cell (80 runs). A comparison is read where its sign holds at every value in every seed.

| | reading | knob sweep |
|---|---|---|
| lock rate `own_reading`, pooled over seeds, optional moves 0.02 | public landlord, `R0 = 1.16`: 0.10, 0.24, 0.52, 0.76 at `g` = 0, 0.005, 0.01, 0.02 | printed |
| households' share of the core `own_reading` | 0.09 to 0.23 at round 50, 0 to 0.04 at round 150; at round 299 zero in 465 of 480 runs, one or two of the 22 core units in the other 15 | printed |
| L2 `own_reading` lock on minus off: production-layer share of net worth | 0 to +0.0025 | not read (sign moves) |
| L2 `own_reading` lock on minus off: round the core leaves households | mean +12 (public) and +26 (listed) rounds at `R0 = 1.16`, `g = 0.005` | not read (sign moves across seeds) |
| L3 `own_reading` public minus listed landlord: production-layer share of net worth | +0.274 to +0.285 | read |

A premium that rises makes owners who may move stay: at Berlin's median premium rising half a percent a
round, about a quarter of the moves that may happen do not. The distribution hardly notices. What the
premium does decide is who holds its rise. An owner who must move must sell, and as the premium climbs no
household can buy the core back, so under residence binding the core ends with the landlord: all 22 units in 465 of 480 runs, all
but one or two in the rest. With a public landlord the rise stays outside the graph and the production layer's share holds at
about 0.417; with a listed landlord it becomes its shareholders' net worth, and at `g = 0.02` the
production layer's share falls from 0.19 to 0.004. In this carrier renters take the cheapest units and
supply exceeds demand, so nobody pays extra to live in the core and it stands empty once households
leave; who would live there needs a carrier with demand for location.

## B127: classic handbags, and the gap between the boutique price and the resale price

`experiments/b127_fetch.py` · `experiments/b127_parse.py` · `experiments/b127_readings.py` · `results/b127_ratio.json` · 2026-09-24

A maker that rations a bag splits one position into two classes of buyer: the client who is
offered the bag pays the boutique price, everyone else pays the resale price. The rival reading is
one price per position (model, size, leather, year), paid alike by every buyer, so resale over
boutique is 1. The object is the price each class pays; who belongs to which class is decided by
the maker and not published, and is not read.

**Carrier.** Every Sotheby's handbag sale from 2021 to 2026 whose results are public: 46 sales,
every lot read from its own page (a sale page shows its first 48 lots, and each lot page lists the
whole sale). Sales whose results show only to a logged-in user (all of 2020, one in 2023) and two
sales still open on the fetch day are not read. On older sales the site removes lots that did not
sell, which leaves lot-number gaps and no unsold row; the lots left are those whose bids met the
reserve, so a ratio on such a sale sits high by an amount bounded by its gap count, printed per
sale. Boutique prices come from price trackers (two agree on every shared figure) and are complete
year by year only for Birkin 25 and 30 in Togo, US and Europe, 2019 to 2026; other currencies are
converted at the European Central Bank reference rate on the closing day.

**Birkin Togo, 395 lots** (23.8 per cent of the sold Birkins). Ratio: final price with buyer's
premium over the boutique price of the same size and leather in the same market and year. Four
settings: each sale against its own market's list or every sale in dollars against the US list;
the list of the sale's year or of the year before. Bands: 500 resamples of whole sales.

| | criterion | detail |
|---|---|---|
| PASS | B127-2 `rival` one price per position: Birkin 25 Togo resells at its boutique price | every band in every year 2021 to 2026 at every setting lies above 1: 1.41 to 3.42 |
| PASS | B127-2b `own_reading` Birkin 35 Togo, where supply is not tight, resells at or under its boutique price | bands 0.59 to 1.03 |
| — | B127-2p `bookkeeping` all three sizes pooled, and Birkin 30 | pooled moves with the settings; Birkin 30 falls from 1.2-2.9 (2021-2023) to 0.8-1.8 (2024-2026) |
| PASS | B127-5 `own_reading` the ratio narrowed from 2022 to 2025 | 2025 minus 2022 median at the four settings: -0.71 to -1.29 |
| FAIL | B127-3 `own_reading` quota bags carry a higher ratio than non-quota bags (2025, 2026) | Picotin 18, non-quota, 1.22 to 1.32; Kelly 28 0.98 to 1.14 and Birkin 35 0.80 to 0.86, both quota |
| PASS | B127-6 `own_reading` the entry tier's share of sold Hermès bags fell from 2022 to 2025 | Evelyne and Picotin: 8.5 per cent of sold Hermès bags in 2022, 2.9 per cent in 2025 |

The three Birkin sizes line up at one date: the smallest, where demand is tightest, keeps about
twice the boutique price, the largest resells at or under it, and the middle size moved from the
first to the second within three years. B127-3 reads the maker's quota list as a measure of how
tight supply is, and it is not one: the list caps how many bags one client may buy a year, while
how hard a given size and colour is to obtain varies inside and outside the list. B127-6 counts
lots at one auction house, whose sales are composed by the house and its consignors; it reads the
entry tier's share of that market, not buyers' purchases at large.

Chanel's Classic Flap, the bag repriced every year and not rationed, has 19 lots in six years at
this house and is not read.

## A49: a loan secured on a commitment to stay, three lenders, and a rental market left to short stays

**RUN: 2026-09-24. Model `src/monetary_topology/housing_rules.py` (switches added, all off by default),
scripts `experiments/a49_block1.py`, `a49_block2.py`, `a49_block3.py`, `a49_grid.py`, records
`results/a49_block1.json` to `a49_block3.json` and `results/a49_grid.json`. Nothing fetched.**

**What is built.** On A47's carrier (levy 0.20, 1.1 dwellings per node, tenancy by unit, cost floor), a
node that can commit to staying at least the holding period of 25 rounds and owns no dwelling may buy
with a down payment of 10 % or 20 %; the lender pays the rest and is repaid in 25 equal instalments plus
interest. Three rounds short and the dwelling goes to the landlord (under residence binding) or the
lender (otherwise), credited against the debt, the rest written off. A tenth of the production layer
stays briefly, must move at 0.25 a round, cannot commit and gets no loan. Three lenders, each the shape of
a lender that exists:

- *treasury*: a public lender that may run the pool below zero by up to the round's levy, the next levy
  bringing it back first; a housing board funded from the budget, as Singapore's HDB loans are (their
  concessionary rate is pegged 0.1 point above the CPF Ordinary Account rate, 2.6 % through 2025);
- *provident fund*: wage receivers pay 5 % or 12 % of their wage into their own account and their
  employers as much again, the pooled cash lends only to contributors at 0 % or 2.85 %, and members spend
  their accounts first; China's housing provident fund is this shape (a floor of 5 % a side, and a
  first-home rate over five years of 2.85 % from 2024-05-18);
- *bank*: the financial layer lends at 2 % a round and is repaid there.

| | criterion | reading |
|---|---|---|
| PASS | A49-1 `instrument` **every new switch off is A48** | A48's stored grid rows, three cells, five seeds, field for field; rerun after each block (A49-1b, A49-1c) |
| PASS | A49-2 `instrument` **the loan book closes** | lent = repaid principal + credited on foreclosure + written off + outstanding, every arm, to `1e-9`; claims conserved every round |
| PASS | A49-3 `instrument` **who borrowed** | no short-stayer ever borrowed; every borrower held the down payment |
| PASS | A49-7 `instrument` **the provident fund's books** | accounts equal contributions less member spending; the fund's cash equals contributions less spending, less what it lent, plus what came back; every provident borrower had contributed |
| PASS | A49-8 `instrument` **the treasury's overdraft** | the pool never ends a round below minus that round's levy (at most 0.82 of it); with the treasury off no pool is ever negative |

Each check has a planted error in its script's `--selftest`, and each is reported.

**Readings.** Grid: regime {unbound, bound} x lender {none, treasury, provident at two rates and two
contribution rates, bank} x down payment {0.1, 0.2} x short stays {none, 0.1}, plus contributions with
no lending, five seeds, 300 runs; the foreclosure lag (1, 6 rounds) and the levy (0.15, 0.25) moved on
eight cells (160 runs). A comparison is read where its sign holds at every value in every seed.

| | reading, bound unless stated, down payment 0.1, short stays 0.1 | knob sweep |
|---|---|---|
| renters left, of whom short-stayers `own_reading` | no loan 156, 10 % short; treasury 15, 95 to 97 % short; bank 12, 96 to 97 %; provident 86, 13 to 17 % | printed |
| renters, with no short-stayers `own_reading` | treasury 0.8, bank 0.5: renting all but disappears | printed |
| M4 `own_reading` renters, loan minus none | treasury −136 to −145, provident −64 to −74, bank −139 to −150 | read |
| M1 `own_reading` renters, unbound minus bound, same loan | treasury +104 to +114, provident +49 to +58, bank +110 to +121 | read |
| M3 `own_reading` production-layer share of net worth, treasury minus bank, provident minus bank | +0.034 to +0.059; +0.117 to +0.130 | read |
| M4 `own_reading` production-layer share, loan minus none | treasury +0.060 to +0.072, provident +0.127 to +0.158; bank +0.001 to +0.034 | treasury and provident read; bank not read |
| contributions alone `own_reading` production-layer share | 0.524 (5 %) and 0.587 (12 %) bound, against 0.413 with neither; 0.127 and 0.231 unbound, against 0.032 | printed |
| M1 `own_reading` foreclosures, unbound minus bound | treasury +1 to +2, provident +4 to +13 per seed; bank mixed; a zero appears at other levy values | direction not read |

Under residence binding, with dwellings at cost and sellable on leaving, a lender without a ceiling on
its cash leaves renting to those who stay briefly: fifteen renters out of 180, nineteen in twenty of them
short-stayers, and with no short stays almost nobody rents. The same loan without binding leaves 110 to
120 more renters, because the price follows the bidders' claims and the down payment follows the price.
The provident fund lends only what wages put in, so it clears the rental market least; it moves the
distribution most, and contributions with no lending at all move it further than any lender does, since
the employer's half is a transfer added to wages and the money waits outside circulation. Interest lent
by the financial layer takes back part of what lending gives: treasury over bank adds 0.03 to 0.06 of the
production layer's share. Foreclosures are more frequent without binding for the treasury and the fund in
every seed, but not at every levy, and the bank forecloses 1.4 to 2.4 times on average under binding too,
so the direction is not read.

## A50: the provident contribution taken apart; money parked outside circulation, and the authority that refills it

**RUN: 2026-09-24. Model `src/monetary_topology/housing_rules.py` (switches added, all at A49's values by
default), scripts `experiments/a50_block1.py`, `a50_grid.py`, `a50_block3.py` to `a50_block7.py` (shared
helpers in `a50_common.py`), records `results/a50_block1.json`, `a50_grid.json`, `a50_block3.json` to
`a50_block7.json`. Nothing fetched.**

**What is built.** A49 found that contributions with no lending moved the production layer's share of net
worth further than any lender. A contribution does two things at once: the employer's half is a transfer
added to wages, and both halves wait in accounts outside circulation. On A49's carrier with no lending
(levy 0.20, short stays 0.1, contribution rate `c` 0.05 and 0.12), switches separate them:

- which side pays (employee, employer, both);
- whether the money is parked in the member's account, or paid straight into the member's holdings the
  same round (the employer's half then is a wage rise of `c`);
- whether a parked account may be spent on a dwelling, or is locked;
- whether the authority sees the accounts: either it counts each round's contributions as arrived
  layer-2 inflow, or its target counts the account balances, converted at the carrier's own baseline
  inflow per unit of circulating claims (0.46 to 0.49 by seed);
- how long money stays parked before it goes back to its owner, `L` rounds. A round carries a trend, not
  a calendar span, so `L` reads as short against long.

The carrier's authority issues `gain` times the shortfall of layer-2 inflow against its baseline, at the
top node (`rule = "endogenous"`, `gain` 1.0).

| | criterion | reading |
|---|---|---|
| PASS | A50-1, 1b, 8, 8b `instrument` **every new switch at its default is A49** | A49's contributions-only grid rows, A48's rows and A49's block previews, field for field, rerun after each new switch |
| PASS | A50-2 `instrument` **the fund's books** | accounts and fund cash equal what was parked less what was spent from accounts and paid back; a returned arm holds nothing and returned exactly what the employer paid; a side that is off paid nothing |
| PASS | A50-4 `instrument` **a locked account** | never spent; holds what was parked less what went back |
| PASS | A50-5 `instrument` **unbound, locked equals parked** | without lending an unbound sale takes holdings only, so the two arms are the same run (an implementation check) |
| PASS | A50-6 `instrument` **the authority written out** | block 2's rows reproduce with the authority set explicitly |
| PASS | A50-9, 11 `instrument` **what the authority withheld** | positive in every run, within `gain` times what was parked; the velocity used is the first round's layer-2 inflow over the initial claims, recomputed from the history |
| PASS | A50-12 `instrument` **paying back** | never more than was parked; `L` = 300 pays nothing back in 300 rounds and equals never paying back, field for field |
| PASS | A50-15 `instrument` **every parked unit accounted for** | parked = spent on dwellings + paid back + still in accounts |

Each check has a planted error in its script's `--selftest`, and each is reported.

**Readings.** Five seeds; the levy (0.15, 0.25) moved on every comparison at `c` 0.12. A difference is read
where its sign holds at every seed and every levy value. Production-layer share of net worth at `c` 0.12,
short stays 0.1, levy 0.20, mean of five seeds, unless stated.

| | reading | sweep |
|---|---|---|
| transfer only (employer's half paid into holdings) minus none `own_reading` | +0.004 to +0.005 (`c` 0.05) and +0.010 to +0.012 (0.12) bound; +0.000 to +0.005 unbound | bound read; unbound at 0.12 not read |
| employee's own money parked minus none `own_reading` | +0.092 to +0.128 bound; +0.041 to +0.118 unbound | read |
| employer's money parked minus the same money returned `own_reading` | +0.089 to +0.122 bound; +0.042 to +0.124 unbound | read |
| locked, never spent, minus none (bound) `own_reading` | +0.210 to +0.222 (`c` 0.05); +0.334 to +0.348 (0.12) | read |
| spendable minus locked (bound) `own_reading` | −0.115 to −0.281, with 18 to 63 more owners and 17 to 65 fewer renters | read |
| refill: extra issuance over money locked `own_reading` | bound 0.99 to 1.04; unbound 0.59 to 0.84 | printed |
| `gain` 0.5 instead of 1.0 `own_reading` | every difference keeps its reading; refill still 0.98 to 1.02 bound | printed |
| no issuance `own_reading` | unbound, a locked account drains circulation from 100 to 0.05 and wages paid in the last 50 rounds fall from 400 to 1.2; bound, the public landlord's pool drains it even with no fund | bound not read |
| authority counts each round's contributions as inflow `own_reading` | withholds what was parked (287 of 288) and issues as much in later rounds (830.1 against 831.7) | printed |
| authority's target counts the balances `own_reading` | locked for good: circulation 0.0003 to 0.19, wages in the last 50 rounds 0.01 to 3.7 of 400; spendable (bound): circulation 187 → 100, wages 400, share 0.530 → 0.603 | printed |
| share over none against `L` (1, 5, 25, 100, never), bound, employee locked `own_reading` | +0.003, +0.012 to +0.014, +0.059 to +0.065, +0.182 to +0.193, +0.334 to +0.348 | every step from 5 up read |
| spendable arm, share at `L` 100 below `L` 25 `own_reading` | money spent on dwellings rises at every step of `L`; at the end, accounts hold 26 to 36 at `L` 25 and 8 to 16 above it | read |

Parking the contribution is what moves the distribution: the employer's half paid as a wage rise flows
back up and moves the share by a hundredth at most, while the employee's own money, which is no transfer
at all, moves it by a tenth once it sits in an account. It moves it because the authority steers
circulation by inflow and does not see the accounts: under binding it issues back exactly what was
locked, so the account is net new wealth for the production layer and circulation is unchanged. Halving
the authority's gain changes only how fast it refills. Without issuance a locked account takes the whole
money stock and wages stop. An authority that counts only the flow into accounts refills anyway, since the
shortfall in circulation persists; one whose target counts the balances accepts less circulation, and
then an account that never pays out stops the economy, while one that is spent on dwellings keeps wages
paid and leaves the production layer a larger share. The effect is a stock: the longer money stays
parked the higher the share, and money paid back or spent on a dwelling rejoins circulation and flows up.
Spending accounts on dwellings under binding buys ownership (more owners, fewer renters) and gives up
share for the same reason.

## B130: Singapore's public housing and A49's prediction; the bound segment owns more, every year

**RUN: 2026-09-24. Scripts `experiments/b130_fetch.py`, `experiments/b130_readings.py`, record
`results/b130_readings.json`, sources `data/b130/raw/` (see `data/SOURCES.md`, B130).**

**What is read.** A49 found that under residence binding, with dwellings at cost and a lender without a ceiling
on its cash, those who can commit to staying buy and renting shrinks to those who cannot; without binding the
same loan leaves many more renters. Singapore runs a bound segment and an unbound one side by side. HDB flats are
bought by citizen or permanent-resident households only, one per household, occupied by the owner through a
five-year minimum occupation period, and let out whole only by citizen owners after it; whole-flat tenants who
are neither citizens nor Malaysians are held to 8 % of a neighbourhood and 11 % of a block. Private
condominiums carry none of these rules. Buyers of both use the Central Provident Fund, and HDB lends on
concessionary terms. Those who cannot enter the bound segment are non-citizens, kept out by statute; they are
read here as A49's class that cannot commit, with the statute named beside every reading.

| | criterion | reading |
|---|---|---|
| PASS | B130-1 `instrument` **sources whole, numbers on their pages** | six files pass their fetch checks; five numbers read from HDB's key statistics are found on the page each is attributed to (pp. 7, 10, 15) |
| PASS | B130-2 `own_reading` **owner-occupied share of resident households, HDB minus condominiums** | positive in all 29 years printed (1980, 1990, 1995, 2000-2025), from +5.4 points (2025) to +15.8 (2005) |
| PASS | B130-3 `own_reading` **who rents HDB flats whole, 2025** | resident non-owners in 3-room and larger HDB flats: 32,406; flats rented out whole: 59,567; so at least 45.6 % of whole-flat tenancies are non-resident, if the 55,883 non-owners in 1- and 2-room flats are public-rental tenants (public rental flats are 1- and 2-room, 63,558 of them). Counting every non-owner as a market tenant gives no floor |
| PASS | B130-4 `rival` **tenure rises with income, whatever the segment's rules** | condominium residents earn 1.94 to 2.40 times as much per household member as residents of the best-paid HDB flat type, every year 2000-2023; the premise then entails a condominium owner-occupied share at least HDB's; it is lower in all 24 years, by 7.3 to 15.8 points. Grid B, 24 years |

The rival criterion records the rival's premise and the step that entails its inequality; it passes when the
inequality fails. Both accounts are read against the same table: the framework's direction (the bound segment
owns more) holds in every year, and the income premise's direction fails in every year it is defined. Landed
properties are printed beside and not scored. The gap between HDB and condominiums narrows from 2005 to 2025;
that trend was not registered and is not read.
